questions.stem: The void ratio of a soil is defined as the ratio of:
options: Volume of voids to volume of solids
Volume of voids to total volume
Volume of water to volume of voids
Volume of air to volume of voids
questions.solution:
**Volume of voids to volume of SOLIDS.**

> **e = V_v / V_s**

The distinction from **porosity** is the whole point of the question:

| Quantity | Definition | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **Void ratio e** | V_v / **V_s** — referred to the volume of **SOLIDS** | **CAN exceed 1** |
| **Porosity n** | V_v / **V** — referred to the **TOTAL** volume | **CANNOT exceed 1** |

Because the denominator of e is only the solid fraction, a very loose soil can have more void volume than solid volume, giving **e > 1** — which is common in soft organic clays. Porosity, whose denominator includes the voids themselves, is necessarily a fraction less than one.

**The conversions:**

> **e = n/(1 − n)**  and  **n = e/(1 + e)**

Option (c) is the **degree of saturation S**, and option (d) is the **air content**.

**Typical values:**

| Soil | Void ratio |
|---|---|
| Dense sand | 0.4 – 0.5 |
| Loose sand | 0.7 – 0.9 |
| Stiff clay | 0.6 – 1.0 |
| **Soft clay** | **1.0 – 2.0** |
| Organic clay, peat | up to 15 |

**Why e rather than n is used** in most soil mechanics relations: the **volume of solids does not change** as the soil compresses, so e changes only through its numerator. That makes it the natural variable for consolidation, where the whole analysis tracks the change in void ratio against effective stress — the e–log σ′ curve.

examTip.trap: **Porosity** is the near-miss and the two are constantly swapped. Porosity is voids over **TOTAL** volume; void ratio is voids over **SOLIDS**.
examTip.trick: Void ratio can exceed 1 (a soft clay may be at e = 1.5); porosity never can, since it is a fraction of the whole. If an option allows a value above 1, it is the void ratio.
examTip.mnemonic: **e = V_v/V_s, n = V_v/V.** Convert with **e = n/(1−n)** and **n = e/(1+e)**.

questions.stem: The fundamental relation connecting void ratio, degree of saturation, water content and specific gravity is:
questions.solution:
**e·S = w·G.**

This single relation, with the definitions of the phase ratios, answers virtually every phase-relation problem set in the examination — and it is worth deriving once so it can be reconstructed rather than merely recalled.

**Derivation.** Take the volume of solids as unity, so V_s = 1 and V_v = e.

> Volume of water **V_w = S · V_v = S e**
> Weight of water **W_w = S e γ_w**
> Weight of solids **W_s = G γ_w** (since V_s = 1)
> Water content **w = W_w/W_s = S e γ_w /(G γ_w) = S e / G**

Rearranging gives **e S = w G**. ∎

**The special case worth memorising:**

> For a **fully saturated** soil, **S = 1**, so **e = w G**

which is how the void ratio of a saturated clay is found from a simple water content test — no volume measurement needed.

**A worked check.** A saturated clay with w = 40% and G = 2.70: **e = 0.40 × 2.70 = 1.08**. A void ratio slightly above 1 is entirely reasonable for a soft saturated clay, which confirms the arithmetic.

**Everything else follows from it**, combined with the unit weight expressions:

> **γ = (G + Se)γ_w/(1 + e)** · **γ_d = Gγ_w/(1 + e)** · **γ_sat = (G + e)γ_w/(1 + e)** · **γ′ = (G − 1)γ_w/(1 + e)**

Each is obtained by writing the total weight over the total volume for the appropriate condition — again with V_s taken as unity.

examTip.trick: This one relation solves most phase problems. Check it at saturation: with **S = 1** it reduces to **e = wG**, which is the standard saturated-soil shortcut.
examTip.mnemonic: **"See Sw-GEE" — eS = wG.** Learn this and the whole phase diagram opens up; almost every other relation can be derived from it plus the definitions.

questions.stem: The submerged (effective) unit weight of a soil is given by:
questions.solution:
**γ′ = (G − 1)γ_w/(1 + e).**

It follows directly from **γ′ = γ_sat − γ_w**:

> γ′ = (G + e)γ_w/(1 + e) − γ_w = [(G + e) − (1 + e)]γ_w/(1 + e) = **(G − 1)γ_w/(1 + e)** ∎

**The four unit weights, and each option here is one of them:**

| Unit weight | Expression | Condition |
|---|---|---|
| **Bulk (moist)** | **(G + Se)γ_w/(1 + e)** | Any degree of saturation |
| **Dry** | **Gγ_w/(1 + e)** | S = 0 (no water weight) |
| **Saturated** | **(G + e)γ_w/(1 + e)** | S = 1 |
| **Submerged (effective)** | **(G − 1)γ_w/(1 + e)** | Below the water table |

Notice that the **bulk** expression reduces to the **dry** value at S = 0 and to the **saturated** value at S = 1 — a useful check that the right formula has been recalled.

**Why the submerged unit weight matters.** Below the water table, the soil is **buoyed up** by the water it displaces, so the **effective** weight causing stress on the soil skeleton is reduced. Computing effective stress below the water table is therefore done in either of two equivalent ways:

> **σ′ = σ − u** (total stress minus pore pressure), **or**
> **σ′ = Σ(γ′ × thickness)** directly, using the submerged unit weight below the water table

The second route is quicker, and the fact that both give the same answer is itself a check on the arithmetic.

**A useful approximation:** for G = 2.65 and a typical e, **γ′ ≈ γ_sat/2 ≈ 9–10 kN/m³**. That is why **a rising water table roughly halves the effective stress** contributed by the submerged soil — and hence roughly halves the frictional component of shear strength, which is the quantitative reason monsoon seepage triggers so many slope failures.

examTip.trap: (G + e)γ_w/(1 + e) is the deliberate distractor — that is the **saturated** unit weight. Submerged is that minus γ_w.
examTip.trick: Derive rather than memorise: **γ′ = γ_sat − γ_w = (G + e)γ_w/(1+e) − γ_w = (G − 1)γ_w/(1+e)** ✓
examTip.mnemonic: **Submerged has G − 1 on top; saturated has G + e.** γ′ is roughly **half** of γ_sat for ordinary soils, which is a useful order-of-magnitude check.

questions.stem: In the Casagrande apparatus, the liquid limit is the water content corresponding to a groove closure at:
questions.solution:
**25 blows.**

The liquid limit is the water content at which the two halves of a soil pat, separated by a standard groove, **close over a length of 12 mm** after exactly **25 blows** of the Casagrande cup falling through **10 mm**.

In practice the test is run at **four or five water contents** giving blow counts between about 15 and 35, and the results plotted as water content against **log(number of blows)** — the **flow curve**, which is a straight line. The liquid limit is then **read off at 25 blows** rather than achieved by trial, which is both quicker and more reliable.

**The slope of that flow curve is the FLOW INDEX I_f**, and it measures how rapidly the soil loses strength as its water content rises.

**The three Atterberg limits**, in **descending** order of water content:

| Limit | Water content at which | Test |
|---|---|---|
| **Liquid limit (LL)** | The soil begins to **flow as a liquid** | **Casagrande, 25 blows**; or cone penetrometer, **20 mm in 5 s** |
| **Plastic limit (PL)** | The soil **ceases to be plastic** and crumbles | Rolled into a **3 mm thread** which just crumbles |
| **Shrinkage limit (SL)** | Further drying causes **no further volume reduction** | Mercury displacement |

**The cone penetrometer method** is now often preferred to the Casagrande cup because it is **less operator-dependent** — the Casagrande result varies with the operator's rate of turning, the hardness of the base, and the exact groove shape, whereas the cone simply falls under gravity.

**Why 25 blows and 12 mm?** They are **conventions**, chosen by Casagrande to give a repeatable value near the true liquid state. Like the 5-day BOD test, the numbers have no physical significance beyond the agreement to use them — which is why the apparatus, the base hardness and the drop height are all specified precisely.

examTip.trick: The full specification matters: a **13 mm groove closure at 25 blows**, with the cup falling **10 mm** each time. Since hitting exactly 25 is luck, the test is run at several water contents and the value read off the **flow curve** at 25.
examTip.mnemonic: **25 blows, 13 mm closure.** The plastic limit is the quite different 3 mm thread test.

questions.stem: The plasticity index of a soil is:
questions.solution:
**Plasticity index PI = liquid limit − PLASTIC limit.**

> **PI = LL − PL**

Substituting the **shrinkage** limit for the plastic limit is the single most frequent error in this topic, and it is why option (a) is offered.

**The derived indices, as a set:**

| Index | Expression | Measures |
|---|---|---|
| **Plasticity index PI** | **LL − PL** | The **RANGE of water content over which the soil is PLASTIC** |
| **Shrinkage index SI** | PL − SL | The range over which it is semi-solid |
| **Liquidity index LI** | (w − PL)/PI | Where the **natural** water content lies within the plastic range |
| **Consistency index CI** | (LL − w)/PI | The complement of LI; **CI + LI = 1** |
| **Flow index I_f** | Slope of the flow curve | Rate of strength loss with water content |
| **Toughness index I_t** | PI / I_f | — |

**What PI means physically:** it is the **width of the water-content band within which the soil behaves plastically** — that is, can be remoulded without cracking and without flowing. A wide band means a highly plastic clay.

| PI | Description |
|---|---|
| **0** | **Non-plastic** (sand) |
| < 7 | Low plasticity |
| 7 – 17 | Medium plasticity |
| **> 17** | **High plasticity** |

**The liquidity index is the practically useful one**, because it relates the soil's **actual** state to its limits:

| LI | State of the soil in the ground |
|---|---|
| **LI > 1** | Water content **above the liquid limit** — the soil is effectively a **liquid** if remoulded; typical of a **sensitive** clay |
| 0 < LI < 1 | Plastic state |
| **LI < 0** | Water content **below the plastic limit** — **semi-solid, stiff** |

A natural clay with **LI close to or above 1** is a warning: it is at or beyond its liquid limit, so **disturbance will destroy its strength**. That is exactly the condition of the quick clays responsible for some of the largest recorded landslides, and it is why sensitivity is measured alongside the limits.

examTip.trick: PI measures the **range of water content over which the soil behaves plastically**. A high PI means a fat clay that stays workable over a wide moisture range; a PI near zero means a silt that goes from stiff to slurry almost at once.
examTip.mnemonic: **PI = LL − PL.** Also worth holding: **liquidity index LI = (w − PL)/PI**, which says where the *natural* water content sits in that range — above 1 and the soil is effectively a liquid.

questions.stem: For a soil to be classified as well graded, the coefficient of curvature C_c must lie between:
questions.solution:
**Between 1 and 3.**

The two grading coefficients must both be satisfied:

> **Uniformity coefficient C_u = D_60 / D_10**
> **Coefficient of curvature C_c = D_30² / (D_10 × D_60)**

| Soil | Well graded requires |
|---|---|
| **Sand** | **C_u > 6** and **C_c between 1 and 3** |
| **Gravel** | **C_u > 4** and **C_c between 1 and 3** |

**The two coefficients test different things**, which is why both are needed:

| Coefficient | Tests |
|---|---|
| **C_u** | The **RANGE of sizes** present — is the grading wide or narrow? |
| **C_c** | The **SHAPE of the curve** — is the range filled smoothly, or is a size band missing? |

A **gap-graded** soil can have a perfectly respectable C_u — the extremes are far apart — while **lacking the intermediate sizes** entirely. C_c detects that: with D_30 displaced toward one end, C_c falls outside the 1 to 3 band.

**Note the direction of C_u**, which candidates routinely invert:

> **A HIGHER C_u means a WIDER range of particle sizes**, hence **better** grading. A **uniform** (single-size) soil has C_u close to 1.

**Why well-graded soils are wanted.** The smaller particles **fill the voids between the larger ones**, so:

| Consequence | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Fewer voids** | Higher density achievable by compaction |
| **Higher shear strength** | Better particle interlock |
| **Lower permeability** | The fines block the flow paths |
| **Less binder or cement needed** | Fewer voids to fill |

That is why a well-graded gravel makes an excellent sub-base and a uniform sand a poor one — and, conversely, why a **uniformly graded** material is deliberately chosen for a **drainage layer**, where high permeability is the object.

**D_10** is the **effective size**, and it correlates with permeability through **Allen Hazen's relation k ≈ C·D_10²** — a reminder that the **finest** 10% of a soil governs its permeability, because the flow must squeeze through the smallest pores.

examTip.trick: Two criteria must be met **together**, and forgetting the second is the usual error: **C_c between 1 and 3**, AND **C_u > 4 for gravel** or **> 6 for sand**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cc between 1 and 3; Cu above 4 (gravel) or 6 (sand).** Well graded means a good spread of sizes, so the small grains fill the voids between the large — which is why it compacts densely and drains predictably.

questions.stem: On the plasticity chart used in the IS classification system, a fine-grained soil plotting ABOVE the A-line is classified as:
questions.solution:
**Clay.**

> **A-line: PI = 0.73 (LL − 20)**
> **ABOVE the A-line → CLAY (C)**
> **BELOW the A-line → SILT (M) or ORGANIC (O)**

**Why plasticity rather than particle size decides** — this is the most important idea in soil classification and is worth stating fully:

> **The engineering behaviour of a FINE-GRAINED soil is governed by its PLASTICITY, not by its particle size.**

Two soils with **identical grading curves** can behave completely differently depending on their **clay mineralogy** — a kaolinite-rich soil is stable and only mildly plastic, while a montmorillonite-rich one of the same grading swells enormously and has a very high plasticity index. A sieve or hydrometer cannot distinguish them; the Atterberg limits can. That is why the classification of fine soils rests on the plasticity chart and not on the grading curve.

**The IS (Unified) classification symbols:**

| First letter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **G** | Gravel |
| **S** | Sand |
| **M** | **Silt** (from the Swedish *mo*) |
| **C** | **Clay** |
| **O** | Organic |
| **Pt** | Peat |

| Second letter (fine soils) | Liquid limit |
|---|---|
| **L** — low compressibility | **LL < 35** |
| **I** — intermediate | **35 ≤ LL ≤ 50** |
| **H** — high | **LL > 50** |

Note that for fine soils the second letter denotes **COMPRESSIBILITY**, not plasticity — so **CH** is a clay of *high compressibility*. Reading it as "high plasticity" is a common slip, and while the two correlate, the code's definition is by liquid limit.

**The U-line, PI = 0.9(LL − 8)**, is an **upper bound above which no natural soil plots**. A result plotting above it is therefore evidence of a **testing error**, not of an unusual soil — a useful and rarely mentioned check on laboratory data.

**Organic soils** plot **below** the A-line like silts, and are distinguished from inorganic silts by the **oven-drying test**: the liquid limit is determined before and after oven drying at 105 °C, and a **reduction of more than about 25%** indicates significant organic content.

examTip.trick: The A-line is drawn as **PI = 0.73(LL − 20)**. Above it the soil is a **clay**; below it a **silt or organic soil**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Above the A-line is Clay** — and the letters help: C above, M (silt) below. The second letter then comes from the LL: **L below 35, I from 35 to 50, H above 50.**

questions.stem: Compared with the standard Proctor test, the modified Proctor test gives:
options: A higher maximum dry density at a lower optimum moisture content
A lower maximum dry density at a higher optimum moisture content
The same maximum dry density and optimum moisture content
A higher maximum dry density at a higher optimum moisture content
questions.solution:
**A HIGHER maximum dry density at a LOWER optimum moisture content.**

**The two tests:**

| | **Standard Proctor** | **Modified Proctor** |
|---|---|---|
| **Layers** | **3** | **5** |
| Blows per layer | 25 | 25 |
| **Rammer** | **2.6 kg** | **4.89 kg** |
| **Drop** | **310 mm** | **450 mm** |
| **Compactive energy** | ~600 kJ/m³ | ~2700 kJ/m³ — about **4.5 times** |

**Greater compactive effort shifts the whole compaction curve UP and to the LEFT.** Understanding why is worth more than memorising the direction:

> **Up**, because more energy packs the particles into a denser arrangement.
> **To the LEFT**, because with more energy available, **less water is needed to lubricate** the particles into that arrangement.

Water in compaction acts as a **lubricant** allowing particles to slide past one another. When the mechanical energy is large, less lubrication is needed to achieve the same rearrangement — and beyond the optimum, additional water simply **occupies volume that solids could have occupied**, which is why the curve falls on the wet side.

**The zero air voids line:**

> **γ_d(zero air voids) = G γ_w / (1 + wG)**

The compaction curve **approaches but never reaches** it, because air can never be entirely expelled. A plotted point lying **on or above** the zero air voids line therefore indicates a **test error** — most often a wrong specific gravity or a weighing mistake — and checking for that is a standard laboratory discipline.

**Which test to specify.** The **modified** test represents the energy delivered by **modern heavy compaction plant**, so it is the basis of specifications for **road and airfield** subgrades and bases (typically 97–100% of modified MDD). The **standard** test suits **earth dams and general fill**, where the higher density of the modified test is neither achievable nor desirable — an earth dam core is deliberately compacted **slightly wet of optimum** to give a **dispersed structure of lower permeability**, and over-compaction would make it brittle and prone to cracking.

**That last point is worth keeping:** the target is not always the maximum density. For a **permeable fill** compaction is done **dry of optimum** (flocculated structure, higher strength, higher permeability); for an **impervious core**, **wet of optimum** (dispersed structure, lower permeability, more flexible).

examTip.trick: The modified test delivers about **4.5 times** the compactive energy of the standard. More energy always pushes the curve **up and to the left**.
examTip.mnemonic: **More energy: higher and drier.** Every compaction curve behaves this way, which is why the OMC falls as the roller gets heavier.

questions.stem: The sand replacement method is preferred to the core cutter method for determining field density when the soil is:
questions.solution:
**Gravelly or hard.**

**The two field density methods and where each fits:**

| Method | Suits | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Core cutter** | **Soft, fine-grained** soils free of stones | A steel cylinder is **driven** into the soil and the intact core weighed |
| **Sand replacement** | **Gravelly, stony or hard** soils | A hole is excavated and its **volume measured by filling with standard sand** |

**The core cutter fails in gravelly ground for a direct physical reason:** the cutter **cannot be driven** without either being damaged by the stones or disturbing and loosening the sample as stones are pushed aside. The resulting core is neither intact nor representative.

**The sand replacement method** avoids the problem by not requiring an intact sample at all: the soil is **excavated** (however stony), weighed, and the **volume of the hole** determined by running **standard uniform sand of known bulk density** into it from a calibrated pouring cylinder.

> **Field dry density = (weight of excavated soil / volume of hole) / (1 + w)**

**Calibration is the critical step**, and it is done twice: the **bulk density of the sand** is determined, and the **weight of sand filling the cone** of the pouring cylinder is measured separately so it can be deducted. An error in either propagates directly into the result.

**Other field density methods:**

| Method | Character |
|---|---|
| **Water displacement / rubber balloon** | Volume by displacing water into a membrane lining the hole |
| **Nuclear density gauge** | **Rapid and non-destructive**; measures density and moisture by gamma and neutron backscatter. Needs licensing and calibration |
| Core cutter, sand replacement | As above |

**Why field density is measured at all:**

> **Relative compaction = field dry density / laboratory maximum dry density × 100%**

and the specification states a minimum — typically **95%** for embankment body, **97%** for subgrade, **100%** for the top 500 mm of a major road subgrade.

**The measurement must be of DRY density**, which is why the moisture content is determined on the same sample. Comparing a wet field density with a laboratory dry density is a straightforward error that flatters the result, and the reason dry density is used is that it measures **how much SOLID has been packed into a unit volume** — which is what compaction actually achieves.

examTip.trick: The core cutter has to be **driven in**, so it fails in anything containing gravel or in stiff, dry ground. The sand replacement method only needs a hole, so it works in both.
examTip.mnemonic: **Core cutter for soft and fine; sand replacement for hard and stony.**

questions.stem: The activity of a clay is defined as the ratio of the plasticity index to the:
options: Percentage of clay-size fraction finer than 2 micron
questions.solution:
**The percentage of the clay-size fraction finer than 2 micron.**

> **Activity A = PI / (% by weight finer than 2 μm)**

**What it identifies is the CLAY MINERAL**, which is its whole purpose:

| Clay mineral | Activity | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **Kaolinite** | **0.3 – 0.5** — **inactive** | Stable; strongly bonded layers; low swelling |
| **Illite** | **0.5 – 1.0** — normal | Intermediate |
| **Montmorillonite** | **1.0 – 7.0** — **ACTIVE** | **Swells enormously** on wetting; very high plasticity |

**Why the ratio works.** The **plasticity index measures how much water the soil can hold in the plastic range**, and that capacity comes almost entirely from the **clay fraction** — the sand and silt contribute nothing. Dividing PI by the clay percentage therefore gives the plasticity **per unit of clay present**, which is a property of the **mineral itself** rather than of how much of it there is.

So two soils with the same PI can have quite different activities: one may be a large quantity of an inactive mineral, the other a small quantity of a very active one — and they will behave differently, because the active one continues to swell as its water content changes.

**Montmorillonite is the mineral responsible for EXPANSIVE (black cotton) soils**, which swell on wetting and shrink on drying with a volume change large enough to:

| Damage | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Crack light structures** | Differential heave beneath a footing |
| **Break pavements** | Seasonal heave and shrinkage |
| **Distort canal linings and pipelines** | — |
| Open **deep desiccation cracks** in the dry season | Which then admit water rapidly at the next rain |

**Treatment of expansive soil:** **remove and replace**, provide a **thick granular capping**, **lime stabilisation** (calcium replaces sodium on the exchange sites, reducing plasticity), **under-reamed piles** anchored below the active zone, or — most fundamentally — **moisture control**, keeping the water content stable so the soil never cycles.

**The free swell index (IS 2720 Part 40)** is the routine screening test: 10 g of oven-dried soil passing 425 μm is placed in water and in kerosene, and

> **Free swell index = (V_water − V_kerosene)/V_kerosene × 100%**

with a value **above about 50%** indicating a soil requiring attention, and above 100% a severely expansive one.

examTip.trick: Activity separates clays by **mineralogy**, not merely by how much clay they contain: **inactive below 0.75** (kaolinite), **normal 0.75–1.25** (illite), **active above 1.25** (montmorillonite).
examTip.mnemonic: **High activity means montmorillonite means trouble** — that is the swelling clay behind black cotton soil and heave damage.

questions.stem: The relative density (density index) of a cohesionless soil is expressed as:
questions.solution:
**I_D = (e_max − e)/(e_max − e_min) × 100%.**

**Check the limiting cases** — the reliable way to identify the right form:

| Condition | Substitution | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **Loosest possible state**, e = e_max | (e_max − e_max)/(…) | **I_D = 0** ✓ |
| **Densest possible state**, e = e_min | (e_max − e_min)/(e_max − e_min) | **I_D = 100%** ✓ |

Option (a) is the same expression **inverted**, giving 100% for the loosest state — which is why testing the limiting cases immediately eliminates it.

**Note the inversion that the definition contains:**

> **A HIGH relative density corresponds to a LOW void ratio.**

That is intuitive once seen — a dense soil has few voids — but the formula's structure conceals it, which is why the check above is worth doing.

**In terms of dry unit weights**, which is how it is often computed:

> **I_D = [(γ_d − γ_d,min)/(γ_d,max − γ_d,min)] × [γ_d,max/γ_d]**

**Classification:**

| I_D | State |
|---|---|
| 0 – 15% | Very loose |
| 15 – 35% | **Loose** |
| 35 – 65% | Medium |
| 65 – 85% | **Dense** |
| 85 – 100% | Very dense |

**It applies to COARSE-grained soils only.** For clays the equivalent descriptors are the **consistency index** and **liquidity index**, because e_max and e_min have no meaning for a soil whose structure depends on its water content and stress history rather than on packing.

**Why relative density rather than void ratio alone?** Because a void ratio of 0.7 tells you nothing on its own — it might be dense for one sand and loose for another, depending on the grading and particle shape. **Relative density places the soil between its OWN limits**, so it is comparable between different sands. A well-graded angular sand has quite different e_max and e_min from a uniform rounded one, and relative density normalises for that.

**Its practical importance:** relative density correlates with **friction angle, compressibility, and liquefaction susceptibility**. A **loose, saturated fine sand (low I_D)** is the classic liquefiable material — which is why relative density, or the SPT N-value that correlates with it, is the first parameter examined in a liquefaction assessment for the Kathmandu Valley.

examTip.trick: The form guarantees the scale: at the loosest state e = e_max and I_D = 0; at the densest e = e_min and I_D = 1. Any option that fails those two checks is wrong.
examTip.mnemonic: **Relative density applies only to COHESIONLESS soil.** For clays it is meaningless — use consistency and the liquidity index instead. Bands: 0–15% very loose, 15–35 loose, 35–65 medium, 65–85 dense, 85–100 very dense.

questions.stem: The specific gravity of soil solids is determined in the laboratory using a:
questions.solution:
**A pycnometer (density bottle).**

The pycnometer is a glass bottle of known volume with a conical screw cap having a small hole at its apex, so that it can be filled to a **precisely repeatable** volume every time. Four weighings give the result:

| Weighing | Contents |
|---|---|
| **W₁** | Pycnometer empty |
| **W₂** | Pycnometer + dry soil |
| **W₃** | Pycnometer + soil + water |
| **W₄** | Pycnometer + water only |

> **G = (W₂ − W₁) / [(W₂ − W₁) − (W₃ − W₄)]**

**Typical values:**

| Soil | G |
|---|---|
| **Most soils** | **2.65 – 2.70** |
| Sand (quartz) | 2.65 |
| Clay | 2.70 – 2.80 |
| Soils with iron minerals | up to 3.0 |
| **Organic soils, peat** | **Lower** — 1.5 – 2.4 |

**Take G = 2.65 when none is given** — the conventional assumption, and quartz's specific gravity, quartz being the dominant mineral in most soils.

**The critical step in the test is REMOVING ENTRAPPED AIR** from the soil-water mixture, by applying a **vacuum** or by **gentle boiling**. Air remaining in the mixture makes W₃ too low, which makes the denominator too large and **understates G** — and because G enters every phase relation, an error there propagates through the whole set of calculations. It is the step most often skimped and the reason results are sometimes low.

**Why the other instruments are wrong:**

| Instrument | Actually measures |
|---|---|
| **Casagrande apparatus** | **Liquid limit** |
| **Hydrometer** | **Grain size distribution of the fine fraction**, by sedimentation using **Stokes' law** |
| **Consolidometer (oedometer)** | **Consolidation properties** — C_c, c_v, m_v |
| Pycnometer | **Specific gravity** |

**Where G is used:** in **every phase relation** (e·S = wG, and all four unit weight expressions), in the **zero air voids line** of the compaction test, in the **hydrometer analysis** (Stokes' law needs the particle density), and in the **critical hydraulic gradient** i_c = (G − 1)/(1 + e) for quick sand. It is a small measurement with a long reach, which is why it is worth doing carefully.

examTip.trick: The pycnometer works by displacement: weigh it with soil and water, then with water alone, and the difference gives the volume the solids occupy. **G is then computed, never read off a dial.**
examTip.mnemonic: **G for most soils is 2.65–2.75** — quartz sand about 2.65, clays a little higher. A result outside that band means an error, not an exotic soil.

questions.stem: In the IS soil classification system, the boundary between coarse-grained and fine-grained soils is the sieve size:
questions.solution:
**75 micron (0.075 mm).**

> A soil is **COARSE grained** if **more than 50% is RETAINED** on the 75 μ sieve, and **FINE grained** if **more than 50% PASSES** it.

That single division determines which branch of the classification applies — the **grading curve** (C_u and C_c) for coarse soils, and the **plasticity chart** for fine soils.

**The other sieve sizes in the options are all real boundaries, which is why they are offered:**

| Size | Boundary |
|---|---|
| **4.75 mm** | Between **GRAVEL and SAND** (also fine/coarse aggregate in concrete) |
| 2.00 mm | Coarse sand / medium sand |
| **425 μ** | The fraction used for the **Atterberg limit** tests |
| **75 μ** | Between **COARSE and FINE grained soil** |
| 2 μ | Between **silt and CLAY size** |

**Particle size ranges (IS 1498):**

| Fraction | Size |
|---|---|
| Boulder | > 300 mm |
| Cobble | 80 – 300 mm |
| **Gravel** | **4.75 – 80 mm** |
| **Sand** | **0.075 – 4.75 mm** (coarse 2–4.75, medium 0.425–2, fine 0.075–0.425) |
| **Silt** | **0.002 – 0.075 mm** |
| **Clay** | **< 0.002 mm (2 μ)** |

**Why 75 μ is the significant boundary** rather than any of the others: it is approximately the **smallest particle visible to the naked eye**, and — far more importantly — it is roughly the size below which **surface forces begin to dominate over gravitational forces**. Above it, a particle's behaviour is governed by its **weight and interlock**; below it, by **electrochemical surface interactions** with water. That is a genuine change of physical regime, and it is why the two halves of the classification system use entirely different criteria.

**It is also the practical limit of sieving.** Below 75 μ, sieves clog and the particles agglomerate, so the grading of the fine fraction is determined instead by **sedimentation** — the **hydrometer or pipette analysis**, using **Stokes' law** to relate settling velocity to particle size.

**Note the distinction between SIZE and BEHAVIOUR** for the fine fraction: a particle smaller than 2 μ is of **clay size**, but whether the soil behaves as a clay depends on its **mineralogy**, which is why the classification of fine soils is decided by the **A-line on the plasticity chart** and not by the percentage finer than 2 μ.

examTip.trick: Two sieve sizes anchor the whole classification: **4.75 mm** separates gravel from sand, and **75 micron** separates sand from silt and clay.
examTip.mnemonic: **4.75 mm and 75 micron.** A soil is coarse-grained if **more than 50%** is retained on the 75 micron sieve.

questions.stem: The sensitivity of a clay is the ratio of:
options: Undisturbed strength to remoulded strength, at the same water content
questions.solution:
**Undisturbed strength to remoulded strength, at the SAME water content.**

> **Sensitivity S_t = q_u(undisturbed) / q_u(remoulded)**

usually measured by the **unconfined compression test** on an undisturbed specimen and then on the same soil remoulded — or in the field by the **vane shear test**, re-shearing the same vane after a full rotation.

**The words "at the same water content" matter**: remoulding must not change the water content, or the comparison measures the effect of drying rather than of disturbance.

**Classification:**

| S_t | Description |
|---|---|
| ~1 | **Insensitive** |
| 1 – 2 | Low sensitivity |
| 2 – 4 | **Medium** |
| 4 – 8 | **Sensitive** |
| 8 – 16 | Extra sensitive |
| **> 16** | **QUICK clay** |

**What causes sensitivity.** A natural clay deposited slowly acquires a **flocculated, edge-to-face structure** with **inter-particle bonding** from cementation and from salts in the pore water. Remoulding **destroys that structure**, breaking the bonds and reorienting the particles into a **dispersed** arrangement — so the strength collapses even though nothing has been added or removed.

**Quick clays** are the extreme case, and their formation is worth knowing: marine clays deposited in **salt water** and later **leached by fresh groundwater** lose the salt that stabilised their flocculated structure, leaving a metastable arrangement of very high void ratio held together only by weak bonds. Disturbed, such a clay can **turn to a liquid** — with **S_t exceeding 100** in the notorious Scandinavian and Canadian deposits, where they have caused enormous flow slides.

**Its practical consequences:**

| Consequence | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **Undisturbed sampling is essential** | A disturbed sample of a sensitive clay grossly understates its strength |
| **Pile driving temporarily destroys capacity** | The clay around the pile is remoulded during driving |
| **THIXOTROPY** recovers part of it | The clay **regains strength with time** at constant water content, as bonds re-form — which is why a driven pile's capacity is re-tested after a **set-up period** of days or weeks |
| Excavation and construction disturbance | Must be minimised |

**Thixotropy is the counterpart of sensitivity** and is worth naming: sensitivity measures **how much strength is lost on remoulding**, thixotropy **how much is regained with rest**. A pile driven into a sensitive clay may show only a fraction of its design capacity immediately and its full capacity a fortnight later — which is why the timing of a pile load test is specified, not incidental.

**Why the other options are different quantities:** (c) contrasts **undrained and drained** strength, which is a question of **drainage conditions**, not disturbance; (d) is the **brittleness or residual strength ratio**, relevant to **progressive failure in slopes**, where a clay strained past its peak falls to a much lower residual strength on a pre-existing slip surface.

examTip.trick: Remoulding destroys the clay's natural structure. The scale runs **1–4 low, 4–8 medium, 8–16 sensitive, above 16 quick**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Sensitive clay loses its strength when disturbed and slowly gets it back — that recovery is THIXOTROPY.** It is why a driven pile's capacity rises for weeks after driving, and why testing too early understates it.

questions.stem: The grain size distribution of the fraction finer than 75 micron is determined by:
questions.solution:
**Hydrometer analysis.**

Below **75 μ**, sieving becomes impracticable: the sieves **clog**, the particles **agglomerate**, and electrostatic forces prevent them passing. The grading of the fine fraction is therefore determined by **sedimentation**, using the **hydrometer** (or the pipette method).

**The principle is STOKES' LAW:**

> **v = g(ρ_s − ρ_w) D² / (18 μ)**

A particle's **settling velocity is proportional to the SQUARE of its diameter**, so at any given time after the suspension is shaken, all particles larger than a calculable size have settled below the measuring depth, and the **density of the suspension at that depth** indicates how much finer material remains. The hydrometer measures exactly that density.

**The procedure:** 50 g of soil is dispersed in water with a **deflocculating agent** (sodium hexametaphosphate — Calgon), shaken, and hydrometer readings taken at intervals (½, 1, 2, 4, 8, 15, 30 minutes, then hours) with corrections for **temperature, meniscus and the dispersing agent**.

**The deflocculating agent is essential**, and the reason is instructive: clay particles in water **flocculate** into clusters that settle as though they were much larger particles, so the analysis would report a far coarser grading than the true one. Calgon disperses them into individual particles by altering the surface charge.

**The assumptions and their limitations** — worth knowing, since a question may probe them:

| Assumption | Reality |
|---|---|
| Particles are **spherical** | Clay particles are **plate-like**, so the result is an **equivalent** diameter, not a true one |
| Settling is **free and independent** | Valid only at low concentration |
| Flow is **laminar** | Fails for particles above about 0.2 mm — hence sieving above 75 μ |
| Particles have **uniform specific gravity** | Approximately true |

Because of the first, hydrometer results are properly described as giving the **equivalent settling diameter**, not the physical size — which is one reason the classification of fine soils rests on plasticity rather than on this curve.

**Combined analysis.** A soil with both coarse and fine fractions is analysed by **wet sieving** to separate at 75 μ, **sieve analysis** on the retained fraction and **hydrometer analysis** on the passing fraction, the two curves then being joined at 75 μ to give a single grading curve.

**Wet sieving** (option b) is a **preparation** step, not a method of determining the fine grading: the soil is washed through the 75 μ sieve to remove the fines from the coarse fraction so that each can be analysed by the appropriate method. It answers *how much* is finer than 75 μ, not *how that fine fraction is distributed*.

examTip.trick: Below 75 micron, sieving is impossible, so the analysis switches to **settling velocity** and Stokes' law. Larger particles fall faster, and the hydrometer reads the changing suspension density.
examTip.mnemonic: **Sieve the coarse, settle the fine.** The two curves are then joined at 75 micron to make one continuous grading.

questions.stem: Compaction differs from consolidation in that compaction:
options: Expels water, while consolidation expels air
Expels air, while consolidation expels water
Is always a slow, time-dependent process
questions.solution:
**Compaction expels AIR, while consolidation expels WATER.**

This pair is confused more often than any other in soil mechanics, and the distinction is complete:

| | **COMPACTION** | **CONSOLIDATION** |
|---|---|---|
| **Expels** | **AIR** | **WATER** |
| **Speed** | **IMMEDIATE** | **SLOW** — months to years |
| **Cause** | **Mechanical energy applied deliberately** | **Applied load** |
| **Applies to** | **Partly saturated** soil | **SATURATED** soil, especially clay |
| Context | A **construction operation** | A **service condition** |
| Water content | Usually **unchanged** | **Reduced** |
| Controlled by | Rolling, rammer, vibration | Permeability and drainage path |

**Compaction** is what a roller does to a fill: it **rearranges the particles into a denser packing, driving out the air**. It happens in the seconds during which the roller passes, and it is a deliberate act of construction.

**Consolidation** is what happens to a saturated clay **beneath** a completed structure: the load is initially carried by the **pore water** (raising the pore pressure), the water then **slowly drains away**, and as it does the load transfers to the soil skeleton while the layer compresses. It happens over years and is a consequence of the structure existing.

**Why compaction cannot occur in a fully saturated soil** — the reason option (c) is wrong, and a genuinely useful point: if the voids are entirely full of water, there is **no air to expel**, and water cannot be expelled quickly because the permeability is low. Applying compactive effort to a saturated clay therefore does not densify it — it **pumps and shears**, which is exactly what happens when a roller works on soil that is too wet, and why compaction is done **at or near the optimum moisture content**.

**The consequences of each:**

| Compaction achieves | Consolidation causes |
|---|---|
| **Increased shear strength and bearing capacity** | **Settlement** |
| **Reduced permeability** | Increased strength (a beneficial side effect) |
| **Reduced compressibility and future settlement** | Reduced void ratio |
| Reduced swelling and shrinkage | — |
| Increased resistance to erosion | — |

**Note the connection between them**, which explains why compaction is worth doing: a **well-compacted** fill has a **low void ratio already**, so there is little further reduction available — and therefore **little consolidation settlement** under the structure. Compaction is, in that sense, consolidation performed deliberately and quickly during construction rather than slowly and inconveniently afterwards.

examTip.trap: This pair is confused more than any other in soil mechanics, and examiners know it.
examTip.trick: Three clean distinctions: compaction is **rapid, mechanical, expels AIR** from a partly saturated soil; consolidation is **slow, load-driven, expels WATER** from a saturated one.
examTip.mnemonic: **Compaction squeezes out AIR in minutes; consolidation squeezes out WATER over years.**

questions.stem: For an undisturbed soil sample, the area ratio of the sampler should not exceed:
questions.solution:
**10%.**

> **Area ratio A_r = (D_o² − D_i²)/D_i² × 100%**

where D_o is the **outside** and D_i the **inside** diameter of the cutting edge. It measures the **volume of soil that the sampler must displace** as a proportion of the volume it collects.

**Why a low area ratio matters.** A thick-walled sampler pushes a large volume of soil aside as it is driven, and that displacement **shears and remoulds** the soil that then enters the tube. The sample recovered is therefore not in its natural state, and its **strength and consolidation properties are altered** — the very properties an undisturbed sample is taken to measure.

**Samplers compared:**

| Sampler | Area ratio | Sample |
|---|---|---|
| **Thin-walled (Shelby) tube** | **< 10%** (typically 6–10%) | **UNDISTURBED** |
| Piston sampler | < 10% | Undisturbed, in soft clay |
| Denison, Pitcher | Moderate | Undisturbed in stiff soil |
| **Split-spoon (SPT) sampler** | **> 100%** | **DISTURBED only** |

**The split-spoon's area ratio exceeding 100%** means it displaces more soil than it collects — which is why the SPT returns a sample suitable for **identification and index tests** but useless for **strength or consolidation** testing. Requesting a triaxial test on a split-spoon sample is a category error, and recognising that is the practical value of the concept.

**Two further sampler criteria:**

| Criterion | Formula | Value | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Inside clearance** | (D_i − D_e)/D_e × 100% | **0.5 – 3%** | So the sample **does not bind** in the tube as it enters; allows slight expansion |
| **Outside clearance** | (D_o − D_w)/D_w × 100% | **0 – 2%** | **Reduces driving friction** on the outside |

**Other factors affecting sample quality**, beyond the geometry: the **method of advance** (pushing is far better than driving), the **rate** (continuous and rapid), the **recovery ratio** (length of sample against depth penetrated — significantly less than 1 indicates loss or compression), **sealing and transport** (to preserve the water content), and **storage** (upright, protected from vibration and temperature change).

**Which tests need an undisturbed sample:**

| Undisturbed required | Disturbed sufficient |
|---|---|
| **Shear strength** (triaxial, direct shear, UCS) | Water content |
| **Consolidation** | Atterberg limits |
| **Permeability** | Grain size |
| In-situ density and void ratio | Specific gravity |
| — | Compaction |

The division follows a clear principle: an **index** property depends only on **what the soil is made of**, so remoulding does not change it — while an **engineering** property depends on **how the soil is arranged**, which remoulding destroys.

examTip.trick: **A_r = (D_o² − D_i²)/D_i² × 100.** Keeping it below 10% limits the soil displaced by the sampler wall, and so limits the disturbance.
examTip.mnemonic: **Under 10% for undisturbed sampling.** A thick-walled split spoon is around 100% — which is exactly why an SPT sample is a disturbed sample and can never be used for a strength test.

questions.stem: According to Terzaghi's principle, the shear strength and volume change of a soil are governed by:
options: The sum of total stress and pore pressure
questions.solution:
**The EFFECTIVE stress.**

> **σ′ = σ − u**

where σ is the **total** stress, u the **pore water pressure**, and σ′ the **effective** stress carried by the soil skeleton through **grain-to-grain contact**.

**Terzaghi's principle is that ONLY σ′ controls strength and volume change.** Total stress does not, and pore pressure alone does not. It is the single most important statement in soil mechanics, and almost everything else in the subject is a consequence of it.

**The consequences, each of which is examinable in its own right:**

| Change | Effect on σ′ | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **Water table RISES** | u rises, **σ′ FALLS** | **Strength falls** — the mechanism of most rain-triggered slope failures |
| Water table falls (pumping) | u falls, **σ′ rises** | **Settlement** — regional subsidence from over-abstraction |
| Load applied to saturated clay | u rises first, σ′ unchanged | **No immediate strength gain**; consolidation follows as u dissipates |
| **Upward seepage** | u rises | σ′ → 0 gives **QUICK SAND** |
| **Submergence** (water added above ground) | **Both σ and u rise EQUALLY** | **σ′ UNCHANGED** |

**The submergence case is the subtle one and is frequently examined.** Adding water **above** the ground surface increases the total stress by γ_w h and the pore pressure by γ_w h — **the same amount** — so σ′ does not change at all. The soil neither strengthens nor settles. That is why a flooded site does not consolidate under the weight of the flood water, which surprises people until the arithmetic is done.

**Computing a profile.** Two equivalent routes:

> **σ = Σ(γ × thickness)**, using **γ_sat below the water table**; then **u = γ_w h_w**; then **σ′ = σ − u**
> or directly **σ′ = Σ(γ′ × thickness)** below the water table, with **γ′ = γ_sat − γ_w**

The second is quicker, and that both give the same answer is a check on the arithmetic.

**Capillary rise** produces **NEGATIVE** pore pressure (suction) above the water table, so σ′ is **INCREASED** there. That apparent cohesion is what allows a damp sand to stand in a vertical cut — and why the cut collapses when the sand dries out **or** is flooded, since either destroys the suction.

examTip.trap: "Total stress" is the intuitive wrong answer. Total stress governs nothing on its own — two soils at the same total stress but different pore pressures behave completely differently.
examTip.trick: **σ′ = σ − u.** Everything that matters — strength, stiffness, volume change — is a function of σ′ alone. This is the single most important equation in the subject.
examTip.mnemonic: **Effective stress does all the work.** Raise the water table and σ is unchanged but σ′ falls, and the soil weakens.

questions.stem: The seepage velocity through a soil is related to the discharge velocity by:
questions.solution:
**v_s = v / n**, where n is the porosity.

**Since n is always less than 1, the seepage velocity is always GREATER than the discharge velocity.**

**The distinction:**

| Velocity | Definition | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **Discharge velocity v** | **v = k i** — flow rate divided by the **GROSS cross-sectional area** | A **fictitious average**; no water actually travels at this speed |
| **Seepage velocity v_s** | The **actual** velocity of water through the **VOIDS** | The real velocity of a water particle |

**The reasoning is simple continuity.** The same discharge Q must pass through the section, but water can only flow through the **void portion** of the area:

> **Q = v × A = v_s × A_v**, and since **A_v = n A**, we get **v_s = v/n** ∎

**A worked illustration.** For a sand with n = 0.35 and a discharge velocity of 1 × 10⁻⁵ m/s:

> v_s = 1 × 10⁻⁵ / 0.35 = **2.86 × 10⁻⁵ m/s** — nearly **three times** the nominal value.

**Which one to use, and when:**

| Problem | Use |
|---|---|
| **Quantity of seepage** (discharge, flow net, pumping) | **Discharge velocity v** — it already refers to the gross area |
| **TIME of travel** of a water particle or a **contaminant** | **Seepage velocity v_s** — the real speed |
| Checking whether flow is **laminar** (Reynolds number) | Seepage velocity |

**The travel-time application is the one that matters practically**: estimating how long it takes a pollutant to reach a well, or a tracer to appear downstream, requires the **actual** velocity. Using the discharge velocity would **overestimate the travel time by a factor of 1/n** — typically two to three times — which for a contamination assessment is a serious error in the unsafe direction.

**Note that even the seepage velocity is an average**: the actual water follows a **tortuous path** through the voids, so its true path length exceeds the straight-line distance and its local velocity varies greatly from pore to pore. v_s is the mean advance rate, which is what the calculation needs.

examTip.trick: Darcy's v is a **fictitious** velocity spread over the whole area; the water actually squeezes through the voids only, so it moves faster by 1/n.
examTip.mnemonic: **Real water moves 2 to 3 times faster than Darcy says**, since n is typically 0.3–0.5. Use **seepage velocity for contaminant travel times** — using v instead overestimates the time by that factor.

questions.stem: For flow parallel to the bedding planes of a stratified soil, the equivalent permeability is the:
options: Harmonic mean of the layer permeabilities, weighted by thickness
Geometric mean of the layer permeabilities
Arithmetic mean of the layer permeabilities, weighted by thickness
Permeability of the least permeable layer
questions.solution:
**The ARITHMETIC mean, weighted by thickness.**

> **Parallel (HORIZONTAL) flow: k_H = Σ(k_i H_i)/ΣH_i** — an **arithmetic** mean
> **Perpendicular (VERTICAL) flow: k_V = ΣH_i / Σ(H_i/k_i)** — a **harmonic** mean

**Therefore k_H is ALWAYS greater than k_V**, typically by a factor of 2 to 10 in natural deposits, and much more in a varved clay.

**Why the two differ, and the electrical analogy makes it immediate:**

| Flow | Analogy | Dominated by |
|---|---|---|
| **Parallel (horizontal)** | Resistances in **PARALLEL** — the current takes the easy path | The **MOST permeable** layer |
| **Perpendicular (vertical)** | Resistances in **SERIES** — all the current must pass through every layer | The **LEAST permeable** layer |

In **parallel** flow the water simply **uses the sandy layer** and largely ignores the clay, so a single permeable seam dominates the total. In **series** flow the water is **held up by the tight layer**, which it cannot bypass — so a single clay seam controls the whole.

**A worked case makes the disparity vivid.** Three 1 m layers with k = 10⁻³, 10⁻⁵ and 10⁻⁷ m/s:

> **k_H = (10⁻³ + 10⁻⁵ + 10⁻⁷)/3 ≈ 3.4 × 10⁻⁴ m/s**
> **k_V = 3 / (10³ + 10⁵ + 10⁷) ≈ 3.0 × 10⁻⁷ m/s**

**A ratio of about 1100** — and note that k_H is close to the **most** permeable layer while k_V is close to the **least**, exactly as the analogy predicts.

**The practical consequences:**

| Consequence | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **Seepage travels far more readily HORIZONTALLY** | Flow nets in stratified ground are strongly elongated |
| A **single sand seam** in a clay dominates horizontal flow | And is a preferential path for seepage under a dam |
| A **single clay seam** in a sand dominates vertical flow | Perching the water table, or blocking a drainage path |
| **Laboratory permeability is unreliable** | A small specimen misses the seams that govern the mass |

The last is why a **field pumping test**, which averages over a large mass, gives a value more useful for a dewatering or seepage problem than any number of laboratory tests — and why the two commonly differ by an order of magnitude.

**For a flow net in anisotropic soil**, the section is **transformed** by scaling the horizontal dimension by **√(k_V/k_H)**, the net drawn on the transformed section, and the discharge computed with the **equivalent permeability √(k_H k_V)** — the geometric mean, which is where option (b) comes from and why it appears as a distractor.

examTip.trick: Reason it physically rather than memorising: **parallel to the layers**, water takes the **easiest** path, so the most permeable layer dominates and the average is **arithmetic**. **Perpendicular**, it must cross **every** layer, so the least permeable controls and the average is **harmonic**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Along the layers, the best one wins (arithmetic). Across them, the worst one wins (harmonic).** Hence k_horizontal is always ≥ k_vertical.

questions.stem: The falling head permeability test is more suitable than the constant head test for:
options: Fine-grained soils such as silt and clay
questions.solution:
**Fine-grained soils such as silt and clay.**

| Test | Suits | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Constant head** | **COARSE** soils — gravel, sand (k > 10⁻⁴ m/s) | The flow is **fast enough to collect and measure a steady discharge** in reasonable time |
| **Falling head** | **FINE** soils — silt, clay (k < 10⁻⁴ m/s) | The flow is far too slow for that, so the **fall of head in a standpipe** is measured instead |

**The reasoning is entirely practical.** In a clay with k = 10⁻⁹ m/s, a constant head test would deliver a few drops of water a day — impossible to measure accurately against evaporation. The falling head arrangement instead uses a **thin standpipe**, so that even a minute volume of flow produces a **measurable fall in level**.

**The formulae:**

> **Constant head: k = QL/(A h t)**
> **Falling head: k = 2.303 (aL)/(A t) · log₁₀(h₁/h₂)**

where **a** is the standpipe area, **A** the specimen area, L its length, and h₁, h₂ the heads at the start and end of time t.

**Note the role of the standpipe area a**: making it **smaller** magnifies the head drop for a given flow, which is how the test is adapted to progressively lower permeabilities. For a very tight clay, a capillary tube is used.

**Typical permeabilities**, spanning **ten orders of magnitude** — which is why soil type matters more here than anywhere else in the subject:

| Soil | k (m/s) | Drainage |
|---|---|---|
| **Clean gravel** | 10⁻¹ – 10⁻² | Very good |
| **Clean sand** | 10⁻² – 10⁻⁵ | Good |
| Silty sand, silt | 10⁻⁵ – 10⁻⁸ | Poor |
| **Clay** | **< 10⁻⁹** | **Practically impervious** |

**Other methods of determining k:**

| Method | Character |
|---|---|
| **Pumping-out test** (field) | Gives a **MASS AVERAGE** over a large volume — the value that actually governs a dewatering or seepage problem |
| Pumping-in / borehole test | Local field value |
| **From the consolidation test** | **k = c_v m_v γ_w** — for very fine soils where direct measurement is impractical |
| **Allen Hazen's formula** | **k ≈ C D₁₀²** for clean sands — a rapid estimate from the grading curve |

**The field pumping test deserves emphasis** because laboratory values are so often misleading: a small specimen cannot contain the **fissures, root holes, laminations and sand seams** that dominate flow through a real soil mass. Laboratory and field values differing by an order of magnitude is normal, and where seepage quantity matters, the **field value is the one to use**.

**Factors affecting permeability:** **grain size** (k ∝ D₁₀², so it is the finest fraction that governs), **void ratio**, **soil structure and stratification**, **degree of saturation** (entrapped air blocks pores and reduces k markedly), and **fluid viscosity** — hence **temperature**, which is why results are corrected to a standard 27 °C.

examTip.trick: In a fine soil the flow through a constant head apparatus would be a few drops an hour — unmeasurable. The falling head test instead measures the **time for the head to drop**, which is long and easy to time precisely.
examTip.mnemonic: **Constant head for coarse and fast; falling head for fine and slow.** Below about 10⁻⁷ m/s, get k from the consolidation test instead.

questions.stem: In a flow net, the quantity of seepage per unit width is given by q = kH(N_f/N_d), where N_f and N_d are respectively the numbers of:
questions.solution:
**Flow CHANNELS and equipotential DROPS.**

> **q = k H (N_f / N_d)**

**N_f and N_d count the SPACES, not the LINES** — which is the distinction the question turns on, and the commonest arithmetic error in flow net problems. Four flow lines bound **three** flow channels; six equipotential lines create **five** drops.

**Properties of a flow net**, each with its reason:

| Property | Why |
|---|---|
| Flow lines and equipotential lines cross at **RIGHT ANGLES** | Flow is always **normal to a line of equal potential** |
| The fields are **curvilinear SQUARES** | So each field has the same ratio of flow to head drop |
| **No two flow lines cross**, and no two equipotentials cross | A point cannot have two velocities or two heads |
| The **discharge between adjacent flow lines is EQUAL** | Hence where the channel **narrows**, the **velocity and gradient INCREASE** |
| The **head drop between adjacent equipotentials is EQUAL** | By construction |

**That fourth property is the one that does the engineering work**: where the flow channel is narrow — typically at the **downstream exit**, close to the end of a sheet pile — the **hydraulic gradient is highest**, and that is exactly where **piping** begins. A flow net therefore shows at a glance where the danger is.

**What a flow net is used for:**

| Output | How |
|---|---|
| **Seepage quantity** | q = kH(N_f/N_d) |
| **Pore pressure at any point** | From the number of drops passed: **u = γ_w[h_total − (n_d/N_d)H − z]** |
| **EXIT GRADIENT** | The head drop in the last field divided by its length — hence **piping safety** |
| **UPLIFT pressure** on a structure's base | From the pore pressures along it |

**Boundary conditions** determine the net and must be identified first:

| Boundary | Type |
|---|---|
| Upstream and downstream ground surfaces | **EQUIPOTENTIALS** |
| An **impervious** surface (the base of a sheet pile, a clay stratum, the underside of a dam) | A **FLOW LINE** |
| The **phreatic (top flow) line** in an earth dam | A free surface at atmospheric pressure — approximated by **Casagrande's parabola** |

**A worked check.** With k = 10⁻⁵ m/s, H = 6 m, N_f = 4 and N_d = 12:

> q = 10⁻⁵ × 6 × (4/12) = **2 × 10⁻⁵ m³/s per metre width** — about 1.7 m³/day per metre.

The flow net is a **graphical solution of Laplace's equation**, and its great merit is that it can be drawn by hand for a boundary shape no formula can handle — which is why it survived long after analytical methods, and why sketching one remains a genuine skill.

examTip.trap: **Count the SPACES, not the LINES.** Five flow lines make four channels; eleven equipotentials make ten drops. Counting lines is the commonest arithmetic error in the whole topic.
examTip.trick: N_f/N_d is the **shape factor** and depends only on geometry — so one flow net serves any permeability and any head.
examTip.mnemonic: **Spaces, not lines.** The net also yields pore pressure, uplift, and the exit gradient that governs piping.

questions.stem: The quick sand condition occurs when the upward hydraulic gradient reaches a critical value approximately equal to:
options: The specific gravity of the soil solids
questions.solution:
**Approximately 1.0.**

> **i_c = (G − 1)/(1 + e)**

and for typical values (**G = 2.65, e = 0.65**): **i_c = 1.65/1.65 = 1.00** — which is why the critical gradient is remembered as **unity**, though it varies slightly with the void ratio.

**Quick sand is a CONDITION, not a type of soil** — the most examined point about it. **Any** cohesionless soil can be brought to the quick condition if the upward gradient is high enough; fine sands and silts are simply the ones in which it is commonly encountered, because they combine low permeability (so gradients can build) with no cohesion.

**The mechanism:**

> Upward seepage exerts a **seepage force** of **j = i γ_w** per unit volume on the soil skeleton. When that upward force **equals the submerged weight** γ′ of the soil, the **effective stress becomes ZERO**:
> **σ′ = γ′z − i γ_w z = 0** when **i = γ′/γ_w = (G − 1)/(1 + e)**

At that point the grains are **no longer in contact under load**, so by Terzaghi's principle the soil has **NO SHEAR STRENGTH AT ALL** — τ = c + σ′ tan φ with c = 0 and σ′ = 0 gives τ = 0. The mixture behaves as a **dense liquid** of unit weight about 2γ_w.

**Note that a person does not "sink out of sight" in quick sand**, contrary to the popular image: the mixture is **denser than the human body**, so a person floats in it more readily than in water. The danger is being unable to extricate oneself, not sinking.

**Where the condition arises in engineering:**

| Situation | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **The bottom of an excavation** below the water table | Upward seepage into the excavation |
| **Downstream of a sheet pile cofferdam** | Flow around the toe emerges upward |
| **Downstream of a weir or dam** on permeable foundation | The exit gradient at the downstream apron |
| Around a **well being pumped** at high rate | Inward and upward gradient |

**Prevention:**

| Measure | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Lengthen the seepage path** — deeper cut-off, sheet piles, upstream blanket | **Reduces the gradient** |
| **Lower the water table** by dewatering **outside** the excavation | Removes the driving head |
| **Increase the downstream weight** — a loading berm, a thicker floor | Increases σ′ at the exit |
| **Inverted filter** at the exit | Allows water out while **retaining the soil** |

**PIPING is the related but distinct failure**, and the two should not be conflated:

| | **Quick sand** | **Piping** |
|---|---|---|
| Condition | σ′ = 0 over an area; the soil **boils** | **Progressive BACKWARD erosion** along a channel |
| Onset | When i reaches i_c | Begins at the exit, works **upstream** |
| Character | A general condition | A **localised, self-accelerating** channel |

Piping is the more dangerous because it is **self-accelerating**: once a channel forms, the flow concentrates into it, the gradient there rises further, and erosion accelerates — which is why it can undermine a structure with little warning and why the safe **exit gradient** is set with a substantial factor of safety (**1/5 to 1/7** depending on the material).

examTip.trick: Derive it: **i_c = (G − 1)/(1 + e)**. With G = 2.65 and e = 0.65 that is 1.65/1.65 = **1.0** — which is why the value is so easy to remember.
examTip.mnemonic: **Critical gradient ≈ 1.** At that point the upward seepage force equals the submerged weight, σ′ drops to zero, and the sand has no strength at all. Design with a factor of safety of **4 to 7** — high, because piping is sudden and self-accelerating.

questions.stem: Khosla's theory showed that the safety of a weir founded on permeable soil is governed principally by:
options: The number of intermediate sheet piles
The exit gradient and the end sheet piles
questions.solution:
**The EXIT GRADIENT and the outer faces of the END sheet piles.**

**The three theories form a progression**, and understanding it as such is more useful than memorising them separately:

| Theory | Assumption | Defect |
|---|---|---|
| **Bligh's creep (1910)** | Creep length = **SUM of horizontal and vertical paths, all equally effective**; head loss **uniform** along it | Horizontal and vertical creep are **not** equally effective; the gradient is **not** uniform; the **exit gradient is ignored** |
| **Lane's weighted creep (1935)** | Horizontal creep weighted at **one third** of vertical | Still empirical; still ignores the exit gradient |
| **KHOSLA (1936)** | **Potential flow theory** — an actual solution of Laplace's equation | Supersedes both |

**Khosla's findings overturned the earlier theories**, and each is worth stating:

| Finding | Consequence for design |
|---|---|
| The actual pressure distribution **differs greatly** from Bligh's uniform assumption | Bligh could be **unsafe at some points and wasteful at others** |
| **The EXIT GRADIENT governs piping** — not the total creep length | Design against a **safe exit gradient** |
| The **OUTER faces of the END piles are far more effective** than the inner faces | **Put the piles at the ends** |
| **INTERMEDIATE sheet piles below the floor are LARGELY INEFFECTIVE** if shorter than the end piles | Money spent on them is **largely wasted** |
| An **upstream** pile reduces **uplift**; a **downstream** pile reduces the **exit gradient** | Each end pile has a **distinct role** |

**The finding about intermediate piles is the one that saved money and lives**: designers following Bligh added intermediate piles to increase the creep length, believing they improved safety. Khosla showed they contribute almost nothing to reducing the exit gradient, which is what actually causes piping — so the expenditure bought little, and the false confidence was itself a hazard.

**The exit gradient:**

> **G_E = (H/d) × 1/(π√λ)**,  where **λ = (1 + √(1 + α²))/2** and **α = b/d**

with b the floor length and d the downstream cut-off depth.

**Safe values:**

| Material | Safe exit gradient |
|---|---|
| **Shingle** | **1/4 to 1/5** |
| **Coarse sand** | **1/5 to 1/6** |
| **Fine sand** | **1/6 to 1/7** |

**Finer material needs a flatter gradient**, because its particles are lighter and more easily lifted — consistent with i_c = (G − 1)/(1 + e) applying to any soil while the **factor of safety** required depends on how easily the particles move.

**The two failures and their two distinct remedies** — the organising idea of the whole topic:

> **PIPING** is resisted by **LENGTH** (deep end cut-offs, upstream apron) and by an **inverted filter** at the exit.
> **UPLIFT** is resisted by **THICKNESS** — floor thickness **t = h/(G − 1)**, with a factor of safety of about 1.33.

Different failures, different remedies; and confusing them leads to a floor that is thick where it should be long, or long where it should be thick.

examTip.trick: Khosla replaced Bligh's crude creep theory with a proper potential-flow solution. The practical outcomes are that the **exit gradient** governs safety and that a **downstream cut-off** is far more effective than a longer horizontal floor.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bligh counted length; Khosla solved the flow.** Bligh treated vertical and horizontal creep as equally effective — they are not, and structures designed on that basis failed.

questions.stem: Immediately after a load is applied to a saturated clay, the increase in stress is carried almost entirely by:
questions.solution:
**The PORE WATER.**

**The mechanism of consolidation, in three stages** — and understanding it as a sequence is worth more than any formula:

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| **1. Load applied (t = 0)** | Water is **incompressible** and cannot escape instantly through a low-permeability clay, so the **PORE WATER takes the whole load**. **u rises by Δσ**; **σ′ is UNCHANGED** |
| **2. Drainage (0 < t < ∞)** | Water **slowly drains out**; **u falls**, **σ′ rises**, and the soil **compresses** |
| **3. Complete (t = ∞)** | u has returned to its original value; **σ′ has risen by the full Δσ**; primary consolidation is complete |

> **Consolidation is therefore the TRANSFER OF LOAD from the WATER to the SOIL SKELETON over time.**

That single sentence explains everything about it: why it is **slow** (water must physically flow out through a material of very low permeability), why it **stops** (there is no more excess pressure left to dissipate), and why the soil **gains strength** as it proceeds (σ′ rises, and strength depends on σ′).

**Two important consequences:**

| Consequence | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **No IMMEDIATE strength gain** | Since σ′ is unchanged at t = 0, the clay is no stronger the moment the load is applied — which is why an embankment on soft clay must be built **slowly, in stages**, allowing consolidation between lifts |
| **The short-term case is critical for a LOADED clay** | Because consolidation subsequently **strengthens** it. Conversely, for an **unloaded** clay (a cutting), swelling subsequently **weakens** it, so the **long-term** case is critical |

**That asymmetry is a favourite examination point** and explains a real phenomenon: **cuttings in clay can fail years after construction**, when the negative pore pressures generated by unloading have finally dissipated and the effective stresses have fallen to their long-term values.

**In SAND the situation is entirely different**: permeability is so high that the water escapes essentially as fast as the load is applied, so **u never rises appreciably**, σ′ increases immediately, and the settlement is **immediate**. That is why consolidation theory is a **clay** subject and settlement in sand is treated as elastic.

**Skempton's pore pressure parameters** quantify the initial response:

> **Δu = B[Δσ₃ + A(Δσ₁ − Δσ₃)]**

with **B = 1 for a fully saturated soil** — which is the formal statement of the answer to this question. A measured **B below 1 means the specimen is not fully saturated**, and it is checked before any triaxial test is accepted, because an unsaturated specimen behaves quite differently.

examTip.trick: Water is essentially incompressible and cannot escape instantly, so at **t = 0** the whole load increment goes into pore pressure: **Δu = Δσ**. As drainage proceeds it transfers to the skeleton, and at **t = ∞**, **Δσ′ = Δσ**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Load goes to water first, soil last.** That transfer IS consolidation, and settlement is its visible consequence.

questions.stem: A clay layer draining from both its top and bottom surfaces will consolidate, compared with the same layer draining from one surface only:
questions.solution:
**FOUR times as fast.**

> **T_v = c_v t / d²**

where **d is the length of the DRAINAGE PATH** — the longest distance a water particle must travel to reach a drainage boundary.

| Drainage | Drainage path d |
|---|---|
| **Single** (one permeable boundary) | **d = H** (the full layer thickness) |
| **Double** (both boundaries permeable) | **d = H/2** |

**Since time varies as d², halving the drainage path divides the time by FOUR:**

> t ∝ d², so (H/2)² = H²/4 ∎

**This is the most useful practical result in consolidation theory**, and it is the basis of the whole technology of accelerating settlement.

**Sand drains and prefabricated vertical drains (PVDs, band drains)** exploit it directly: vertical drains installed on a grid of perhaps **1 to 3 m** spacing convert the drainage from **vertical over the layer thickness** (which might be 10 m) to **radial over the drain spacing** (perhaps 1 m).

> Reducing the drainage path from 10 m to 1 m reduces the consolidation time by a factor of **100**.

So a settlement that would have taken **twenty years** occurs in a matter of **months** — which is exactly what a preloading scheme needs, since the object is to complete the settlement **before** construction rather than after it.

**The essential point about drains, and it is often misunderstood:**

> **Vertical drains do NOT change HOW MUCH settlement occurs — only HOW FAST.**

The total settlement is determined by the **stress increase and the compressibility**, neither of which the drains affect. They change only the **rate**. A question suggesting that drains reduce the total settlement is offering a wrong answer.

**Useful time factor values:**

| Degree of consolidation U | T_v |
|---|---|
| 50% | **0.197** |
| 90% | **0.848** |
| 100% | ∞ (approached asymptotically) |

and approximately **T_v = (π/4)U²** for U < 60%.

**Note that consolidation is never strictly complete** — U approaches 100% asymptotically — which is why design is to **90% or 95%** consolidation, and why a preloading period is specified to reach a stated degree rather than to finish.

**Determining c_v from the test data** uses either **Casagrande's logarithm-of-time** fitting method (taking T_v = 0.197 at U = 50%) or **Taylor's square-root-of-time** method (T_v = 0.848 at U = 90%). The two often disagree somewhat, which is an honest reflection of the fact that real clay does not exactly obey the idealised theory.

examTip.trick: **t ∝ d²**, where d is the **longest drainage path**. Draining both faces halves d, and halving a squared term divides the time by **four**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Double drainage, quarter the time.** The same square law is why **vertical drains** work so dramatically — cutting the path from 10 m to 1 m cuts the time by a hundred.

questions.stem: A clay whose preconsolidation pressure exceeds its present effective overburden pressure is described as:
questions.solution:
**Over-consolidated.**

> **OCR = preconsolidation pressure σ′_c / present effective overburden σ′₀**

| OCR | State | Behaviour under load |
|---|---|---|
| **= 1** | **Normally consolidated** | Follows the **virgin compression line**; settles substantially |
| **> 1** | **OVER-consolidated** | Follows the much **flatter RECOMPRESSION line**; settles **far less**, until σ′_c is exceeded |
| **< 1** | **Under-consolidated** | Still consolidating under its **own weight**; a recent fill or deposit |

**Why a clay becomes over-consolidated** — it has **carried a greater load in the past** and been unloaded:

| Cause | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Erosion of overburden** | Soil above has been removed by weathering or a river |
| **Melting of an ice sheet** | Glacial loading removed |
| **Demolition of a former structure** | — |
| **Desiccation** | Drying generates large suctions, which act like a load |
| **Groundwater level rise** | A previously higher effective stress has been reduced |
| Ageing, cementation | Produces an apparent preconsolidation |

**Why it matters so much practically:**

> Recognising over-consolidation can reduce a settlement estimate by an **ORDER OF MAGNITUDE**, because the recompression index **C_r is typically only 1/5 to 1/10 of the compression index C_c**.

The settlement calculation must therefore use **C_r while the stress remains below σ′_c**, switching to **C_c** for any part of the increase beyond it:

> **If σ′₀ + Δσ ≤ σ′_c:  S = (C_r H/(1+e₀)) log₁₀[(σ′₀+Δσ)/σ′₀]**
> **If σ′₀ + Δσ > σ′_c:  S = (C_r H/(1+e₀)) log₁₀(σ′_c/σ′₀) + (C_c H/(1+e₀)) log₁₀[(σ′₀+Δσ)/σ′_c]**

Using C_c throughout for an over-consolidated clay **grossly overestimates** the settlement and can lead to an unnecessary and expensive foundation.

**Finding σ′_c: Casagrande's construction** on the e – log σ′ curve:

1. Locate the **point of minimum radius of curvature**.
2. Draw a **horizontal** line and a **tangent** at that point.
3. **Bisect** the angle between them.
4. **Extend the straight virgin portion** of the curve backwards.
5. Their **intersection** gives **σ′_c**.

**Skempton's correlation** gives a check on C_c where no test is available:

> **C_c = 0.009 (LL − 10)** for remoulded, normally consolidated clay

**A practical consequence worth carrying:** because the recompression line is so flat, a structure whose **net** pressure increase does not exceed the preconsolidation pressure will settle very little. That is one of the arguments for a **deep basement** — excavating removes overburden, so the **net** stress increase is small, and the ground behaves in recompression rather than virgin compression.

examTip.trick: OCR = σ′_c/σ′_0. **OCR = 1 normally consolidated; OCR > 1 over-consolidated.** Causes include erosion of overburden, past glaciation, and desiccation.
examTip.mnemonic: **Over-consolidated clay has been squeezed harder before, so it settles far less now** — it follows the flat **recompression** line until the past maximum is exceeded. Using C_c instead of C_r for an OC clay overestimates settlement several-fold.

questions.stem: The depth to which a significant increase of vertical stress extends below a loaded footing is generally taken as:
questions.solution:
**1.5 to 2 times the footing width.**

This follows from the **pressure bulb** — the region within which the stress increase is significant. Conventionally the boundary is taken at the **isobar of 20% (or 10%) of the applied pressure**, and for a square or circular footing of width B the **20% isobar reaches a depth of about 1.5 B**, the 10% isobar about 2 B.

**Why the stress decays so quickly.** By **Boussinesq's** solution for a point load on an elastic half space:

> **σ_z = (3Q / 2πz²) × [1/(1 + (r/z)²)]^{5/2}**

the stress **falls roughly as 1/z²** on the axis. Doubling the depth quarters the stress, so by 2 B below the footing the added stress is a small fraction of the applied pressure — small enough that further compression of the soil is negligible compared with the layers above.

**The practical consequences are three, and they are the reason the concept is examined:**

| Consequence | Application |
|---|---|
| **Depth of soil EXPLORATION** | Boreholes are taken to **1.5 to 2 B** below foundation level — deeper is wasted, shallower misses a compressible layer that matters |
| **Which layers contribute to SETTLEMENT** | Only those within the bulb; a soft layer well below it can be ignored |
| **Overlapping bulbs** | Where adjacent footings are close, their bulbs **overlap** and the combined stress reaches **deeper** — so the group must be treated as one larger loaded area |

**The overlapping-bulb point is the one most often missed** and it matters: a raft or a closely spaced group of footings has a pressure bulb governed by the **overall dimension**, not by the individual footing width. A borehole taken to 1.5 × (individual footing width) would then be far too shallow, and a deep compressible layer would be discovered only by the settlement.

**The corresponding rules for exploration depth:**

| Foundation | Depth of exploration |
|---|---|
| **Isolated footing** | 1.5 – 2 × width B |
| **Raft** | 1.5 – 2 × the **shorter** plan dimension |
| **Pile group** | 1.5 × the group width **below the pile tips** |
| Rock encountered | **3 m into sound rock**, to confirm it is not a boulder |

**Other stress distribution theories:**

| Theory | Assumption | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **Boussinesq** | **Homogeneous, isotropic, elastic** half space | The standard |
| **Westergaard** | A **layered** soil with rigid horizontal reinforcement | **LOWER** stresses at depth — more realistic for stratified deposits |
