| **2:1 approximate method** | The load spreads over an area widening at **2 vertical to 1 horizontal** | Crude but adequate for many settlement estimates |
| **Newmark's influence chart** | Graphical | Handles a loaded area of **any shape** |

**The 2:1 method** is worth knowing for its simplicity: **σ_z = Q/[(B + z)(L + z)]**. It gives results reasonably close to Boussinesq for the depths that matter, and it requires no chart — which is why it survives as a check on a computed value.

examTip.trick: The conventional cut-off is where the added stress falls to about **10–20%** of the applied pressure — below that it contributes little settlement.
examTip.mnemonic: **Investigate to 1.5–2 B below the footing.** For a pile group the bulb is far deeper, which is why a group settles much more than a single test pile suggests.

questions.stem: In an earth dam, the top flow line of the seepage through the dam body is called the:
questions.solution:
**The phreatic line (seepage line).**

It is the **top flow line** of the seepage through the dam body, and it is a **free surface at ATMOSPHERIC pressure** — so along it the **pore pressure is zero** and the total head equals the elevation head.

**It is approximated by CASAGRANDE'S PARABOLA**, a base parabola with corrections at the entry and exit.

**Why controlling it is central to earth dam design:**

> The phreatic line **must be kept WITHIN the body of the dam and AWAY from the DOWNSTREAM SLOPE.**

**If it emerges on the downstream slope:**

| Consequence | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| Seepage water **exits on the face** | Visible as a wet patch or a spring |
| The soil there becomes **saturated** | Its **effective stress falls**, and with it its shear strength |
| The slope **SLOUGHS** progressively | Each small failure exposes more saturated soil |
| **Internal erosion** may begin | If the exiting water carries soil particles |

**The remedies are internal drainage features**, and their purpose is precisely to **draw the phreatic line down and away from the face**:

| Feature | Function |
|---|---|
| **Chimney (inclined) filter drain** | Intercepts the seepage **within** the dam and leads it down |
| **Horizontal drainage blanket** | Carries it to the toe |
| **Toe drain / rock toe** | Collects and discharges it safely |
| **Filters** (graded) around all of them | Pass water while **retaining the soil** |

**The filter is the component whose omission causes failure**, and its criterion is the standard one: **coarse enough to pass water freely, fine enough to retain the adjacent soil**. Without it, the seepage carries fine core particles into the coarse drain, forming a pipe that enlarges progressively — **internal erosion**, responsible for a large share of embankment dam failures.

**Why the other options are wrong:**

| Term | Actually means |
|---|---|
| **Equipotential line** | A line of **equal total head** — it crosses flow lines at right angles |
| **Hydraulic grade line** | Pressure head + datum head, in **pipe or channel** flow |
| **Energy line (TEL)** | HGL + velocity head, in pipe or channel flow |

The last two belong to **hydraulics**, not seepage, and are offered because the names are superficially similar.

**Monitoring the phreatic line** in a completed dam is done with **piezometers** installed at intervals through the section. A **rising piezometric level**, an **increase in measured seepage** at the toe, or — most seriously — **seepage that becomes CLOUDY** (carrying soil, hence internal erosion in progress) are the signs of developing trouble. **Cloudy seepage is an emergency**, and recognising it as such is a genuine professional obligation.

examTip.trick: The phreatic line is the **top streamline**, and on it the **pore pressure is atmospheric** — so pressure head is zero and the total head equals the elevation. That boundary condition is what makes the flow net solvable.
examTip.mnemonic: **Keep the phreatic line inside the dam.** If it emerges on the downstream face, the face saturates and sloughs — which is why a downstream filter drain is provided to draw it back down.

questions.stem: Secondary compression of a clay occurs:
options: At constant effective stress, after primary consolidation is complete
Only under a rapidly applied load
Simultaneously with the expulsion of air from the voids
questions.solution:
**At constant effective stress, AFTER primary consolidation is complete.**

**The three components of total settlement:**

| Component | Cause | Timescale | Dominant in |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Immediate (elastic)** | Distortion at constant volume | **During construction** | **Sand and gravel** |
| **Primary consolidation** | **Expulsion of pore WATER**; effective stress rising | **Months to years** | **Saturated clay** |
| **Secondary compression (creep)** | **Creep of the soil STRUCTURE at CONSTANT effective stress** | **Years to decades** | **Organic and highly plastic** soils, peat |

> **Total settlement = immediate + primary consolidation + secondary compression**

**The defining feature of secondary compression is that the EFFECTIVE STRESS IS NO LONGER CHANGING.** Primary consolidation ends when the excess pore pressure has fully dissipated and σ′ has risen by the whole of the applied increment. Yet the soil **continues to compress** — slowly, and without any further change in σ′ — because the **soil structure itself creeps**: particles reorient, adsorbed water films are squeezed, and inter-particle bonds slowly adjust.

That is why it is also called **creep**, and why it cannot be accelerated by drainage: there is no water to expel and no gradient to drive it.

**Quantified by the secondary compression index:**

> **C_α = Δe / Δ(log t)**,  and  **S_s = (C_α H/(1 + e_p)) log₁₀(t₂/t₁)**

Note that the settlement is **linear in the LOGARITHM of time** — so it never quite stops, but each successive doubling of time produces the same increment. That is why it is significant over decades in a structure's life while being negligible over a few months.

**When it matters:**

| Soil | C_α/C_c ratio | Significance |
|---|---|---|
| Inorganic clay | 0.04 | Usually **minor** |
| Silt | 0.04 | Minor |
| **Organic clay** | **0.05** | Significant |
| **PEAT** | **0.06 and above** | **Dominant** — can exceed the primary settlement |

**In peat and highly organic soils, secondary compression can exceed the primary consolidation settlement** — which is why building on peat is avoided where possible, and why preloading, which accelerates primary consolidation, does **not** solve the problem: the creep continues regardless.

**Why the other options are wrong:**

| Option | Error |
|---|---|
| Before primary begins | It **follows** primary consolidation by definition |
| Only under rapid loading | It occurs under any **sustained** load, however applied |
| With expulsion of **air** | That is **compaction**, an entirely different process in partly saturated soil |

**A practical note on measurement:** the boundary between primary and secondary is identified on the **settlement–log time** curve from the oedometer test, where the steep primary portion gives way to a flatter straight line. Casagrande's construction locates the **end of primary (100% consolidation)** at the intersection of the two, and the slope of the flatter portion gives C_α.

examTip.trick: Primary consolidation is driven by **pore pressure dissipating**; secondary compression is **creep of the soil skeleton** and continues after the excess pore pressure has gone.
examTip.mnemonic: **Primary = water leaving. Secondary = the skeleton slowly rearranging.** Usually minor in inorganic clay, but it can **dominate in PEAT and organic soils** — which is why building on peat is treated as a special problem.

questions.stem: An inverted filter provided at the downstream exit of a hydraulic structure is graded:
options: Fine at the bottom against the soil, becoming coarse upward
Coarse at the bottom, becoming fine upward
With the coarsest material in the middle
questions.solution:
**FINE at the bottom against the soil, becoming COARSE upward.**

Hence the name **inverted** filter — it is the reverse of the intuitive arrangement, and the reason is precise.

**The two requirements it must satisfy simultaneously:**

| Requirement | Achieved by |
|---|---|
| **RETAIN the soil** — prevent particles being carried out by the seepage | The **FINE layer immediately against the soil** |
| **RELIEVE the pressure** — let the water out freely, without building up head | The **COARSE layers above**, offering no resistance |

**So the grading runs fine → coarse in the direction of FLOW**, which for upward seepage at a downstream exit means fine at the bottom and coarse at the top.

A filter graded the other way would either **block** (fine material on top, clogged by the water it must pass) or **fail to retain** (coarse against the soil, whose particles wash straight through).

**The filter criteria** (Terzaghi), where D refers to the **filter** and d to the **protected soil**:

| Criterion | Requirement | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **Retention (piping) criterion** | **D₁₅ < 4 to 5 × d₈₅** | The filter voids are small enough to **retain** the soil particles |
| **Permeability criterion** | **D₁₅ > 4 to 5 × d₁₅** | The filter is **at least 4–5 times more permeable** than the soil, so it does not impede flow |
| Additional | D₅₀ < 25 d₅₀; the filter must not be **gap graded** or **segregate** | — |

**Note that the two criteria pull in OPPOSITE directions** — retention wants the filter fine, permeability wants it coarse — and the design is the band between them. Where the soil is very fine, a **single** filter layer cannot satisfy both against the soil and against the drain, so a **graded filter of two or three layers** is used, each satisfying the criteria against the one beneath.

**Where inverted filters are used:**

| Location | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Downstream of a weir or barrage** | Relieves uplift and prevents **piping** at the exit |
| **Downstream toe of an earth dam** | Controls the phreatic line and prevents internal erosion |
| **Behind a retaining wall** | Drains the backfill, preventing hydrostatic pressure |
| Around a **subsurface drain pipe** | Prevents fines clogging the perforations |
| Under **riprap** and slope protection | Prevents the bank material washing out through the joints |

**Geotextiles** are the modern alternative, performing the same two functions in a single manufactured layer: the fabric's **pore size** retains the soil while its **permittivity** passes the water. They are quicker to install and require no grading, but their long-term behaviour depends on **not clogging** — which is why the fabric must be selected against the soil's grading, exactly as a granular filter would be.

**A launching apron of loose stone** is usually placed over the filter at a river structure, so that as the bed scours the stone **launches down the developing slope** and continues to protect the filter beneath.

examTip.trap: The grading direction is easy to reverse under pressure, and reversing it makes the filter useless.
examTip.trick: The filter must be **fine enough to hold the soil in** and **coarse enough to let water out**. Two criteria, both required: **D₁₅(filter)/D₈₅(soil) < 4–5** and **D₁₅(filter)/D₁₅(soil) > 4–5**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fine against the soil, coarse against the drain.** Get it upside down and the soil pipes straight through.

questions.stem: The coefficient of consolidation c_v has the dimensions of:
questions.solution:
**Area per unit time** — typically **cm²/s** or **m²/year**.

**Check it from the definition:**

> **c_v = k / (m_v γ_w)**

| Quantity | Dimensions |
|---|---|
| k (permeability) | **L/T** |
| m_v (coefficient of volume change) | **1/(F/L²)** = L²/F |
| γ_w (unit weight of water) | **F/L³** |

> c_v = (L/T) ÷ [(L²/F)(F/L³)] = (L/T) ÷ (1/L) = **L²/T** ✓

And it is confirmed by the time factor being dimensionless: **T_v = c_v t/d²** requires c_v to have dimensions of **length² / time**.

**The consolidation parameters as a set**, since questions often ask which is which:

| Parameter | Symbol | Definition | Units | Governs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Compression index** | **C_c** | Slope of the **virgin** portion of the **e – log σ′** curve | Dimensionless | **HOW MUCH** settlement |
| Recompression index | C_r | Slope of the reloading curve | Dimensionless | Settlement below σ′_c |
| **Coefficient of compressibility** | **a_v** | −de/dσ′ | m²/kN | — |
| **Coefficient of volume change** | **m_v** | a_v/(1 + e₀) | **m²/kN** | Settlement per unit stress per unit thickness |
| **Coefficient of consolidation** | **c_v** | **k/(m_v γ_w)** | **m²/year** | **HOW FAST** — the rate |
| Secondary compression index | C_α | Δe/Δ(log t) | Dimensionless | Creep |

**The essential division is between MAGNITUDE and RATE:**

> **C_c (or m_v) determines HOW MUCH settlement occurs.**
> **c_v determines HOW FAST it occurs.**

A clay may be highly compressible but drain quickly (a silty clay), or only moderately compressible but drain extremely slowly (a plastic clay) — and the two questions are answered by different parameters and different parts of the test data.

**Typical values of c_v:**

| Soil | c_v (m²/year) |
|---|---|
| **Highly plastic clay** | **0.3 – 1** |
| Medium clay | 1 – 10 |
| Silty clay | 10 – 50 |
| **Sandy silt** | **> 100** |

**Note the enormous range**, which follows from c_v being proportional to **k** — and permeability spans ten orders of magnitude across soils. It is why a settlement that takes six months in one deposit takes fifty years in another.

**Determining c_v from the oedometer test:**

| Method | Fitting point |
|---|---|
| **Casagrande's log-time** method | **T_v = 0.197 at U = 50%** |
| **Taylor's √time** method | **T_v = 0.848 at U = 90%** |

The two commonly give somewhat different values, which is an honest reflection of real clay not exactly obeying the idealised theory — and a reason to treat c_v as an estimate with a range rather than a precise constant. Field values back-calculated from observed settlement are frequently **several times higher** than laboratory values, because the laboratory specimen lacks the fissures and silt partings that provide drainage in the field.

examTip.trick: Read it off the formula: **T_v = c_v t/d²**, and T_v is dimensionless, so c_v must be **d²/t** — length squared over time, that is **m²/year**.
examTip.mnemonic: **c_v says how FAST; m_v and C_c say how MUCH.** Keeping those two questions apart is the organising idea of consolidation — a clay can be very compressible yet drain quickly, or barely compressible yet take decades.

questions.stem: Above the water table, capillary action produces pore water pressures that are:
options: Negative, and therefore increase the effective stress
Positive, and therefore reduce the effective stress
Negative, and therefore reduce the effective stress
questions.solution:
**Negative, and therefore INCREASE the effective stress.**

**The reasoning follows directly from σ′ = σ − u.** Above the water table, capillary action holds water in the pores under **tension**, so **u is NEGATIVE**. Subtracting a negative quantity **increases** σ′:

> **σ′ = σ − (−u) = σ + |u|**

**Capillary rise** in a soil is governed by the same relation as in a tube, with the pore size in place of the tube diameter:

> **h_c = 4σ_s cos θ/(γ_w d)**, or approximately **h_c ≈ C/(e·D₁₀)**

| Soil | Capillary rise |
|---|---|
| **Coarse sand** | **0.03 – 0.15 m** |
| Medium sand | 0.12 – 1.1 m |
| Fine sand | 0.3 – 3.5 m |
| Silt | 1.5 – 12 m |
| **Clay** | **> 10 m** |

**Finer soils give greater capillary rise**, because rise is inversely proportional to the pore size — and clay's pores are minute.

**The practical consequences of that negative pressure:**

| Effect | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **APPARENT COHESION** in damp sand | The suction holds the grains together, so a damp sand **stands in a vertical cut** — a sandcastle |
| **Bulking of sand** | Moisture films push the grains apart, increasing the volume by **20–40%** |
| **Increased effective stress** and hence strength | Temporarily |
| **FROST HEAVE** | Capillary water drawn up to a freezing front forms **ice lenses** that lift the pavement |
| Damp in masonry | Rising damp through the fine pores |

**The apparent cohesion is TEMPORARY and unreliable**, which is the professional point:

> A trench in damp sand standing unsupported is held by **suction alone**. It collapses **without warning** if the sand **dries out** (the suction disappears) **or is flooded** (the suction is destroyed). Neither event is under the excavator's control.

That is why **temporary works design never relies on apparent cohesion in a granular soil**, and why trench collapses kill people who saw the sides standing perfectly well the previous day.

**Frost heave** deserves note for high-altitude Nepali roads: water is **drawn upward by capillarity to a freezing front**, where it forms **ice lenses** that grow and lift the surface. The requirements for it are a **frost-susceptible soil (silt is the worst)**, a **water source within capillary reach**, and **freezing temperatures**. Remove any one and the problem disappears — which is why the standard remedies are a **non-frost-susceptible granular capping** and **lowering the water table**, rather than any attempt to prevent the freezing.

**Above the capillary fringe** the soil is partly saturated and the pore pressure is governed by **matric suction**, which is the subject of unsaturated soil mechanics — a field beyond this syllabus but the correct framework for the slope stability of the partly saturated hillside soils that fail in Nepal's monsoon.

examTip.trick: Water above the table is held in **tension** by the menisci, so u is negative. Since **σ′ = σ − u**, a negative u makes **σ′ greater than σ**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Suction makes soil stronger — until it is wetted.** That is exactly the apparent cohesion holding a sandcastle or a trench face in damp sand, and it vanishes completely on saturation. Many trench collapses follow rain for this reason.

questions.stem: In a flow net, the head loss between two successive equipotential lines is:
options: Proportional to the distance between them
Greatest where the flow channel is widest
questions.solution:
**The same between every pair.**

A flow net is constructed so that the **total head drop H is divided into N_d EQUAL parts**, one for each equipotential drop:

> **Head loss per drop = H / N_d**

That equality is a **construction rule of the net**, not a property of the soil — the equipotentials are drawn where they are precisely so that each interval carries the same head loss.

**The consequences follow immediately, and they are what makes the net useful:**

| Because the head drop is equal everywhere | It follows that |
|---|---|
| **Where the fields are SHORT** (equipotentials close together) | The **hydraulic gradient i = Δh/Δl is HIGH** |
| **Where the fields are LONG** | The gradient is **low** |
| **The gradient is greatest where the net is most crowded** | Which is at the **DOWNSTREAM EXIT**, near the toe of a sheet pile |

**So option (a) has the relation backwards**: the head loss is the same regardless of the distance, and it is the **GRADIENT** — head loss per unit length — that varies with the distance. Where the equipotentials crowd together, the same head is lost over a shorter path, so the gradient rises.

**That is why the flow net is read for danger at the DOWNSTREAM EXIT.** The crowding there gives the highest gradient, and it is the **exit gradient** that governs **piping** — as Khosla established.

> **Exit gradient G_E = (H/N_d) / Δl_last**, where Δl_last is the length of the last field at the exit.

**The parallel property for flow channels:**

| Property | Consequence |
|---|---|
| The **discharge in every flow channel is EQUAL** (= q/N_f) | Where the channel **narrows**, the **velocity increases** |
| The fields are **curvilinear SQUARES** | So the two properties are consistent — equal Δq and equal Δh together require b ≈ l in each field |

**The square-field requirement is what ties the construction together**, and it is worth seeing why. For a field of width b and length l, the discharge is **Δq = k(Δh/l)b**. For Δq and Δh to be the same in every field, **b/l must be constant** — and it is conventionally taken as **1**, giving curvilinear squares. That single choice makes the net drawable by eye and the formula q = kH(N_f/N_d) valid.

**Computing the pore pressure at a point** uses the same equal-drop property: if a point lies after **n_d** drops from the upstream boundary,

> **Total head at the point h = h_upstream − n_d (H/N_d)**
> **Pore pressure u = γ_w (h − z)**, with z the elevation of the point

which is how the **uplift pressure diagram** beneath a dam or weir floor is constructed — reading the number of drops at successive points along the base and converting each to a pressure.

examTip.trick: It is true by construction — the net is drawn so each field is a curvilinear square, which forces equal head drops. Each drop is **Δh = H/N_d**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Equal drops, equal flows.** Where the fields get **small**, the gradient is **steep** — which is why the smallest field at the downstream exit is where piping is checked.

questions.stem: For a saturated clay tested under undrained conditions, the angle of shearing resistance is:
options: Zero, so the strength is independent of the confining pressure
Equal to the effective angle of friction
Equal to the angle of repose
questions.solution:
**Zero, so the strength is independent of the confining pressure.**

> **For a saturated clay under undrained conditions: φ_u = 0, and τ = c_u**

**Why φ_u = 0.** In an undrained test on a **saturated** soil no water can leave, so the **volume cannot change**. Applying a higher cell pressure therefore raises the **pore pressure by the same amount** (Skempton's B = 1), leaving the **effective stress unchanged**. Since strength depends only on effective stress, the measured strength is the same whatever the cell pressure — and the **total-stress Mohr circles all have the same diameter**, giving a **horizontal** failure envelope, that is φ_u = 0.

**The two limiting cases that cover most examination problems:**

| Soil | Parameters | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **Pure sand (cohesionless)** | **c = 0**, τ = σ′ tan φ | Strength is **ZERO at zero confinement** — sand cannot stand in a vertical cut |
| **Saturated clay, undrained** | **φ_u = 0**, τ = c_u | Strength is **INDEPENDENT of confinement** — clay can stand vertically for a while |

That pair explains a great deal of practice: a trench in sand collapses immediately unless supported, while one in stiff clay stands unsupported — until it softens.

**The critical distinction, and a serious error if missed:**

> **φ_u = 0 is the UNDRAINED, TOTAL-STRESS angle. The EFFECTIVE angle φ′ for a clay is NOT zero** — it is typically **20° to 30°**.

Confusing them makes the long-term strength of a clay vanish, which is both wrong and dangerously unconservative for a cutting or a permanent slope.

**Consequences of φ_u = 0:**

| Result | Expression |
|---|---|
| Unconfined compressive strength | **q_u = 2 c_u** |
| Failure plane | At **45°** to the major principal plane |
| Bearing capacity factors | **N_c = 5.14 (Prandtl) or 5.7 (Terzaghi)**, **N_q = 1**, **N_γ = 0** |
| Bearing capacity of clay | **INDEPENDENT of footing width** |

**The last is a striking consequence** and is examined directly: since N_γ = 0, the width term disappears from Terzaghi's equation, so **widening a footing on clay does not increase the pressure it can carry** — only the total load. On sand, where c = 0 and the width term dominates, it does.

**Consistency of clay by undrained strength:**

| c_u (kPa) | Description | Field test |
|---|---|---|
| < 12 | **Very soft** | Squeezes between the fingers |
| 12 – 25 | Soft | Easily moulded |
| 25 – 50 | Medium | Moulded by strong pressure |
| 50 – 100 | **Stiff** | Indented by the thumb |
| 100 – 200 | Very stiff | Indented by the thumbnail |
| > 200 | **Hard** | Difficult to indent |

examTip.trick: Under undrained loading a saturated clay cannot change volume, so the extra confining pressure goes **entirely into pore pressure**. The effective stress is unchanged, so the strength is unchanged — the Mohr envelope is **horizontal**.
examTip.mnemonic: **φ_u = 0 for saturated clay, undrained.** All Mohr circles have the same diameter, and **c_u = q_u/2**. Note this is a property of the TEST, not of the clay — the same clay has a real φ′ of 20–30° in drained terms.

questions.stem: In a soil with an angle of internal friction φ, the failure plane is inclined to the major principal plane at:
questions.solution:
**45° + φ/2.**

From the geometry of **Mohr's circle**, the point of tangency with the Mohr–Coulomb envelope lies at an angle **2θ = 90° + φ** from the major principal stress point — so the failure plane is at **θ = 45° + φ/2** to the **major principal plane**.

**Note carefully what the angle is measured FROM.** It is **45° + φ/2 from the MAJOR PRINCIPAL PLANE**, which in a triaxial test is the **horizontal** plane (since σ₁ is vertical). So the failure plane appears in the specimen inclined at that angle **to the horizontal**.

**The corresponding principal stress relation:**

> **σ₁ = σ₃ tan²(45° + φ/2) + 2c tan(45° + φ/2)**

where **tan²(45° + φ/2) = (1 + sin φ)/(1 − sin φ) = K_p**, the coefficient of passive earth pressure — which is not a coincidence, since passive failure is exactly this condition.

**Two special cases worth carrying:**

| Soil | φ | Failure plane |
|---|---|---|
| **Saturated clay, undrained** | **φ_u = 0** | **45°** — and **σ₁ − σ₃ = 2c_u**, so **q_u = 2c_u** |
| **Dense sand** | 40° | **65°** |
| Loose sand | 30° | 60° |

**The φ = 0 case is why an unconfined compression specimen of clay fails on a plane at 45°**, which is readily observed in the laboratory and is a quick check that the test behaved as expected.

**Why the failure plane is NOT at 45°** for a frictional soil — the physical reason is worth understanding. On a plane at 45° the **shear stress is greatest**, so a purely cohesive material fails there. But in a frictional material, a plane with slightly **lower shear stress but much lower normal stress** may be closer to failure, because the available strength (c + σ tan φ) falls with the normal stress. The failure plane therefore **rotates away from 45°** by exactly φ/2, balancing the two effects.

**Related results from Mohr's circle:**

| Quantity | Expression |
|---|---|
| **τ_max** | **(σ₁ − σ₂)/2**, on planes at **45°** |
| Normal stress on the failure plane | σ_n = (σ₁+σ₃)/2 + [(σ₁−σ₃)/2]cos 2θ |
| Shear stress on the failure plane | τ = [(σ₁−σ₃)/2] sin 2θ |

**Note that τ_max does NOT act on the failure plane** when φ ≠ 0 — the maximum shear stress is at 45°, while failure occurs at 45° + φ/2. The soil fails where the **ratio of shear stress to available strength** is greatest, not where the shear stress alone is greatest, and that distinction is the substance of the Mohr–Coulomb criterion.

examTip.trap: 45° is the standing wrong answer — correct only for **φ = 0** (saturated clay, undrained). For any frictional soil the plane is steeper.
examTip.trick: Read it off Mohr's circle: the failure point sits at **2θ = 90 + φ** from the σ axis, so **θ = 45 + φ/2**. For φ = 30°, the plane is at **60°**.
examTip.mnemonic: **45 + φ/2.** Friction rotates the failure plane steeper than the pure-shear 45°.

questions.stem: The consolidated undrained (CU) triaxial test with pore pressure measurement is appropriate for modelling:
options: The end-of-construction condition of a rapidly built embankment
The long-term stability of a permanent cutting
Sudden drawdown of a reservoir behind an earth dam
The compaction of a fill in layers
questions.solution:
**Sudden drawdown of a reservoir behind an earth dam.**

**The choice of test is a MODELLING decision, not a laboratory preference** — the question is whether the field loading is **fast or slow relative to the soil's drainage**.

| Test | Consolidation | Shearing | Models |
|---|---|---|---|
| **UU** (unconsolidated undrained) | **None** | **Undrained**, fast | **END OF CONSTRUCTION** — an embankment built quickly on soft clay, before any consolidation |
| **CU** (consolidated undrained, with u measured) | **Full**, under σ₃ | Undrained | **SUDDEN LOADING or DRAWDOWN after the soil has consolidated** |
| **CD** (consolidated drained) | Full | **Drained**, very slow | **LONG-TERM** stability — a permanent cutting or natural slope |

**Why CU fits sudden drawdown exactly.** The upstream slope of an earth dam has been submerged for years, so the soil has **fully consolidated** under the reservoir. Then the reservoir is **drawn down rapidly** — the loading changes far faster than the low-permeability fill can drain, so the response is **undrained**. Consolidated, then sheared undrained: precisely the CU condition.

**Why sudden drawdown is so severe** is worth stating, because it explains why the upstream slope is often the flatter one:

> During drawdown the **external water pressure supporting the slope is removed**, while the **pore pressures inside the fill remain high**. The slope therefore carries the **full weight of saturated soil with high internal pore pressure and no external support** — the worst possible combination.

**The critical condition for each slope of an earth dam:**

| Slope | Critical condition |
|---|---|
| **UPSTREAM** | **SUDDEN DRAWDOWN** |
| **DOWNSTREAM** | **STEADY SEEPAGE** at full reservoir |
| Both | **End of construction** (high construction pore pressures in a clay core) |
| Both | **Earthquake**, combined with the above |

**The general rule for which case governs**, which is the most useful thing in the topic:

> For a **LOADED** clay (a foundation, an embankment), the **SHORT-TERM undrained** case is critical — because consolidation subsequently **STRENGTHENS** the soil.
> For an **UNLOADED** clay (a cutting, an excavation), the **LONG-TERM drained** case is critical — because swelling subsequently **WEAKENS** it.

That asymmetry explains a real and dangerous phenomenon: **cuttings in clay can fail years after construction**, when the negative pore pressures generated by unloading have finally dissipated and the effective stresses have fallen to their long-term values. The slope that stood perfectly well for a decade fails in the eleventh year, and nothing visible changed.

**Why the triaxial test is the most versatile:** it **controls drainage** and can **measure pore pressure**, so it yields **either total or effective** stress parameters as required. The **direct shear box** can do neither, and it forces failure on a **predetermined plane** which may not be the weakest.

examTip.trick: Match the test to the drainage history of the real problem. **UU** = load applied fast on a soil that has not consolidated (end of construction). **CU** = soil consolidated under one condition, then loaded fast (drawdown, staged construction). **CD** = everything slow (long-term slope stability).
examTip.mnemonic: **Sudden drawdown: the dam has consolidated under the full reservoir, then the water disappears in hours.** Consolidated, then undrained — CU exactly.

questions.stem: The unconfined compressive strength q_u of a saturated clay is related to its undrained cohesion c_u by:
questions.solution:
**q_u = 2 c_u**, so **c_u = q_u/2**.

**The derivation is immediate from the φ = 0 condition.** In an unconfined compression test the **confining pressure σ₃ = 0** and the axial stress at failure is σ₁ = q_u. With φ_u = 0 the failure envelope is **horizontal at τ = c_u**, and the Mohr circle of radius (σ₁ − σ₃)/2 must be tangent to it:

> **(q_u − 0)/2 = c_u**, hence **q_u = 2 c_u** ∎

The same follows from the general relation σ₁ = σ₃ tan²(45+φ/2) + 2c tan(45+φ/2) with σ₃ = 0 and φ = 0.

**The unconfined compression test:**

| Detail | Value |
|---|---|
| Specimen | Cylindrical, **height ≈ 2 × diameter** |
| Confining pressure | **ZERO** — the specimen stands unsupported |
| Rate of strain | 0.5 – 2% per minute |
| Failure | At the peak load, or at **20% axial strain** if no peak occurs |
| Correction | The **area increases** as the specimen shortens: **A = A₀/(1 − ε)** |

**The area correction is the step most often omitted**, and it matters: at 15% strain the area has increased by nearly 18%, so using the original area **overstates the stress** by that amount.

**Its limitations, which define where it can be used:**

| Limitation | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Applies ONLY to saturated CLAY** | A specimen must stand unsupported, which sand cannot |
| **Gives total-stress c_u only** | No effective stress parameters |
| Assumes **φ_u = 0** | Valid only for full saturation |
| **Not suitable for fissured clay** | The specimen fails on a fissure, understating the strength |
| Not suitable for very soft clay | The specimen cannot stand |

**Its virtues** are that it is **quick, cheap and needs no cell** — which is why it remains the routine test for the undrained strength of a clay, and why the **pocket penetrometer** and **torvane**, which correlate with it, are standard site tools for a rapid check.

**Its most valuable use is measuring SENSITIVITY:**

> **S_t = q_u(undisturbed) / q_u(remoulded)**

run on the same soil at the same water content, before and after remoulding. A high sensitivity warns that the clay will lose most of its strength if disturbed — by pile driving, by excavation, or by an earthquake.

**The alternative in the field** is the **vane shear test**, which gives c_u in situ:

> **c_u = T / [π D²(H/2 + D/6)]**

and is preferred for **soft, sensitive** clays precisely because it avoids the disturbance of sampling — the soil is tested where it lies.

examTip.trick: In the unconfined test the cell pressure is zero, so σ₃ = 0 and σ₁ = q_u. With **φ_u = 0** the Mohr circle's radius is c_u, and the radius is q_u/2.
examTip.mnemonic: **c_u = q_u/2 — halve it.** Consistency bands: very soft below 25 kPa, soft 25–50, medium 50–100, stiff 100–200, very stiff above 200.

questions.stem: The stability of an infinite slope in a dry cohesionless soil depends on:
options: The height of the slope only
The slope angle and the angle of internal friction only
The height and the unit weight
questions.solution:
**The slope angle and the angle of internal friction only.**

> **F = tan φ / tan β**

where β is the slope angle. The slope is **stable while β < φ**, and — the striking result —

> **The stability of a dry cohesionless slope is INDEPENDENT OF ITS HEIGHT.**

**Why height does not appear.** Consider an element of the slope. Both the **driving force** (the down-slope component of its weight) and the **resisting force** (friction, proportional to the normal component of the same weight) are **proportional to the weight**. The weight therefore **cancels** in the ratio — and with it the depth, the unit weight and the height all disappear:

> F = (W cos β tan φ)/(W sin β) = **tan φ / tan β** ∎

So a sand slope at its **angle of repose** is equally stable whether it is 1 m or 100 m high, which is why a sand pile always forms the same cone angle however much sand is added.

**The contrast with a COHESIVE slope is the point of the question:**

| Slope | Stability depends on |
|---|---|
| **Cohesionless (c = 0)** | **β and φ only — NOT the height** |
| **Cohesive (c > 0)** | **β, φ, c, γ AND the HEIGHT** |

A cohesive slope is **height-dependent** because cohesion provides a strength that does **not** scale with the weight — so as the slope grows, the driving force grows while the cohesive resistance per unit area does not.

> **Taylor's stability number S_n = c/(F γ H)** captures exactly that, and it is why a clay cutting has a **critical height** while a sand slope does not.

**The effect of SEEPAGE**, which is what makes this practically important:

> With **seepage parallel to the slope** (the monsoon condition), **F = (γ′/γ_sat)(tan φ/tan β)**

and since **γ′/γ_sat ≈ 0.5**, the factor of safety is **roughly HALVED**.

That single result is the quantitative reason **so many granular hill slopes fail in the monsoon**: a slope standing comfortably at F = 1.6 in the dry season falls to F = 0.8 when the water table rises to the surface and seepage runs parallel to it. Nothing about the soil has changed — only the water.

**With seepage EMERGING from the slope** (flow at an angle out of the face), the position is worse still, because the seepage force has a component directly down-slope.

**The practical conclusions:**

| Measure | Effect |
|---|---|
| **DRAINAGE** — surface, catch water, sub-horizontal drains | **Removes the water**, restoring the dry-case factor of safety. **The most effective and cheapest measure** |
| Flattening the slope | Reduces tan β |
| Toe weighting | Adds resistance |
| Vegetation | Interception, transpiration, root reinforcement |

**Drainage first, always** — it addresses the actual trigger, costs least, and acts on the whole mass rather than a local strip.

examTip.trick: For an infinite slope in dry sand, **F = tan φ/tan β** — the height cancels out entirely and the depth of the slip surface is irrelevant.
examTip.mnemonic: **Dry sand stands at its angle of repose, whatever its height.** A sand slope is stable if β < φ and unstable if β > φ, full stop. Add seepage parallel to the slope and F is roughly **halved** — which is why sand slopes fail in the monsoon.

questions.stem: The critical height of an unsupported vertical cut in a purely cohesive soil is:
questions.solution:
**H_c = 4c/γ.**

From the **Rankine active earth pressure** distribution in a cohesive soil:

> **p_a = K_a γ z − 2c√K_a**,  and for **φ = 0** (so K_a = 1): **p_a = γz − 2c**

The pressure is **negative (tensile) near the top** and becomes positive below. Setting the **net thrust to zero** — the condition for the cut to stand unsupported — the positive and negative areas must balance, which gives

> **H_c = 4c/γ**  (in general, **H_c = 4c/(γ√K_a)**)

**Two related depths, and confusing them is the standard error:**

| Depth | Expression | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **Tension crack depth z₀** | **2c/γ** | The depth to which the pressure is **negative**, so a **crack opens** |
| **Critical height H_c** | **4c/γ** | The height at which the **total thrust becomes zero** — the cut just stands |

So the **critical height is exactly TWICE the tension crack depth**, which is a useful check.

**A worked case.** A stiff clay with c_u = 50 kPa and γ = 19 kN/m³:

> **H_c = 4 × 50/19 = 10.5 m**

which is why a trench in stiff clay stands unsupported to several metres — and why that fact is so dangerous.

**The professional warning is the substance of this question**, and it deserves stating plainly:

> **H_c is a THEORETICAL LIMIT with a factor of safety of ONE.** It assumes the soil is homogeneous, that c_u does not change, and that no tension crack fills with water. **None of those holds for long.**

What actually happens:

| Change | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Rain fills the tension crack** | Adds a **full hydrostatic thrust** exactly where the soil is weakest |
| **The clay SOFTENS** as it absorbs water | c_u falls, so H_c falls |
| **Desiccation cracks** open in dry weather | Then admit water rapidly at the next rain |
| **Vibration** from plant or traffic | Reduces the effective strength |
| **Surcharge** at the crest — spoil, plant, stacked material | Increases the driving force |

So a trench standing perfectly well in the morning can collapse in the afternoon, **without warning**, and trench collapse kills more construction workers than almost any other single cause.

**Practice therefore does not rely on H_c:**

> **Excavations deeper than about 1.2 m are SUPPORTED**, regardless of how well the sides appear to stand — by **timbering, sheeting, trench boxes, or battering** to a safe slope.

A design factor of safety of at least **1.5** would in any case reduce the permitted unsupported height to about 7 m in the worked example, and the practical rules cut it far below that.

**Taylor's stability number** generalises the result to a sloping cut:

> **S_n = c/(F γ H)**

read from charts against the slope angle and depth factor — the systematic method where the vertical-cut formula does not apply.

examTip.trick: **H_c = 4c/γ**, which is exactly **twice** the depth of the tension crack, 2c/γ. Deriving it from the Rankine active pressure diagram is one line: the negative and positive areas balance at that depth.
examTip.mnemonic: **4c over gamma — and halve it for the tension crack.** In practice a factor of safety is applied, so an unsupported cut is limited to about **H_c/2**.

questions.stem: Compared with the ordinary method of slices, Bishop's simplified method:
options: Satisfies vertical equilibrium of each slice and is more accurate
Ignores the weight of the slices
Gives a lower factor of safety
questions.solution:
**It satisfies vertical equilibrium of each slice and is more accurate.**

**The method of slices** divides the assumed failure mass above a trial circular surface into vertical slices, and takes **moments about the centre of the circle**:

> **F = Σ(c′Δl + N′ tan φ′) / Σ(W sin α)**

where N′ is the effective normal force on the base of each slice and α its inclination.

**The difficulty is that the problem is statically INDETERMINATE**: the **inter-slice forces** (the forces each slice exerts on its neighbours) are unknown, and different assumptions about them give different methods.

| Method | Assumption about inter-slice forces | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **Ordinary / Fellenius (Swedish)** | **IGNORED entirely** | Simplest; **CONSERVATIVE** — underestimates F, sometimes by 10–20% |
| **BISHOP'S SIMPLIFIED** | Resultant inter-slice force is **HORIZONTAL** — satisfies **vertical equilibrium** of each slice | **More accurate**; the standard method |
| Janbu | Satisfies force equilibrium | For non-circular surfaces |
| **Morgenstern–Price, Spencer** | Satisfy **all** equilibrium conditions | Rigorous; used in software |

**Bishop's method requires ITERATION**, because F appears on both sides of its equation:

> **F = (1/Σ W sin α) × Σ[(c′b + (W − ub)tan φ′)/m_α]**,  where **m_α = cos α(1 + tan α tan φ′/F)**

A value of F is assumed, the right side evaluated, and the process repeated until it converges — usually within three or four cycles. That iterative requirement is what made the method impractical before calculators, and why the cruder Fellenius method was used for so long.

**Option (d) is the trap**: the **ordinary** method gives the **lower** (more conservative) factor of safety, not Bishop's. Bishop's is more accurate, and because Fellenius under-estimates, **Bishop's usually gives a HIGHER F** — which means using Fellenius is safe but wasteful.

**Points that apply to every slice method:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Many trial circles must be tried** | The analysis is a **SEARCH for the critical circle**, not a single calculation — which is why it is done by software |
| The **critical circle** gives the lowest F | It must be located, not assumed |
| **Total or effective stress** must be chosen to match the case | Undrained (φ = 0) for short term; effective for long term |
| **Pore pressure** enters through **u** or the ratio **r_u = u/γh** | From a flow net or from piezometers |
| **Non-circular surfaces** may govern | Where a weak layer exists — then Janbu or a wedge analysis is used |

**Types of failure surface**, distinguished by where they emerge:

| Type | Surface |
|---|---|
| **Face (slope) failure** | Emerges **above** the toe |
| **Toe failure** | Passes **through** the toe |
| **Base failure** | Passes **below** the toe, through the foundation soil |

**Base failure** occurs where a **weak stratum underlies** the slope, and it is the most damaging because it mobilises a much larger mass — which is exactly the case a purely circular search through the slope body would miss if the weak layer were not modelled.

**Minimum factors of safety**: **1.5** for the long-term steady case, **1.2 to 1.3** for transient cases such as **sudden drawdown** or **seismic** loading — the lower value being accepted because those conditions are short-lived and their loading is already conservatively estimated.

examTip.trick: The ordinary (Fellenius) method ignores the interslice forces entirely and is **conservative by 10–20%**. Bishop satisfies vertical equilibrium of each slice, which recovers most of that.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fellenius is simple and pessimistic; Bishop is iterative and closer to the truth.** Bishop needs iteration because F appears on both sides of its equation.

questions.stem: Liquefaction during an earthquake is most likely in:
options: Dense gravel above the water table
questions.solution:
**Loose, saturated, fine sand.**

**The mechanism, in four steps:**

1. **Cyclic shearing** from the earthquake tries to **densify** the loose sand.
2. Because the sand is **saturated** and the loading is **rapid**, the water **cannot escape** in time.
3. The tendency to contract is therefore transferred to the water, and the **pore pressure RISES** cycle by cycle.
4. When **u reaches the total stress, σ′ = 0** — and by Terzaghi's principle the soil has **no shear strength at all**. It behaves as a **heavy liquid**.

**The four conditions that must ALL be present:**

| Condition | Why |
|---|---|
| **LOOSE** (low relative density) | A **dense** sand **dilates** on shearing, which generates **negative** pore pressure and makes it stronger, not weaker |
| **SATURATED** | Dry or partly saturated soil has air in the voids, which compresses harmlessly — no pore pressure builds |
| **Fine to medium SAND**, uniformly graded | Fine enough that water cannot drain quickly; coarse enough to be cohesionless. **Gravel drains too fast; clay has cohesion** |
| **Cyclic (earthquake) loading** | Repeated reversals are what accumulate the pore pressure |

**Each option in the question fails a different condition**, which is why the set is instructive: dense gravel fails **loose** and **fine** and **saturated**; stiff clay fails **cohesionless** and **loose**; dry sand fails **saturated**.

**Dilatancy is the reason density matters so much**, and it is worth understanding rather than memorising:

| Sand | On shearing it tries to | Pore pressure | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| **LOOSE** | **CONTRACT** | **RISES** | **Weakens — liquefaction** |
| **DENSE** | **DILATE (expand)** | **FALLS (negative)** | **Strengthens** |

A dense sand must expand to shear, because the grains have to ride over one another. In undrained conditions that expansion sucks the pore pressure **down**, raising σ′ and making the sand temporarily **stronger** — the opposite of liquefaction.

**Consequences of liquefaction:**

| Effect | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Loss of bearing capacity** | Buildings **sink, tilt or overturn** — often intact, having simply lost their support |
| **FLOTATION** of buried structures | Empty tanks, pipes and manholes **float up** through the liquefied soil |
| **Lateral spreading** | The ground moves sideways on a gentle slope or toward a free face |
| **Sand boils** | Water and sand ejected at the surface |
| Settlement | On re-consolidation after the event |

**Nepal's context makes this a first-order concern.** The **Kathmandu Valley is a former lake basin** filled with **young, loose, saturated fine sediments** and has a **shallow water table** — the combination liquefaction requires. **Widespread liquefaction occurred in the 2015 Gorkha earthquake**, and **NBC 105:2020** requires liquefaction assessment for susceptible sites.

**Assessment** is normally by the **simplified (Seed–Idriss) procedure**, comparing the **Cyclic Stress Ratio (CSR)** imposed by the design earthquake with the **Cyclic Resistance Ratio (CRR)** of the soil, estimated from the corrected **SPT N-value** or the CPT cone resistance. A factor of safety below about 1.2 indicates a liquefiable layer.

**Mitigation:**

| Measure | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Densification** — vibro-compaction, dynamic compaction, **stone columns** | Raises the relative density so the sand dilates rather than contracts |
| **Drainage** — stone columns also act as drains | Lets the pore pressure dissipate as fast as it builds |
| **Lowering the water table** | Removes the saturation |
| Grouting, soil mixing | Cements the grains |
| **Deep foundations** through the layer | Avoids the problem rather than solving it |

**Stone columns are the common choice** because they act **both** ways at once — densifying the surrounding sand during installation **and** providing a permanent drainage path.

examTip.trick: Four conditions must coincide: **loose**, **saturated**, **fine sand** (or non-plastic silt), and **cyclic** loading. Remove any one and liquefaction does not occur.
examTip.mnemonic: **Loose sand CONTRACTS on shearing, so pore pressure RISES until σ′ = 0.** Dense sand dilates and generates *negative* pore pressure, which is why it is safe. This is a live concern for the Kathmandu Valley's saturated silty sands.

questions.stem: The direct shear (shear box) test has the disadvantage that it:
options: Cannot be used for cohesionless soils
Forces failure on a predetermined plane and cannot control drainage
Cannot measure the angle of internal friction
questions.solution:
**It forces failure on a predetermined plane and cannot control drainage.**

**The two defects are distinct and both are serious:**

| Defect | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Failure is forced on the PLANE OF THE BOX SPLIT** | That plane **may not be the weakest** in the specimen, so the measured strength can **overestimate** the true value |
| **Drainage cannot be CONTROLLED** | The test is effectively **drained** for sand (fast enough to drain) but **indeterminate** for clay, where neither fully drained nor fully undrained conditions are assured |
| Pore pressure **cannot be measured** | So only **total** stress parameters are obtained for a clay |
| **Stress distribution is non-uniform** | Stress concentrations at the edges of the box |
| The area **changes** during shear | Requiring correction |
| Principal stress **rotation** is uncontrolled | The stress path is not known |

**The comparison with the triaxial test:**

| | **Direct shear box** | **Triaxial** |
|---|---|---|
| Drainage | **NOT controlled** | **Controlled** |
| Pore pressure | **Not measured** | **Measured** |
| Failure plane | **Predetermined** | **Free to develop** on the weakest plane |
| Stress distribution | Non-uniform | Reasonably uniform |
| Effective stress parameters | **Not obtainable** for clay | **Obtainable** |
| **Simplicity and speed** | **Simple, quick, cheap** | Slower, more equipment |
| Suits | **Sand**; residual strength by reversal | **Everything**, especially clay |

**Where the shear box nonetheless remains useful**, and it genuinely does:

| Use | Why the box suits it |
|---|---|
| **SAND** | Drains freely anyway, so the drainage defect does not bite; quick and cheap |
| **RESIDUAL strength of clay** | The box can be **reversed repeatedly**, shearing the same plane over and over until the strength falls to its **residual** value — which a triaxial cannot easily do |
| **Interface friction** — soil against concrete, steel or geotextile | The interface is placed at the split |
| Rapid routine testing | Where a check rather than a design parameter is wanted |

**The residual strength application is the important one**, and it is worth understanding why the box is uniquely suited to it: a **pre-existing slip surface** in a clay slope has already been sheared through a large displacement, so its strength has fallen from **peak** to **residual** — often by a factor of two or more. The box, by reversing, reproduces exactly that large displacement on a single plane. A **ring shear** apparatus does it better still, by shearing continuously in one direction without limit.

**Peak and residual strength** matter for **progressive failure**: a slope containing a pre-existing shear surface must be analysed at **residual** strength, not peak — and using peak parameters on a reactivated landslide is a classic and dangerous error, because the strength that resisted the first movement is no longer there.

**Option (a) is the reverse of the truth**: the shear box is **particularly suitable** for cohesionless soils, and is often the preferred test for sand precisely because sand drains freely and the test is quick.

examTip.trick: The box has to split along its own horizontal plane, which may not be the weakest plane in the soil, and there is no way to seal it — so pore pressure can be neither measured nor controlled.
examTip.mnemonic: **Shear box: cheap, quick, and blind.** Fine for a drained sand test; use the **triaxial** whenever pore pressure matters, which is whenever clay is involved.

questions.stem: In Skempton's pore pressure equation, the parameter B for a fully saturated soil equals:
questions.solution:
**B = 1.0.**

> **Δu = B[Δσ₃ + A(Δσ₁ − Δσ₃)]**

| Parameter | Represents |
|---|---|
| **B** | The response to an **all-round (isotropic)** stress change |
| **A** | The response to the **deviator** stress (σ₁ − σ₃) |

**Why B = 1 for full saturation.** Water is **effectively incompressible** compared with the soil skeleton, so when an all-round pressure is applied to a saturated soil that cannot drain, the **water takes the entire increment**:

> **Δu = Δσ₃**, hence **B = 1** ∎

If **air is present** in the voids, the air **compresses** and absorbs part of the increment, so **B < 1** — falling rapidly as saturation decreases:

| Degree of saturation | B (approximate) |
|---|---|
| **100%** | **1.00** |
| 99% | 0.9 |
| 95% | 0.5 |
| 90% | 0.2 |
| **Dry** | **≈ 0** |

**The practical use of B is as a SATURATION CHECK**, and it is standard laboratory procedure:

> Before shearing a triaxial specimen, the cell pressure is raised and the pore pressure response measured. **If B is significantly below 1, the specimen is NOT fully saturated**, and the test must not proceed.

Saturation is then achieved by applying a **back pressure** — raising the pore pressure and cell pressure together — which dissolves the remaining air into the pore water. B is re-checked until it reaches about **0.95 or better**.

**Skipping the B check invalidates the test**, because an unsaturated specimen behaves quite differently: its pore pressure response is muted, its measured strength is higher, and the φ_u = 0 assumption fails.

**The A parameter** varies with the soil's **stress history and its tendency to contract or dilate**, and its value at failure is diagnostic:

| Soil | A at failure | Behaviour on shearing |
|---|---|---|
| **Very loose sand, sensitive clay** | **+2 to +3** | Strongly **CONTRACTIVE** — large positive pore pressure |
| **Normally consolidated clay** | **+0.5 to +1.0** | Contractive |
| Lightly over-consolidated clay | 0 to +0.5 | — |
| **Heavily over-consolidated clay** | **−0.5 to 0** | **DILATANT** — **negative** pore pressure |
| **Dense sand** | **Negative** | Dilatant |

**A negative A means the soil DILATES on shearing**, sucking the pore pressure down and temporarily **strengthening** itself — which is exactly the behaviour that makes dense sand resistant to liquefaction, and heavily over-consolidated clay strong in the short term but weaker in the long term as those negative pressures dissipate.

**That last point connects to the earlier result about cuttings**: a heavily over-consolidated clay cutting generates **negative** pore pressures on excavation, is therefore **strongest immediately** after being cut, and **weakens for years** as the suctions equalise. It is the mechanism behind delayed failures in clay cuttings, and A is the parameter that quantifies it.

examTip.trick: **Δu = B[Δσ₃ + A(Δσ₁ − Δσ₃)]**. B measures how completely the pore water carries an all-round pressure change; if the voids hold no air, it carries all of it.
examTip.mnemonic: **B = 1 means fully saturated — and checking B is the standard way to CONFIRM saturation before a triaxial test.** The A parameter varies with soil type: about 1 for soft NC clay, and **negative for dense sand**, which dilates.

questions.stem: The most effective and usually the cheapest measure for stabilising an unstable slope is:
options: Drainage to lower the pore water pressure
Constructing a retaining wall at the toe
questions.solution:
**Drainage, to lower the pore water pressure.**

**Why drainage comes first** — the reasoning follows directly from the Mohr–Coulomb criterion:

> **τ = c′ + σ′ tan φ′**, and **σ′ = σ − u**

So **raising u lowers σ′, which lowers the available strength**. Rainfall infiltration is the dominant **trigger** of slope failure precisely because it raises u — and **nothing about the soil itself changes**. Removing the water therefore restores the strength that was there before, which is why drainage is both effective and cheap.

**Its three advantages over every other measure:**

| Advantage | Explanation |
|---|---|
| It addresses the **actual TRIGGER** | Not a symptom, and not a substitute for the strength that was lost |
| It acts on the **WHOLE MASS** | A retaining wall protects only the strip it occupies |
| It is **cheap** | Open drains and catch water drains cost a fraction of any structure |

**Drainage measures:**

| Measure | Function |
|---|---|
| **Catch water (intercepting) drain** above the slope | **Diverts hillside runoff BEFORE it reaches the unstable area** — the single most valuable measure |
| Surface drains, sealing of cracks | Prevents infiltration |
| **Sub-horizontal (bored) drains** | Drain the mass from within, lowering the water table |
| Counterfort / trench drains | Deep drainage trenches filled with granular material |
| **Toe drains** | Relieve pressure at the toe, where it most matters |
| Vertical wells with pumping | Where the mass is large |

**The full range of stabilisation measures**, organised by which side of the stability equation each addresses:

| Category | Measures |
|---|---|
| **Reduce the DRIVING force** | **Flatten** the slope; **bench** it; **remove material from the CREST**; lighten the fill |
| **Increase the RESISTING force** | **Toe weighting** — a berm or buttress; **retaining structures** (gravity wall, gabion, crib, piles); **soil nails and anchors** |
| **Increase the SOIL STRENGTH** | **Drainage** (raises σ′); grouting; lime or cement stabilisation; **vegetation and root reinforcement** |

**Note that removing material from the CREST and adding it at the TOE both help**, while doing the reverse — a common site practice — is precisely what causes failures:

> **Cutting the TOE** (to widen a road) removes the resistance; **loading the CREST** (with spoil or a building) adds to the driving force. Both are routine in Nepali hill construction and both are routine causes of failure.

**Bio-engineering** deserves emphasis for Nepal, where it is promoted by the Department of Roads:

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| Uses **local species and local labour** | Cheap; the skills exist in the community |
| **STRENGTHENS with time** as roots develop | Unlike a structure, which only deteriorates |
| Addresses **both water and reinforcement** | Interception, transpiration, and root reinforcement together |
| Maintainable by the community | Sustainable without an agency |

Its limitations are real: it takes **one or two growing seasons** to become effective, it reinforces only the **shallow** rooted zone, and it needs **protection from grazing** while establishing.

**So the standard practice is a COMBINATION** — **drainage first**, a **structural toe** (gabion or masonry) where the slope is actively attacked, and **bio-engineering on the face above**. Each does what the others cannot, and the sequence reflects both effectiveness and cost.

examTip.trick: Water is almost always the culprit, and **σ′ = σ − u** says why: lowering u raises σ′ and therefore raises the shear strength everywhere on the slip surface at once.
examTip.mnemonic: **Drain it first.** Cheaper than regrading, far cheaper than a retaining structure, and it treats the cause rather than resisting the effect. Surface drains stop infiltration; subsurface drains lower the water table.

questions.stem: The vane shear test is particularly suitable for determining the shear strength of:
questions.solution:
**Soft, sensitive clay in situ.**

> **c_u = T / [π D²(H/2 + D/6)]**

where T is the torque at failure, D the vane diameter and H its height (usually **H = 2D**).

**Why it suits soft sensitive clay above all other tests:**

| Reason | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **The soil is tested WHERE IT LIES** | No sampling, so **no disturbance** — decisive for a **sensitive** clay, which loses most of its strength if remoulded |
| An undisturbed sample **cannot be recovered** from very soft clay | It deforms under its own weight during extrusion |
| The test is **quick and simple** | A profile can be taken at close intervals down a borehole |
| It gives **c_u directly** | No interpretation needed |
| **Sensitivity is measured in the same operation** | By re-shearing after a full rotation |

**Measuring sensitivity is a particular strength of the test**: after the peak torque is recorded, the vane is **rotated rapidly through ten complete revolutions** to remould the soil, and the torque re-measured. The ratio of the two gives

> **S_t = undisturbed strength / remoulded strength**

in a single in-situ operation — something no laboratory test can do without two separate specimens and the disturbance of sampling.

**Why it does NOT suit the other options:**

| Soil | Why the vane fails |
|---|---|
| **Dense gravel** | The vane **cannot be pushed in**, and stones would jam it |
| **Compacted fill** | Too stiff; and the fill is usually granular, where φ not c_u governs |
| **Rock** | Absurd |
| **Stiff or fissured clay** | The vane may **not shear the weakest surface**, and the strength is overestimated |
| **Sand** | Drains during the test, so it is not an undrained measurement |

**Its known limitations**, which are examinable:

| Limitation | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Assumes the soil is **isotropic** | Real clays are **anisotropic**; the vane shears both a vertical cylindrical surface and two horizontal ends, mixing the two strengths |
| Assumes **uniform stress** on the failure surface | Approximate |
| **Rate effects** | The standard rotation rate is slow (0.1°/s); faster rotation gives a higher apparent strength |
| **Over-estimates** the strength for design | Hence **Bjerrum's correction factor μ**, applied to the measured value |

**Bjerrum's correction** deserves note because it is a real and substantial adjustment:

> **c_u(design) = μ × c_u(vane)**, with **μ falling from about 1.0 at PI = 20 to about 0.6 at PI = 100**

It was derived by back-analysing embankment failures on soft clay, which consistently occurred at strengths **lower** than the vane predicted — the discrepancy being greatest for **highly plastic** clays. Applying the vane value uncorrected to a highly plastic clay overestimates its strength by up to 40%.

**The other in-situ strength tests**, for comparison:

| Test | Measures |
|---|---|
| **SPT** | Correlates with **relative density** (sand); **unreliable in soft clay** |
| **CPT** | Continuous profile of cone resistance; c_u from **q_c** by a cone factor |
| **Pressuremeter** | In-situ stress–strain and modulus |
| **Plate load test** | Bearing capacity and settlement, but only to a **shallow** depth |

**The SPT's unreliability in soft clay** is the complementary point: the blow count there is so small (often 0 to 2) that it cannot resolve differences in strength — which is precisely why the vane exists.

examTip.trick: The vane is pushed into the ground and turned, so the clay is **never sampled, transported or trimmed** — which is the whole point for a sensitive clay that would lose most of its strength on handling.
examTip.mnemonic: **Vane test = strength in place.** Turning the vane further after failure also gives the **remoulded** strength, so a single test yields the **sensitivity** directly.

questions.stem: A dense sand sheared under undrained conditions tends to:
options: Contract, generating positive pore pressure and weakening
Dilate, generating negative pore pressure and strengthening
questions.solution:
**Dilate, generating NEGATIVE pore pressure and STRENGTHENING.**

**Why a dense sand dilates.** In a dense packing the grains are closely interlocked, so **shearing requires them to RIDE OVER one another** — which increases the volume. That is **dilatancy**, and it is a purely geometric consequence of the packing.

**Under UNDRAINED conditions the water cannot enter to fill the expanding voids**, so the pore pressure is **sucked DOWN** — it becomes **negative**. By **σ′ = σ − u**, a negative u **increases** the effective stress, and by **τ = σ′ tan φ** the sand becomes **temporarily STRONGER**.

**The contrast with loose sand is complete:**

| | **LOOSE sand** | **DENSE sand** |
|---|---|---|
| On shearing tries to | **CONTRACT** | **DILATE** |
| Undrained pore pressure | **RISES (positive)** | **FALLS (negative)** |
| Effective stress | **Falls** | **Rises** |
| Result | **WEAKENS — liquefaction risk** | **STRENGTHENS** |
| Stress–strain curve | No peak; strength rises to a plateau | **Distinct PEAK, then softening** |
| Volume change (drained) | Decreases | **Increases** |

**Both converge on the CRITICAL STATE** — the condition at which the soil shears **continuously at constant volume and constant stress**. A loose sand contracts toward it; a dense sand dilates past its peak and then softens toward it. The **critical state friction angle φ_cv** is a genuine material property, independent of the initial density.

**The important practical consequence** follows from that:

> **The PEAK friction angle of a dense sand is a function of its PACKING, not a permanent property.** It is available only while the dense state persists, and it falls to **φ_cv** once the soil has been sheared through enough strain.

So the peak φ should be used with caution in design — particularly where **large strains** can occur (a progressive failure, a flexible retaining structure, a seismic event), or where the sand may be **loosened** by disturbance. Many codes recommend designing on **φ_cv** for that reason.

**The dilatancy angle ψ** quantifies it, with the peak angle related to the critical state angle approximately by **φ_peak ≈ φ_cv + 0.8ψ**.

**Why this matters for liquefaction** — it is the whole reason density is the first thing assessed:

> A **dense** sand cannot liquefy, because it **dilates** and generates **negative** pore pressure under cyclic loading — the opposite of what liquefaction requires. Densification (vibro-compaction, stone columns, dynamic compaction) therefore works by converting a contractive soil into a dilatant one.

**And for clays the analogue holds**: a **normally consolidated** clay is contractive (Skempton's A ≈ +1), while a **heavily over-consolidated** clay is dilatant (A negative) — which is why an over-consolidated clay cutting is strongest immediately after excavation and weakens over the following years as the negative pore pressures dissipate.

examTip.trick: Dense grains are interlocked and must **ride up over one another** to shear, so the sample tries to expand. Undrained, it cannot — so the pore pressure goes **negative**, σ′ rises, and the sand gets stronger.
examTip.mnemonic: **Dense dilates and strengthens; loose contracts and liquefies.** This single contrast explains why liquefaction affects loose deposits and never dense ones.

questions.stem: Taylor's stability number for a slope is defined as:
questions.solution:
**S_n = c / (F γ H).**

It is a **dimensionless** grouping — check: c has units of kN/m², γ of kN/m³ and H of m, so γH has units of kN/m² and the ratio is dimensionless ✓. That dimensional check identifies the correct option immediately, since options (c) and (d) are not dimensionless.

**How it is used.** **Taylor's charts** give S_n against the **slope angle β** and the **depth factor D_f** (the ratio of the depth to a hard stratum to the slope height), for various friction angles. The chart is then entered in one of two ways:

| Given | Find |
|---|---|
| The slope angle and height, and the soil properties | The **factor of safety F** |
| The soil properties and a required F | The **maximum safe HEIGHT**, or the **safe slope angle** |

**Its value is that it collapses several variables into one dimensionless number**, so a single chart covers all combinations — which is why it remained the standard rapid method for decades before computers.

**The contrast with a cohesionless slope is the conceptual point:**

| Slope | Stability governed by | Height matters? |
|---|---|---|
| **Cohesionless (c = 0)** | **F = tan φ/tan β** | **NO** — independent of height |
| **Cohesive (c > 0)** | **S_n = c/(F γ H)** | **YES** — F falls as H rises |

A cohesive slope is height-dependent because **cohesion provides a strength that does not scale with the weight**, while the driving force does. Doubling the height doubles γH and therefore **halves** the factor of safety, all else equal.

**Special results from Taylor's analysis:**

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| **Vertical cut in pure clay (β = 90°, φ = 0)** | **S_n = 0.261**, giving **H_c = 3.83c/γ ≈ 4c/γ** |
| Slope angle β > 53° with φ = 0 | **Toe failure** always |
| β < 53° with φ = 0 | **Base failure** possible, depending on the depth factor |
| φ > 3° | Toe failure is the usual mode |

**The 53° threshold is worth knowing**: below it, the critical circle may pass **beneath the toe** through the foundation soil, so the depth to a hard stratum becomes relevant and the **depth factor** must be considered. Above it, the circle passes through the toe and the depth factor is irrelevant.

**Taylor's method assumes:**

| Assumption | Note |
|---|---|
| **Homogeneous** soil | Real slopes are layered |
| **Circular** failure surface | A weak layer may force a non-circular one |
| **No pore pressure** in the basic charts | Charts with r_u exist for the seepage case |
| Total stress (φ = 0) or effective, consistently | Must match the case being analysed |

**So it is a rapid preliminary method**, appropriate for a homogeneous slope and for checking a computed result — while a real layered slope with seepage requires the **method of slices** with the actual stratigraphy and pore pressures. Its enduring value is that it gives an answer in a minute and shows immediately how the factor of safety responds to a change in height or angle, which a software run does not.

examTip.trick: S_n is **dimensionless** — c, γ and H combine to cancel — which is what lets one chart serve every slope of a given angle and φ.
examTip.mnemonic: **Taylor's charts give the number from the slope angle and φ; the formula then gives the safe height.** Note H is inversely proportional to S_n, so a small stability number means a tall safe slope.

questions.stem: A slope failure in which the failure surface passes below the toe through the foundation soil is called a:
questions.solution:
**Base failure.**

**The three types of circular slope failure**, distinguished by **where the failure surface emerges**:

| Type | Failure surface | Occurs when |
|---|---|---|
| **Face (slope) failure** | Emerges **ABOVE the toe**, on the face | The slope is **steep**, or a **weak layer** exists in the upper part |
| **Toe failure** | Passes **THROUGH the toe** | The **usual** case; steep slopes and soils with φ > 3° |
| **BASE failure** | Passes **BELOW the toe**, through the **FOUNDATION soil** | A **WEAK STRATUM UNDERLIES** the slope, and the slope is **flat** (β < 53° for φ = 0) |

**Base failure is the most damaging** because it mobilises a **much larger mass** — the failure surface extends well beyond the toe, taking in ground that appeared to be nowhere near the slope. Structures and roads at a distance from the crest can be involved.

**When to expect it:**

| Condition | Reason |
|---|---|
| A **soft clay layer beneath** a stronger slope | The circle finds the weak path below |
| **Flat** slopes (β below about 53° with φ = 0) | A deeper circle becomes critical |
| An **embankment on soft ground** | The classic case — the fill is stronger than what it sits on |
| A **thick soft stratum** with no hard layer close beneath | The circle can develop fully |

**The depth factor D_f** governs whether base failure is possible:

> **D_f = depth from the top of the slope to a hard stratum / height of the slope**

A **hard stratum close beneath the toe (D_f near 1)** prevents a deep circle from forming, and toe failure governs. A **deep soft deposit (large D_f)** allows base failure.

**Why this matters for the ANALYSIS**, which is the practical point:

> A slope stability search restricted to circles **through the toe** will **MISS a base failure entirely** — and report a comfortable factor of safety for a slope that is in fact unsafe.

So the trial circles must include **deep circles passing below the toe** wherever a soft foundation stratum exists. That is one reason the analysis is a **search** rather than a calculation, and why the stratigraphy must be modelled rather than the slope treated as homogeneous.

**Non-circular failures** are the further case: where a **distinct weak layer** exists — a clay seam, a bedding plane, an old slip surface, a soil-rock interface — the failure surface follows **it** rather than any circle. Such cases need:

| Method | For |
|---|---|
| **Wedge analysis** | A planar or two-plane surface, often in rock or along a bedding plane |
| **Janbu's method** | A general non-circular surface |
| **Morgenstern–Price, Spencer** | Rigorous, any surface |

**In Nepal's hills the non-circular case is often the real one**, because failures commonly occur along the **interface between the colluvium (the loose surface mantle) and the underlying rock** — a planar or gently curved surface determined by the geology, not by soil mechanics. Analysing such a slope with a circular search through a homogeneous soil model can miss it completely, which is why the **engineering geology** of a hill slope matters as much as its soil parameters.

examTip.trick: Three named cases, distinguished by where the surface emerges: **face** failure (above the toe), **toe** failure (through the toe — the commonest), **base** failure (below the toe, through the foundation).
examTip.mnemonic: **Base failure needs a weak layer under the slope**, typically soft clay, and it is favoured by a flat slope on a deep soft stratum. If a hard layer lies close beneath, the surface cannot get down there and toe failure results.

questions.stem: In the Mohr-Coulomb equation the term c represents the strength that is:
questions.solution:
**The strength that is INDEPENDENT of the normal stress.**

> **τ = c + σ tan φ**

The equation is the sum of **two physically distinct** contributions, and separating them is the substance of the criterion:

| Term | Name | Depends on normal stress? | Physical source |
|---|---|---|---|
| **c** | **COHESION** | **NO — independent** | **Electrochemical bonding** between clay particles, **cementation**, and negative pore pressure (apparent cohesion) |
| **σ tan φ** | **FRICTION** | **YES — proportional** | **Interlocking and sliding resistance** between grains |

**The graphical statement is the failure envelope**: a straight line of **intercept c** on the τ axis and **slope tan φ**. The intercept is the strength available at **zero normal stress** — which is precisely what "independent of normal stress" means.

**The two limiting cases, and each corresponds to one term vanishing:**

| Soil | Parameters | Envelope |
|---|---|---|
| **Pure sand** | **c = 0** | A line **through the origin** — no strength at zero confinement, so **sand cannot stand in a vertical cut** |
| **Saturated clay, undrained** | **φ_u = 0** | A **HORIZONTAL** line at τ = c_u — strength **independent of confinement**, so **clay CAN stand vertically** for a while |

That pair explains the everyday observation that a trench in sand collapses at once while one in stiff clay stands — and it follows entirely from which term is present.

**Sources of cohesion**, and they are not all equally reliable:

| Source | Character |
|---|---|
| **True cohesion** — electrochemical bonding in clay | Genuine and permanent |
| **Cementation** — carbonate, iron oxide, silica | Genuine, but can be destroyed by disturbance or leaching |
| **APPARENT cohesion** — negative pore pressure (suction) in a damp soil | **TEMPORARY and UNRELIABLE** |

**Apparent cohesion deserves the warning**, because it is what holds a damp sand cut standing and it is not to be relied upon:

> It **disappears** when the soil **dries out** (the suction is lost) **or is flooded** (the suction is destroyed). Neither is under the excavator's control, which is why temporary works design **never relies on apparent cohesion in a granular soil**.

**In effective stress terms** the criterion becomes

> **τ = c′ + σ′ tan φ′**

and it is this **effective stress form that is fundamental** — the total stress form is a convenient shortcut valid only for a specific drainage condition.

**Typical values:**

| Soil | φ′ | c′ |
|---|---|---|
| Loose sand | 28 – 32° | 0 |
| **Dense sand / gravel** | **35 – 45°** | 0 |
| Silt | 27 – 35° | small |
| **Normally consolidated clay** | 20 – 30° | **≈ 0** |
| **Over-consolidated clay** | 15 – 25° | **10 – 50 kPa** |

**Note that c′ is essentially ZERO for a normally consolidated clay** — the cohesion such a clay exhibits in an undrained test is not true cohesion but a consequence of the undrained condition. Assuming a c′ for a normally consolidated clay in a long-term analysis is unconservative, and it is a genuine error in slope stability work.

examTip.trick: **τ = c + σ tan φ** is the equation of a straight line: **c is the intercept** and **tan φ the slope**. The intercept is by definition the strength when σ = 0.
examTip.mnemonic: **c is the strength at zero normal stress; φ supplies the strength that grows with confinement.** Pure sand has c = 0 through the origin; saturated clay tested undrained has φ = 0 and a horizontal line.

questions.stem: For the long-term stability analysis of a permanent cutting in clay, the appropriate parameters are:
options: Undrained total stress parameters c_u and φ_u = 0
Effective stress parameters c′ and φ′
The peak strength measured in a UU test
questions.solution:
**Effective stress parameters c′ and φ′.**

**The rule, and it is the most useful judgement in the topic:**

> For a **LOADED** clay (a foundation, an embankment), the **SHORT-TERM undrained** case is critical.
> For an **UNLOADED** clay (a **CUTTING**, an excavation), the **LONG-TERM drained** case is critical.

**Why the asymmetry.** It comes down to which way the pore pressure moves, and therefore whether the soil gets stronger or weaker with time:

| Situation | Immediate pore pressure | Over time | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|
| **LOADING** (embankment, footing) | **RISES** (positive) | Dissipates, **σ′ increases** | **INCREASES** — so the short term is worst |
| **UNLOADING** (cutting, excavation) | **FALLS** (negative) | Equalises, **σ′ decreases** | **DECREASES** — so the long term is worst |
