A cutting is therefore **strongest immediately after excavation** and **weakens for years** afterwards, as the negative pore pressures generated by the unloading slowly dissipate and the water content rises to its equilibrium value.

**The consequence is a real and dangerous phenomenon:**

> **Cuttings in clay can fail YEARS after construction** — sometimes decades. The slope stood perfectly well through many monsoons, nothing visible changed, and then it failed. The cause is the slow approach to the long-term equilibrium pore pressure.

That is why an **undrained (φ_u = 0) analysis of a permanent cutting is not merely approximate but WRONG** — it analyses the strongest condition the slope will ever have, and pronounces it safe.

**How the effective stress analysis is done:**

| Step | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Obtain **c′ and φ′** | From **CD** triaxial tests, or **CU with pore pressure measurement** |
| Establish the **long-term pore pressure** | From a **flow net**, from a **pore pressure ratio r_u = u/γh**, or from piezometers |
| Analyse by the **method of slices** in effective stress | Bishop's simplified, or a rigorous method |
| Factor of safety | **≥ 1.5** for a permanent slope |

**Establishing the long-term pore pressure is the difficult part**, and it is where the judgement lies: it depends on the eventual groundwater regime, which depends on the drainage provided, the surrounding hydrology and the climate. A conservative assumption is often the water table at or near the ground surface — which is the monsoon condition in Nepal in any case.

**Where the undrained analysis IS appropriate:**

| Case | Why |
|---|---|
| **Immediate stability of an excavation** during construction | Days or weeks, so undrained |
| **End of construction** of an embankment on soft clay | The fill is placed faster than the clay can consolidate |
| **Bearing capacity** of a footing on clay, immediately after loading | Short term governs |
| **Sudden drawdown** (with CU parameters) | Rapid unloading of a consolidated fill |

**Option (d), remoulded strength**, is wrong here but names a real parameter used elsewhere: the **residual** strength applies to a slope containing a **pre-existing slip surface**, where the clay has already been sheared through a large displacement and its strength has fallen from peak to residual. Analysing a **reactivated landslide** at peak strength is a classic and dangerous error — the strength that resisted the first movement is no longer there.

examTip.trick: Decide by the **timescale of drainage** against the timescale of loading. Permanent works are long-term, so the excess pore pressures have dissipated and the drained parameters apply.
examTip.mnemonic: **Short term → total stress (c_u, φ_u = 0). Long term → effective stress (c′, φ′).** And note which is critical: for a **CUTTING** the long term is worse (pore pressures rise back to equilibrium after unloading), while for an **EMBANKMENT** the short term is worse. Getting that pairing the wrong way round is a real design error.

questions.stem: In the Standard Penetration Test, the N value is the number of blows required for a penetration of:
options: The last 300 mm of a 450 mm drive
questions.solution:
**The LAST 300 mm of a 450 mm drive.**

**The test procedure:**

| Detail | Value |
|---|---|
| Sampler | **Split-spoon**, 50 mm outside diameter |
| **Hammer** | **63.5 kg** |
| **Free fall** | **750 mm** |
| Total drive | **450 mm**, in three increments of 150 mm |
| **N value** | Blows for the **SECOND and THIRD increments** — the **last 300 mm** |
| Refusal | 50 blows for any one increment |

**Why the first 150 mm is DISCARDED** — this is the point of the question:

> The bottom of the borehole is **DISTURBED by the drilling**: loosened by the boring tool, possibly heaved by water pressure, and littered with cuttings. The blow count through that disturbed zone means nothing.

The first increment is therefore the **seating drive**, taking the sampler through the disturbed material into undisturbed soil, and only the subsequent 300 mm is counted.

Omitting that and reporting the blows for the full 450 mm is the standard error, and it **overstates** N by roughly 50%.

**Corrections to the measured N**, applied in this order:

| Correction | Reason |
|---|---|
| **OVERBURDEN pressure** | The **same sand** gives a **higher N at depth** simply because it is more confined. Corrected to a standard overburden of 100 kPa, giving **N₆₀** or (N₁)₆₀ |
| **DILATANCY** (fine sand or silt below the water table) | Negative pore pressure generated during driving **inflates** N |
| Energy ratio, rod length, borehole diameter, sampler type | Equipment differences between rigs and countries |

**The dilatancy correction (IS 2131):**

> **N_c = 15 + ½(N − 15)** when **N > 15**; no correction when N ≤ 15

So a measured N of 35 in saturated fine sand becomes **15 + ½(20) = 25** — a substantial reduction, and one that matters because it is in the **safe** direction.

**Interpretation:**

| N | Sand | N | Clay |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 – 4 | **Very loose** | < 2 | Very soft |
| 4 – 10 | Loose | 2 – 4 | Soft |
| 10 – 30 | Medium | 4 – 8 | Medium |
| 30 – 50 | Dense | 8 – 15 | Stiff |
| **> 50** | **Very dense** | > 30 | **Hard** |

**Why the SPT survives despite being crude**: it is **quick, cheap, performed in any borehole with simple equipment**, it recovers a **sample** for identification, and — decisively — an enormous body of **empirical correlation** has been built on it, for **relative density, φ, bearing capacity, settlement and LIQUEFACTION susceptibility**. That last is why it is mandatory for Kathmandu Valley sites under NBC 105.

examTip.trap: "450 mm" is the whole drive and is the obvious wrong pick. The **first 150 mm is the seating drive and is DISCARDED.**
examTip.trick: The spoon is driven 450 mm in three 150 mm increments; N is the sum of the **second and third** only.
examTip.mnemonic: **150 seating, 300 counted.** The hammer is 63.5 kg falling 750 mm.

questions.stem: The Standard Penetration Test is least reliable in:
questions.solution:
**Gravel and very soft clay** — the two extremes, each for its own reason.

| Soil | Why the SPT fails |
|---|---|
| **GRAVEL** | A **single stone jams the split spoon**, giving a spuriously **high** N that reflects the stone and not the soil |
| **VERY SOFT CLAY** | The blow count is **too small to resolve** — N of 0, 1 or 2 cannot distinguish a soft clay from a very soft one, yet their strengths may differ by a factor of three |

**The alternatives for each:**

| Soil | Better test | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Gravel** | **Plate load test**, large-diameter penetration test, or **geophysical** methods | No small sampler to be jammed |
| **Soft clay** | **VANE SHEAR** (in situ) or laboratory **triaxial / UCS** | The vane measures c_u directly and resolves small differences |

**The SPT's other limitations**, which questions probe:

| Limitation | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Highly operator- and equipment-dependent** | Hammer type, rope-and-drum versus automatic trip, rod length, borehole diameter all affect the **energy delivered** — hence the correction to **N₆₀** (60% of theoretical free-fall energy) |
| **The sample is DISTURBED** | Area ratio over 100%, so **no strength or consolidation testing** is possible on it |
| It is a **crude, empirical** index | It measures penetration resistance, not any fundamental property |
| **Borehole disturbance** at the base | Partly addressed by discarding the seating drive |
| **Below the water table**, the borehole must be kept topped up | Otherwise water flows in and **loosens** the base, understating N |

**The last point is a practical one worth carrying**: if the water level in the borehole falls below the surrounding water table, an **upward gradient** develops at the base and the sand there is **loosened** — sometimes to the quick condition. The measured N is then far too low. Keeping the borehole **full of water or drilling mud at all times** is therefore part of the standard procedure, not a refinement.

**The Static Cone Penetration Test (CPT)** addresses several of these limitations and is increasingly preferred:

| CPT advantage | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **CONTINUOUS profile** | A **thin weak layer** that a borehole sampled at 1.5 m intervals would miss entirely is detected |
| **Operator-independent** | The cone is pushed at a standard rate; there is no hammer |
| **Repeatable** | Far less scatter than the SPT |
| Measures **cone resistance AND sleeve friction** | Their ratio identifies the soil type |
| No borehole needed | Faster |

Its limitation is that it **recovers no sample** — so it cannot identify the soil directly, only infer it — and it cannot penetrate gravel or rock. In practice the two are **complementary**: CPT for a continuous profile and stratigraphy, boreholes with SPT and undisturbed sampling at selected locations for identification and laboratory testing.

examTip.trick: The test fails at both ends of the scale. In **gravel** a single stone jams the shoe and gives an absurdly high N; in **very soft clay** the spoon sinks under its own weight and N is meaningless.
examTip.mnemonic: **Too coarse or too soft and the SPT lies.** Two corrections always apply: **overburden** (N₁) and **dilatancy** in saturated fine sand, where N above 15 is corrected to 15 + ½(N − 15).

questions.stem: The depth of soil exploration below a footing is normally taken as:
questions.solution:
**1.5 to 2 times the footing width.**

**The reason is the PRESSURE BULB**: the depth to which a **significant** increase of vertical stress extends. Conventionally bounded by the **isobar of 20% (or 10%) of the applied pressure**, it reaches about **1.5 B** for the 20% contour and about **2 B** for the 10%.

Below that depth the added stress is a small fraction of the applied pressure, so **further compression of the soil is negligible** compared with the layers above — and exploring deeper gains nothing.

**Boussinesq's solution** gives the stress falling roughly as **1/z²** on the axis, so doubling the depth quarters the stress. By 2 B the increment is only a few percent of the applied pressure.

**The rules for different foundations:**

| Foundation | Depth of exploration |
|---|---|
| **Isolated footing** | **1.5 – 2 × width B** |
| **Raft** | 1.5 – 2 × the **SHORTER plan dimension** |
| **Pile group** | **1.5 × the group width, BELOW the pile tips** |
| Adjacent footings whose bulbs overlap | Treat as **one larger loaded area** |
| Rock encountered | **3 m into sound rock** |

**The overlapping-bulb rule is the one most often missed** and it matters greatly:

> Where footings are **closely spaced**, their pressure bulbs **OVERLAP** and the combined stress reaches **far deeper** than any individual footing's would. The group must then be treated as a **single loaded area of the overall dimension**.

A borehole taken to 1.5 × (individual footing width) on such a site would be far too shallow, and a compressible layer at depth would be discovered only by the settlement of the completed building.

**Why 3 m into rock** — the reason is specific and practical: a **BOULDER can be mistaken for bedrock**. A borehole that stops on the first hard material may have stopped on a single large stone within a soft deposit, and founding a structure on it would be a serious error. Penetrating 3 m confirms continuity.

**Number and spacing of boreholes:**

| Situation | Spacing |
|---|---|
| Building, uniform conditions | **15 – 30 m** |
| Erratic conditions | Closer |
| Road or pipeline | Along the alignment at intervals |
| Minimum | At least **one at each corner and one at the centre** for a building |

The governing principle is that the boreholes must be enough to **interpolate confidently between them** — which depends on the **variability actually found**, not on a fixed rule. Erratic results call for more boreholes; consistent ones justify fewer.

**Methods of exploration** and where each fits:

| Method | Character |
|---|---|
| **Trial pit** | **Direct visual inspection**; the most informative per rupee, but **shallow** (to ~3 m) |
| **Auger boring** | Above the water table in cohesive soil |
| **Wash boring** | Fast and cheap, but **cuttings are washed up so stratification is poorly identified** |
| **Percussion boring** | Boulders and hard strata; disturbs the soil |
| **Rotary drilling** | **Rock coring**; gives the **RQD** |
| **Geophysical** — seismic refraction, electrical resistivity | **Rapid, non-intrusive, covers large areas**; indirect, so it must be **calibrated against boreholes** |

**Geophysical methods are complementary, not alternative**: they interpolate cheaply over a large site between boreholes, but they cannot replace a sample.

examTip.trick: It is the same 1.5–2 B as the significant stress depth — the two questions are the same physics. Explore as deep as the footing stresses the ground.
examTip.mnemonic: **Explore the pressure bulb.** For a pile group, measure from the pile TIPS, not from ground level — and for a raft, B is the whole raft width, which can mean very deep boreholes.

questions.stem: The plate load test can give misleading results for:
options: Clay with a compressible layer at depth
questions.solution:
**Clay with a compressible layer at depth.**

**The reason is the SIZE of the plate.** A test plate is **300 to 750 mm** across, so its **pressure bulb extends only about 1.5 times that — perhaps 0.5 to 1 m**. A real footing several metres wide has a bulb reaching **several metres**.

> The plate therefore **CANNOT DETECT a compressible layer that lies below its own shallow influence zone but WITHIN the footing's** — and it reports a comfortable result for a site where the real foundation will settle badly.

That is the classic failure of the test, and it is why the plate load test must always be read alongside a **borehole log** showing what lies below.

**Scaling the results — and the rules differ fundamentally between sand and clay:**

| Soil | Bearing capacity | Settlement |
|---|---|---|
| **SAND (φ soil)** | **q_footing/q_plate = B_footing/B_plate** — capacity **increases** with width | **S_f/S_p = [2B_f/(B_f + B_p)]²** — settlement **increases** with width |
| **CLAY (c soil)** | **q_footing = q_plate** — capacity is **INDEPENDENT of width** | **S_f/S_p = B_f/B_p** — settlement **proportional** to width |

**The clay result for capacity follows from Terzaghi**: with φ = 0, **N_γ = 0**, so the width term vanishes from the bearing capacity equation entirely. Widening a footing on clay does **not** increase the pressure it can carry — only the total load.

**The sand settlement relation** shows that settlement **increases with width** even at the same pressure, which is why a plate test on sand **understates** the settlement of a large footing — and why the test is more useful for **capacity** than for settlement even on sand.

**Test procedure (IS 1888):**

| Detail | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Plate | **300 to 750 mm** square or circular, at least 25 mm thick |
| Test pit | **At the proposed founding level**, width at least **5 × the plate** |
| Loading | In **increments of about one fifth** of the estimated safe load |
| Settlement recorded | Until the rate falls below **0.02 mm/min**, or for a stated time |
| Failure | Taken at a defined settlement, or at the clear break in the load–settlement curve |

**Making the pit at least five plate-widths wide** matters: a narrow pit **confines** the plate, giving a falsely high capacity.

**Its genuine strengths:**

| Strength | Note |
|---|---|
| **Direct** measurement of bearing capacity and settlement | No correlation or theory needed |
| **Rapid** | A day's work |
| Well suited to **granular** soils | Where sampling is difficult and settlement is immediate |
| Good for **compaction checks** on a fill | Where the layer tested is the whole of what matters |

**And its limitations, as a set:**

| Limitation | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Shallow influence zone** | Misses deeper layers — the point of this question |
| **Short duration** | Gives **immediate** settlement only; **consolidation settlement of a clay is not measured at all** |
| Size effect | Scaling rules must be applied, and they differ by soil type |
| Only tests one point | Several tests needed on a variable site |

**The consolidation point is the second reason the test misleads on clay**: a plate test lasting a few hours captures the **immediate elastic** settlement, while the **primary consolidation** of the clay — which may be several times larger — takes years and is entirely invisible to the test.

examTip.trap: The plate test looks authoritative because it loads real ground — which is exactly what makes its failure mode dangerous.
examTip.trick: A **300–750 mm plate** stresses only about a metre of soil. A **real footing** stresses several metres. A soft layer below the plate's bulb but inside the footing's is **completely invisible** to the test.
examTip.mnemonic: **Small plate, small bulb, big blind spot.** Reasonable on uniform sand, actively misleading on layered clay.

questions.stem: Rankine's coefficient of active earth pressure for a cohesionless soil is:
questions.solution:
**K_a = (1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ)**, equivalently **tan²(45° − φ/2)**.

**The three coefficients and their ORDERING**, which must be automatic:

| State | Coefficient | Wall movement | For φ = 30° |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ACTIVE** | **K_a = (1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ)** | Wall moves **AWAY** from the backfill | **1/3** |
| **AT REST** | **K₀ = 1 − sin φ** (Jaky) | **NO** movement | **0.5** |
| **PASSIVE** | **K_p = (1 + sin φ)/(1 − sin φ) = 1/K_a** | Wall moves **INTO** the backfill | **3** |

> **K_a < K₀ < K_p** — always.

Those three numbers for φ = 30° (**1/3, 0.5, 3**) are worth memorising as a check on any computed value: a coefficient of 3 cannot be active, and one of 1/3 cannot be passive.

**Option (b) is K_p** and **option (d) is also K_p** (since tan²(45 + φ/2) = K_p) — so two of the four distractors are the passive coefficient in different forms, which is exactly the confusion the question tests. **Option (c) is K₀.**

**Why the direction of movement decides which applies** — the physical reasoning:

| State | Who is pushing | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **ACTIVE** | The **SOIL pushes the wall** | The soil **mobilises its own strength** to resist collapsing, so the pressure it exerts is **REDUCED** below at-rest |
| **PASSIVE** | The **WALL pushes the soil** | The soil **resists**, mobilising its full strength **against** the wall, so the pressure is greatly **INCREASED** |

**The movement required differs by an order of magnitude**, and this has a real design consequence:

| State | Movement to mobilise |
|---|---|
| **Active** | Small — about **0.001 to 0.005 H** |
| **Passive** | Large — about **0.01 to 0.05 H**, roughly **TEN TIMES** more |

> Because passive resistance needs so much movement, the **passive resistance of soil in front of a wall is often DISCOUNTED or heavily FACTORED** in design — by the time it is fully mobilised, the structure has moved unacceptably.

**A wall that cannot move at all** — a basement wall restrained by the floor slabs, a bridge abutment restrained by the deck, a rigid box culvert — must be designed for **AT REST pressure K₀**, which is **50% higher than active** for φ = 30°. Designing such a wall for active pressure is a genuine and common error, and it is why the restraint conditions must be established before the coefficient is chosen.

**Note also that K₀ depends on stress history**: for an **over-consolidated** soil, **K₀ = (1 − sin φ)(OCR)^{sin φ}**, which can exceed 1 — meaning the horizontal stress **exceeds** the vertical. A heavily over-consolidated clay can therefore exert far more lateral pressure than its unit weight suggests, and excavating into it releases that stored horizontal stress.

examTip.trick: Two ways to check you have it the right way up: **K_a < 1 < K_p**, and **K_p = 1/K_a**. If your expression gives a number above 1 you have written K_p.
examTip.mnemonic: **Active has (1 − sin φ) on TOP.** For φ = 30° the numbers are clean: **K_a = 1/3, K_p = 3.** Also **K_a = tan²(45 − φ/2).**

questions.stem: The resultant active thrust on a vertical wall retaining a dry cohesionless backfill of height H acts at:
questions.solution:
**H/3 above the base.**

**The pressure distribution is TRIANGULAR:**

> **p_a = K_a γ z** — increasing **linearly with depth**

so the resultant acts at the **centroid of a triangle**, which is at **one third of the height from the base**:

> **P_a = ½ K_a γ H²**, acting at **H/3 above the base**

**The same reasoning applies to hydrostatic pressure on a dam** (½γH² at H/3), and for the same reason — a linearly increasing distribution has its centroid at one third of the depth.

**Where the resultant acts for other loadings** — the set worth holding:

| Loading | Distribution | Resultant | Acts at |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Soil, dry cohesionless** | **Triangular** | **½ K_a γ H²** | **H/3** |
| **Uniform SURCHARGE q** | **RECTANGULAR** | **K_a q H** | **H/2** |
| **Water** (submerged backfill) | Triangular | **½ γ_w H²** | H/3 |
| Line load, point load | Complex | By Boussinesq or approximate methods | Varies |

**The surcharge acting at H/2 rather than H/3** is the distinction most often missed: a surcharge adds a **constant** pressure at every depth, so its distribution is a **rectangle** and its centroid is at mid-height. Where both act, the resultant of the combined trapezoidal distribution is found by taking moments of the two parts separately.

**A submerged backfill deserves particular attention**, because it is where the largest errors are made:

> For a backfill below the water table, the pressure is **K_a γ′ z (from the soil) PLUS the FULL γ_w z (from the water)**.

**The water pressure is NOT reduced by K_a.** Water has no shear strength, so it transmits pressure equally in all directions — there is no "active" state for a fluid. Applying K_a to the water component **grossly underestimates** the thrust, and it is a genuine and dangerous error.

**A worked comparison** for H = 5 m, φ = 30° (K_a = 1/3), γ = 18 kN/m³ dry and γ_sat = 20:

| Case | Thrust |
|---|---|
| **Dry backfill** | ½ × (1/3) × 18 × 25 = **75 kN/m** |
| **Fully submerged** | ½ × (1/3) × 10.2 × 25 + ½ × 9.81 × 25 = 42.5 + 122.6 = **165 kN/m** |

> **The submerged case is more than TWICE the dry one** — even though the soil's contribution has nearly halved, because the water contributes so much more than the soil it replaces.

**That is why DRAINAGE behind a retaining wall matters so much**, and why most retaining wall failures are drainage failures rather than structural ones. A wall designed for the dry case and then allowed to accumulate water behind it receives **two to three times** its design thrust.

The measures — **weep holes, a granular filter, a longitudinal drain at the base, a geotextile filter, and surface sealing at the crest** — are therefore not details but the primary defence.

examTip.trick: The pressure diagram is a **triangle** (pressure grows linearly with depth), and a triangle's centroid is at one third of its height from the base.
examTip.mnemonic: **Triangular pressure → resultant at H/3.** With **P_a = ½K_aγH²**, the overturning moment about the base is P_a × H/3. Note P_a goes as **H²**, so doubling the wall height quadruples the thrust and increases the moment eightfold.

questions.stem: In a cohesive backfill, the depth over which the active pressure is negative and a tension crack may form is:
questions.solution:
**z₀ = 2c/(γ√K_a).**

The active pressure in a cohesive soil is

> **p_a = K_a γ z − 2c√K_a**

The **cohesion term is NEGATIVE and constant with depth**, so near the surface the computed pressure is **negative** — that is, tensile. Setting p_a = 0:

> **K_a γ z₀ = 2c√K_a**, hence **z₀ = 2c/(γ√K_a)** ∎

For **φ = 0** (K_a = 1) this reduces to **z₀ = 2c/γ**.

**Soil cannot sustain tension against a wall**, so a **TENSION CRACK opens** to that depth, and the wall receives no pressure at all over it.

**The related depth**, and confusing the two is the standard error:

| Depth | Expression | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **Tension crack z₀** | **2c/(γ√K_a)** | Depth to which the pressure is negative |
| **Critical height H_c** | **4c/(γ√K_a)** | Height at which the **NET thrust is zero** — an unsupported cut just stands |

> **H_c is exactly TWICE z₀** — a useful check.

**Why this makes cohesive backfill a POOR choice**, which is the practical point:

| Problem | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **The tension crack FILLS WITH WATER** | The wall then receives the **FULL HYDROSTATIC pressure over the crack depth** — exactly where the calculation assumed **zero** pressure |
| Clay **swells** on wetting | Generating swelling pressure against the wall |
| Clay **holds water** | So the drainage system cannot function |
| Clay is **difficult to compact** | And compaction-induced pressures are high |
| Clay **creeps** | Long-term pressures exceed the computed active values |

**The water-filled crack is the serious one**, and it reverses the apparent benefit of cohesion:

> The engineer computes a **reduced** thrust because of the cohesion, and the crack that the same cohesion creates then **fills with water and delivers a thrust larger than if the cohesion had never existed**.

**Conservative practice therefore IGNORES the negative pressure entirely** — the pressure diagram is taken as zero from the surface to z₀ and the positive triangle below, with **no credit for the negative area**. Many codes go further and require the crack to be assumed **full of water**.

**The design conclusion:**

> **Use FREE-DRAINING GRANULAR backfill.** Where clay is unavoidable, provide **enhanced drainage**, ignore the negative pressure, and consider the water-filled crack case.

**A note on where cohesion IS legitimately used**: in a **temporary** excavation, the cohesion of a stiff clay genuinely allows an unsupported cut for a short period — but as the earlier question on critical height set out, that is a factor of safety of one, with no allowance for softening, rain or surcharge, and practice supports excavations deeper than about 1.2 m regardless.

examTip.trick: Set the Rankine active pressure to zero: **σ_a = γzK_a − 2c√K_a = 0** gives **z = 2c/(γ√K_a)** ✓
examTip.mnemonic: **Tension crack depth is HALF the critical unsupported height (4c/γ√K_a... for φ=0, 2c/γ and 4c/γ).** Soil cannot pull, so the negative block is ignored — and the crack **fills with water**, which is why the design must add a water thrust that is often larger than the earth pressure it replaced.

questions.stem: Compared with Rankine's theory, Coulomb's earth pressure theory:
options: Ignores the weight of the backfill
Cannot be applied to cohesionless soils
Takes account of wall friction and permits an inclined wall back
questions.solution:
**It takes account of wall friction and permits an inclined wall back.**

**The comparison:**

| | **RANKINE (1857)** | **COULOMB (1776)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Wall friction δ** | **IGNORED** — smooth wall assumed | **INCLUDED** |
| **Wall back** | **Vertical** | May be **INCLINED** |
| Backfill surface | Level or uniformly sloping | **Any** |
| **Failure surface** | **PLANAR** | **PLANAR** |
| Method | Stress states within the soil mass | **Force equilibrium of a trial WEDGE** |
| Character | Simpler; **CONSERVATIVE for active** | More general |

**Note that BOTH assume a planar failure surface** — so option (a) is wrong for Coulomb as well as for Rankine. The real failure surface is **curved**, and that fact is the source of Coulomb's principal defect.

**Coulomb's method** considers a trial wedge of soil bounded by the wall, the ground surface and an assumed plane failure surface, and finds the wedge giving the **maximum** thrust (active) or **minimum** resistance (passive) by trial — the **trial wedge** or, graphically, **Culmann's construction**.

**Its defect, and it is important:**

> **Coulomb's PASSIVE value is UNSAFE for large wall friction.**

Because the real passive failure surface is **strongly CURVED** (a logarithmic spiral near the wall), the assumption of a plane surface **overestimates the resistance** — by up to **two or three times** for large δ. So the passive case must be computed by a **curved-surface method** (log spiral, or the coefficients of Caquot–Kerisel) where wall friction is significant.

**The active case is much less affected**, because the active failure surface is nearly planar, and **Coulomb's active value is close to correct**.

**The effect of wall friction, and it is worth understanding:**

| On the ACTIVE side | On the PASSIVE side |
|---|---|
| Wall friction acts **UPWARD** on the wall as the soil settles | Acts **DOWNWARD** as the soil is pushed up |
| **REDUCES** the active thrust — by perhaps 10–20% | **INCREASES** the passive resistance — substantially |

**So ignoring wall friction (Rankine) is CONSERVATIVE for active and CONSERVATIVE for passive** — it overestimates the thrust and underestimates the resistance. That is why Rankine's simpler theory is safe to use, and why it remains the standard for routine design despite being less general.

**Typical wall friction values:**

| Interface | δ |
|---|---|
| Smooth concrete against sand | **⅓ to ½ φ** |
| Rough concrete or masonry against sand | **⅔ φ** |
| Steel sheet pile against sand | ⅓ to ½ φ |
| Soil against soil (a virtual back) | **φ** |

**The "virtual back" trick** lets Rankine be applied to a wall with a projecting heel: a **vertical plane through the heel** is taken as the boundary, the soil above the heel is treated as part of the wall's weight, and along that plane the friction is **soil against soil (δ = φ)** — which Rankine's assumption of no wall friction handles correctly because the plane is a plane of the soil itself, not a wall interface. It is why Rankine's theory can be used for a cantilever retaining wall despite the wall stem being rough.

examTip.trick: Rankine is simpler but assumes a **smooth vertical wall** and a plane backfill surface. Coulomb allows **wall friction δ**, an **inclined back**, and a **sloping surface** — so it is the general theory and Rankine a special case of it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rankine: smooth and vertical. Coulomb: rough and any shape.** Wall friction *reduces* the active thrust, so ignoring it is conservative — one reason Rankine survives despite being less general.

questions.stem: A retaining wall must be checked for overturning, sliding, bearing capacity and:
options: Overall (deep-seated) slope failure through the wall and foundation
questions.solution:
**Overall (deep-seated) slope failure through the wall and foundation.**

**The four stability checks, with their minimum factors of safety:**

| Check | Minimum F | Expression |
|---|---|---|
| **Overturning** about the toe | **2.0** | Σ stabilising moments ÷ Σ overturning moments |
| **Sliding** along the base | **1.5** | (ΣV·μ + adhesion + passive) ÷ ΣH |
| **Bearing pressure** at the base | **3.0** on ultimate capacity | p = ΣV/B ± 6ΣV·e/B² |
| **OVERALL slope failure** | **1.5** | A slip circle passing **through or beneath** the wall |

**The fourth is the one most often OMITTED**, and the consequence is exactly what makes it worth a question:

> A wall can be **perfectly stable in itself** — satisfying overturning, sliding and bearing with comfortable margins — and still **ride down on a slip surface passing BENEATH it**, taking the whole hillside with it.

That is precisely what happens on **hill roads built on marginally stable slopes**: the retaining wall is designed as a structure, the slope is never analysed, and the wall is found some distance downhill after the monsoon, intact and undamaged, having simply moved with the ground it was built on.

**Checking it requires a SLOPE STABILITY analysis** — the method of slices, with trial circles passing below the wall's foundation — using the soil properties of the **whole slope**, not merely the backfill. It is a geotechnical calculation, not a structural one, which is part of why it is skipped.

**The other three checks in more detail:**

**Overturning** is taken about the **toe**, with the stabilising moments from the wall's weight and the soil on the heel, and the overturning moment from the active thrust. **Passive resistance in front is usually IGNORED**, because the soil there may be excavated for services, may be eroded, or may not have moved enough to mobilise.

**Sliding** is resisted by **friction on the base (ΣV tan δ)** plus any **adhesion**, and possibly by passive resistance in front — again usually discounted. Where sliding governs, the remedies are a **base key (shear key)** projecting down into the soil, a **wider base**, or **battering the base** to incline the resistance favourably.

**Bearing pressure** must satisfy both the maximum value and the **no-tension** requirement:

> **e ≤ B/6** — the resultant within the **middle third** of the base

If the resultant falls outside the middle third, **the heel lifts off**, the contact area is reduced, and the pressure under the toe rises sharply — which both threatens a bearing failure and reduces the overturning resistance.

**Types of retaining wall:**

| Type | Resists by | Height |
|---|---|---|
| **Gravity** (masonry, mass concrete) | Its **own weight** | Up to ~3 m |
| **Cantilever** (RCC, L or T stem) | Weight **plus the weight of soil on the base slab** | 3 – 8 m |
| **Counterfort** | As cantilever, with ribs on the **EARTH** side, in **TENSION** | Over 8 m |
| **Buttress** | Ribs on the **EXPOSED** side, in **COMPRESSION** | Over 8 m |
| **Gabion / crib** | Weight, but **flexible and permeable** | Hill roads, river banks |
| Reinforced soil (MSE) | Tensile reinforcement within the fill | Tall walls |
| Sheet pile, soil nails, anchors | Embedment or tension | Excavations, cuttings |

**The counterfort/buttress distinction is examinable**: counterforts on the **earth** side act in **tension** (concrete is weak in tension, so they need reinforcement); buttresses on the **exposed** side act in **compression** (structurally better) but occupy usable space and look worse — which is why counterforts are more common despite being the structurally inferior arrangement.

examTip.trick: Three checks are local to the wall; the fourth looks at the **whole hillside**. A wall can pass every internal check and still ride down the slope on a deeper failure surface that passes underneath it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Overturning 2.0, sliding 1.5, bearing 3.0, overall slope 1.5.** The overall check is the one most often skipped, and on a Nepali hillside it is frequently the one that governs.

questions.stem: The most common cause of retaining wall failure in practice is:
questions.solution:
**Inadequate drainage behind the wall.**

**The reason is quantitative**, and the arithmetic makes it unarguable:

> Soil pressure is **reduced by K_a** (perhaps to one third). **WATER pressure is NOT** — water has no shear strength, so it transmits pressure equally in all directions.

**A worked comparison** for a 5 m wall, φ = 30° (K_a = 1/3), γ = 18 kN/m³ dry, γ_sat = 20 kN/m³:

| Condition | Thrust per metre |
|---|---|
| **Drained (dry)** | ½ × ⅓ × 18 × 25 = **75 kN/m** |
| **Water table at the surface** | ½ × ⅓ × 10.2 × 25 + ½ × 9.81 × 25 = 42.5 + 122.6 = **165 kN/m** |

> **The undrained case is more than TWICE the design thrust** — and the overturning moment rises similarly, since both act at H/3.

A wall designed for the drained case has a factor of safety of about 2 against overturning; fill it with water and that becomes **less than 1**. The wall does not have a marginal problem — it has no reserve at all.

**The drainage measures, and each has a distinct role:**

| Measure | Function |
|---|---|
| **Weep holes** (75–100 mm, at 1–1.5 m centres) | Let the water **out through the wall** |
| **Granular filter / drainage blanket** behind the wall | **Conducts water down to the weep holes** without clogging |
| **Longitudinal perforated drain** at the base | **Collects and carries it away** |
| **Geotextile filter** | Prevents **fines migrating** into the granular layer and blocking it |
| **Surface sealing at the crest** | Stops infiltration **in the first place** |
| **Free-draining granular backfill** | So the water can reach the drains at all |

**Weep holes alone are not enough**, which is the detail most often got wrong: without a **granular layer connecting the backfill to them**, the weep holes drain only the few centimetres of soil immediately around each one, and the rest of the backfill stays saturated. The filter layer is what makes the weep holes work.

**Equally, a filter without a geotextile clogs**: fines from the backfill migrate into the granular layer, fill its voids, and within a few seasons it ceases to drain. The geotextile (or a properly graded filter) is what makes the drainage **durable**.

**Why clay backfill is poor** — it compounds every problem:

| Problem | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Holds water** | The drainage system cannot function |
| **Swells** on wetting | Adds swelling pressure |
| Develops a **tension crack** which **fills with water** | Full hydrostatic pressure where the design assumed none |
| **Creeps** | Long-term pressure exceeds the active value |
| Difficult to compact | High compaction-induced pressures |

**Compaction near the wall needs care in BOTH directions**, which is a subtler point: too little and the fill settles and the surface subsides; **too much** and **compaction-induced lateral pressure** from a heavy roller working close to the wall can **exceed the at-rest value** and push the wall forward. **Light plant only within about 1 m of the wall** is the standard rule.

**The professional summary**: a retaining wall is a **water problem disguised as a structural one**. The structural design is routine; the drainage detailing is where the walls that fail were lost.

examTip.trap: Candidates reach for a structural cause — undersized section, insufficient reinforcement. In practice the wall is usually strong enough and simply loaded far beyond what was assumed.
examTip.trick: Water behind a wall does two things at once: it adds a **full hydrostatic thrust** (γ_w = 9.81 vs an effective soil thrust often around 6 kN/m³) and it **reduces the soil's own strength**. The design load can easily double.
examTip.mnemonic: **Weep holes and a granular filter drain are not a detail — they are the design.** Blocked weep holes have brought down more walls than any calculation error.

questions.stem: A basement wall restrained against movement by the floor slabs should be designed for:
questions.solution:
**At rest earth pressure, K₀.**

> **K₀ = 1 − sin φ** (Jaky's relation for a normally consolidated soil)

**The reason is that active pressure requires MOVEMENT to develop:**

| State | Requires the wall to |
|---|---|
| **At rest (K₀)** | **NOT MOVE at all** |
| **Active (K_a)** | Move **AWAY** from the soil by about **0.001 to 0.005 H** |
| **Passive (K_p)** | Move **INTO** the soil by about **0.01 to 0.05 H** |

A basement wall is **restrained top and bottom by the floor slabs**, so it cannot move enough for the soil to mobilise its own strength and reduce the pressure to the active value. The soil therefore remains in its **at rest** state.

**The magnitude of the error if this is missed**, for φ = 30°:

> **K_a = 0.33, K₀ = 0.50** — the at rest pressure is **50% HIGHER**

Designing a restrained wall for active pressure therefore under-designs it by half, which is a serious error and a common one.

**Structures that must be designed for K₀:**

| Structure | Why restrained |
|---|---|
| **Basement walls** | Held by the floor slabs |
| **Bridge abutments** with an integral deck | Held by the deck |
| **Box culverts and underpasses** | A closed box cannot move |
| **Rigid unyielding walls** on rock | No foundation movement possible |
| Braced excavations (in part) | Struts prevent movement |

**And those that may use K_a:**

| Structure | Why free to move |
|---|---|
| **Free-standing gravity or cantilever** retaining wall | Can tilt and translate slightly |
| **Gabion and crib walls** | Flexible |
| Reinforced soil walls | Deform to mobilise the active state |

**The general principle is worth stating:**

> **The earth pressure a structure experiences depends on how much it MOVES — which depends on the structure, not on the soil alone.** A stiffer structure attracts more load.

That is a general truth of soil–structure interaction, and it runs counter to the intuition that a stronger structure is always safer: making a retaining wall **more rigid** increases the pressure it must carry.

**For an OVER-CONSOLIDATED soil**, K₀ is higher still:

> **K₀ = (1 − sin φ)(OCR)^{sin φ}**

which **can exceed 1** for a heavily over-consolidated clay — meaning the **horizontal stress EXCEEDS the vertical**. Excavating into such a clay releases that stored horizontal stress, causing the excavation to close in, and a rigid wall built into it can attract very large pressures indeed. It is why K₀ for stiff over-consolidated clays is measured rather than assumed.

**Braced excavations** are a related case with their own rules: because the struts are installed progressively as the excavation deepens, the wall's movement pattern is neither active nor at rest, and the pressure distribution is **not triangular**. **Empirical apparent-pressure diagrams (Terzaghi and Peck)** — rectangular or trapezoidal — are used instead, derived from measured strut loads rather than from theory.

examTip.trick: The three states depend entirely on **movement**: away from the soil gives **active** (minimum), toward it gives **passive** (maximum), **no movement** gives **at rest** (in between).
examTip.mnemonic: **No movement, no active state.** **K₀ = 1 − sin φ** for normally consolidated soil — roughly **0.5**, against K_a of about 0.33. Designing a restrained basement wall for active pressure under-designs it by about half.

questions.stem: Gabion retaining structures are widely used on Nepali hill roads principally because they are:
options: Flexible and permeable, and built from local boulders without cement
questions.solution:
**Flexible and permeable, and built from local boulders without cement.**

**Each property answers a specific difficulty of the Nepali hill setting:**

| Property | Why it matters there |
|---|---|
| **Built from LOCAL boulders** | The rivers and hillsides supply the stone; **no transport of manufactured material** to a site that may have no road |
| **NO CEMENT, no formwork, no skilled labour** | Can be built by a **local workforce** in a remote location, with no curing water and no plant |
| **FLEXIBLE** | Tolerates **settlement and undermining** by **deforming and continuing to function**, where a rigid concrete wall **cracks and fails** |
| **PERMEABLE** | **Pore pressure cannot build up behind it** — which removes the commonest cause of retaining wall failure |
| **Modular** | Can be **extended or repaired incrementally**, a course at a time |
| Vegetation establishes in the voids | Improves appearance and adds root reinforcement over time |

**The flexibility and permeability are the two that matter most**, and they are the properties a concrete wall lacks:

> A hillside settles, creeps and is undermined by scour. A **rigid** wall responds by **cracking** — and once cracked it has failed. A **gabion** wall **deforms**, its wire baskets redistributing the load, and it goes on retaining the soil while visibly leaning.

> And because it is **permeable**, the water that would build up behind a solid wall simply **passes through**. Given that inadequate drainage is the commonest cause of retaining wall failure, a structure that cannot accumulate water behind it has eliminated the principal risk by its construction rather than by a detail that might be omitted.

**Option (a) is plainly wrong** — a gabion wall is far weaker than reinforced concrete in any structural sense. Its merit is not strength but **tolerance**.

**Option (d) is also wrong**, and its weaknesses should be known:

| Weakness | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Wire CORROSION** | Mitigated by **galvanising or PVC coating**, but finite |
| **ABRASION of the mesh** by boulders in a steep torrent | Limits its use in the steepest boulder reaches, where the bed load destroys it |
| Vandalism, wire theft | Real in some locations |
| Appearance | Improves as vegetation establishes |

So gabions require **inspection and repair** — a broken wire allows the stones to spill, and the failure propagates along the course.

**Design requirements**, since they are not merely stacked:

| Requirement | Detail |
|---|---|
| Stone size | Larger than the mesh opening; **hard, durable, angular** |
| Filling | **Hand-packed at the faces**, machine-filled behind; well graded to minimise voids |
| **Wire** | Galvanised, or **PVC coated** in aggressive conditions |
| **Lacing** | Baskets **laced together** at every edge, or the wall acts as separate boxes |
| **Filter** behind | Geotextile or graded stone, to prevent the backfill washing through the gabions |
| Foundation | Below scour depth; on a level, firm base |
| Batter | The face is usually **stepped or inclined back** |

**The filter behind is the detail most often omitted**, and it defeats the whole structure: without it the fine backfill **washes out through the stone**, the ground behind subsides, and the wall is left retaining a void.

**Related techniques used with gabions** in Nepal: **bio-engineering** on the slope above, **launching aprons** of loose stone at the toe where a river attacks, and **gabion check dams** in gullies to arrest erosion. The Department of Water Induced Disaster Management and the Department of Roads both publish standard details.

examTip.trick: Every property suits the terrain: **flexible** so it tolerates the differential settlement normal on hill ground without cracking; **permeable** so no water pressure can build behind it; **local boulders** so no cement or aggregate has to be hauled up the road.
examTip.mnemonic: **A gabion bends instead of breaking.** A rigid concrete wall on the same ground cracks at the first settlement, and then fails at the crack.

questions.stem: The passive resistance of soil in front of a retaining wall is often ignored in design because:
options: It acts in the same direction as the active thrust
It requires large wall movement to mobilise and the soil may be removed or eroded
questions.solution:
**It requires large wall movement to mobilise, and the soil may be removed or eroded.**

**Two independent reasons, and both are sufficient on their own:**

**1. The movement required.**

| State | Movement to fully mobilise |
|---|---|
| **Active** | **0.001 to 0.005 H** — small |
| **Passive** | **0.01 to 0.05 H** — roughly **TEN TIMES** more |

> By the time the passive resistance is **fully mobilised**, the wall has moved so far that it has already **failed in serviceability terms** — leaning visibly, cracking its coping, and distressing anything it supports.

So counting on full passive resistance is counting on a condition the structure must not be allowed to reach.

**2. The soil may not be there.**

| Cause | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Excavated for services** — a water main, a cable trench | Removed, possibly years later, by someone unaware of its structural role |
| **Scoured or eroded** by a watercourse | Removed by nature |
| **Softened** by water | Its strength reduced |
| Removed for landscaping or road widening | — |

The soil in front of a wall is **shallow, exposed and unprotected**, and nothing marks it as structurally essential. Designing a wall to depend on it is designing a wall that a trench can undermine.

**Standard practice therefore:**

| Approach | Application |
|---|---|
| **Ignore passive resistance entirely** | The usual, and always for the **top 0.5 to 1 m** |
| Apply a **large factor** to it (2 to 3, beyond the overall F) | Where it is relied on and the soil is protected |
| Use only the resistance **below a stated depth** | Discounting the vulnerable upper zone |

**Where passive resistance IS legitimately relied on:**

| Structure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Sheet pile walls** | Their whole stability depends on passive resistance below dredge level — but it is **factored**, and a **dredge-level allowance** is deducted |
| **Anchor blocks and deadmen** | Passive resistance is the mechanism |
| **Shear keys** under a wall base | The key mobilises passive resistance to resist sliding |
| Braced excavations | The soil below formation |

**Even there the value is reduced** — commonly by taking a factored φ, by using the **curved-surface** (Caquot–Kerisel) coefficients rather than Coulomb's, and by assuming an over-dig.

**A further reason to be cautious with passive values**: Coulomb's theory **overestimates passive resistance** when wall friction is significant, because the real failure surface is **curved** while Coulomb assumes it planar. The error can be a factor of two or three for large δ — so a passive resistance computed by Coulomb and then relied upon compounds two unconservative assumptions.

**The general principle**, which recurs throughout geotechnical design:

> **Be conservative about the forces you rely on to RESIST, and generous about the forces that DRIVE.** Passive resistance resists; it should therefore be treated sceptically. Water pressure drives; it should be assumed present unless drainage is certain.

examTip.trick: The asymmetry is large: the **active** state needs a wall movement of about **0.1–0.4% of H** to mobilise, but the **passive** state needs **2–5% of H** — ten times more, which is far beyond the tolerable movement of a real wall.
examTip.mnemonic: **Passive resistance arrives too late to help.** And the soil in front is exactly the soil that gets excavated for a service trench. Ignoring it is prudence, not conservatism.

questions.stem: In a counterfort retaining wall, the counterforts are provided on the:
options: Exposed face, and act in compression
Earth side, and act in tension
questions.solution:
**On the EARTH side, and they act in TENSION.**

**The distinction from a buttress wall:**

| | **COUNTERFORT wall** | **BUTTRESS wall** |
|---|---|---|
| Ribs on the | **EARTH (backfill) side** — buried | **EXPOSED side** — visible |
| Ribs act in | **TENSION** | **COMPRESSION** |
| Structurally | **Inferior** — concrete is weak in tension, so the counterforts need **substantial reinforcement** | **Better** — concrete is strong in compression |
| Appearance | **Better** — the ribs are hidden | Worse — the ribs project into the visible face |
| Space | Does not occupy usable space in front | **Occupies usable space** in front |
| Common? | **More common** | Less common |

**Why counterforts are in tension.** The stem spans horizontally between the counterforts and is pushed **outward** by the earth pressure. The counterforts, being on the earth side, must **HOLD THE STEM BACK** against that push — so they are **pulled**, that is, in tension. A buttress on the far side would instead be **pushed**, and would resist in compression.

**The paradox is that the structurally inferior arrangement is the more common one**, and the reason is not structural at all:

> **Counterforts are buried in the backfill** and therefore **invisible**, while **buttresses project into the space in front of the wall** — which is usually the space the wall was built to create. Architecture and usable area win over structural efficiency.

**When either is used:**

| Wall height | Type |
|---|---|
| Up to ~3 m | **Gravity** |
| **3 – 8 m** | **Cantilever** |
| **Over 8 m** | **Counterfort or buttress** |

**Why a cantilever wall becomes uneconomical above about 8 m** is worth understanding: the stem is a **vertical cantilever**, so its bending moment increases as the **CUBE of the height** (M ∝ γH³). Doubling the height multiplies the moment eightfold, and the stem thickness required at the base becomes prohibitive.

**Counterforts change the structural action entirely:** instead of a tall vertical cantilever, the stem becomes a **slab spanning HORIZONTALLY between the counterforts** — a span of perhaps 3 m instead of a cantilever of 10 m. The moment falls dramatically, and the stem can be thin. The counterforts themselves act as **vertical cantilevers of T section**, with the stem as their flange.

**Structural design of the elements:**

| Element | Designed as |
|---|---|
| **Stem** | A **continuous slab spanning horizontally** between counterforts (with cantilever action at the top, above the topmost counterfort) |
| **Counterfort** | A **vertical cantilever of T section**, in **tension** at the earth face — its main reinforcement placed along the **sloping back face** |
| **Heel slab** | Spans **between counterforts**, loaded **downward** by the soil above |
| **Toe slab** | A **cantilever** from the stem, loaded **upward** by soil pressure |

**The counterfort's main reinforcement runs along the SLOPING back face**, which is the tension face — a detail that is examined and that is easy to get wrong on a drawing, since intuition suggests the vertical face.

**Counterfort spacing** is typically **0.3 to 0.6 times the wall height**, balancing the stem's horizontal span against the number of counterforts.

examTip.trap: **Buttresses** are the mirror image and are the standard confusion: buttresses go on the **front (opposite) face** and work in **compression**.
examTip.trick: Ask which way the stem bends. The earth pushes the stem outward, so the earth face is in **tension** — and the counterfort ties it back.
examTip.mnemonic: **Counterfort: earth side, tension, hidden. Buttress: front side, compression, visible and in the way.** Counterforts win because the buttress occupies usable space. Both become economical above about **6 m** height.

questions.stem: Geophysical methods of soil exploration are best described as:
options: Rapid and non-intrusive, but indirect and requiring calibration against boreholes
questions.solution:
**Rapid and non-intrusive, but INDIRECT and requiring calibration against boreholes.**

**The two principal methods:**

| Method | Principle | Detects |
|---|---|---|
| **Seismic refraction** | Times the travel of an induced **seismic wave**; velocity **increases with density and stiffness** | **Depth to bedrock**, thickness of overburden, rippability of rock |
| **Electrical resistivity** | Measures the soil's **resistance to an electric current** | **Water table**, changes in soil type, **contamination**, cavities |

Others: ground penetrating radar (shallow, high resolution), seismic reflection, cross-hole seismic, magnetic and gravity surveys.

**Their advantages:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **RAPID** | A large area covered in a day |
| **NON-INTRUSIVE** | No excavation, no damage, works over roads and structures |
| **CONTINUOUS coverage** | Interpolates between boreholes rather than sampling points |
| **Cheap per unit area** | Especially for large sites — a dam, a road corridor, a canal alignment |
| Reaches inaccessible ground | — |

**Their fundamental limitation:**

> They measure a **PHYSICAL PROPERTY** (seismic velocity, electrical resistivity) — **NOT** an engineering property. The relation between the two must be **inferred**, and the inference requires **calibration against boreholes** at known locations.

**Specific ambiguities**, which is why interpretation needs judgement:

| Ambiguity | Example |
|---|---|
| Different materials give **similar readings** | A dense saturated sand and a weathered rock may have the same seismic velocity |
| **A low-velocity layer beneath a high-velocity one is INVISIBLE** to seismic refraction | Weak rock beneath a strong crust is missed entirely — a serious and classic failure |
| Resistivity is dominated by **water and salinity** | A change in reading may mean a change in pore water, not in soil type |
| **No sample** is recovered | The material cannot be identified or tested |

**The hidden low-velocity layer is the most dangerous limitation**, and it is worth stating: seismic refraction works by detecting waves that travel faster in a deeper layer and refract back. If a **slower** layer lies beneath a faster one, no such refraction occurs and the layer is **not detected at all** — so a weak stratum beneath a hard crust is completely missed.

**The correct use is COMPLEMENTARY:**

> **Boreholes** give **exact information at a few points**. **Geophysics** gives **approximate information everywhere between them**. Used together, the boreholes **calibrate** the geophysical interpretation and the geophysics **interpolates** the borehole data.

That combination is far better than either alone, and is standard practice on any large site.

**Where geophysics is particularly valuable:**

| Application | Why |
|---|---|
| **Dam and reservoir sites** | Large area, depth to rock critical |
| **Road and canal alignments** | Long corridor, many kilometres |
| **Tunnel routes** | Depth and rock quality along the line |
| **Locating buried features** | Old foundations, cavities, services |
| **Rippability assessment** | Seismic velocity indicates whether rock can be ripped or must be blasted — a large cost difference |

**The rippability application** is a good example of the method used well: the contractor needs to know whether excavation will be by ripper or by blasting, the answer depends on the rock's seismic velocity, and geophysics measures exactly that — with a borehole or two to confirm the rock type.

examTip.trick: Seismic refraction and electrical resistivity cover ground **fast and cheaply** and find the shape of the bedrock surface — but they measure a **physical property**, not the soil itself.
examTip.mnemonic: **Geophysics maps between the boreholes; it never replaces them.** Use it to decide where to drill, then calibrate the interpretation against what the drilling actually finds.

questions.stem: A shear key is provided beneath the base of a retaining wall primarily to:
options: Reduce the earth pressure on the stem
questions.solution:
**To increase the resistance to SLIDING.**

**How it works.** A **shear key** is a downward projection from the base slab, cast into the soil beneath. It increases the sliding resistance in two ways:

| Mechanism | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Mobilises PASSIVE resistance** in front of the key | The soil in front of the key must be pushed forward for the wall to slide |
| **Forces the failure surface deeper**, into **soil rather than along the concrete–soil interface** | The friction angle available becomes **φ (soil on soil)** instead of **δ (soil on concrete, typically ⅔φ)** |

**The second mechanism is the more reliable**, and it is often overlooked. Sliding resistance along the base is **ΣV tan δ**, with δ perhaps two thirds of φ. A key that forces the failure plane down into the soil raises that to **ΣV tan φ** — an increase of perhaps 20–30% with no reliance on passive resistance at all.

**Where to place the key** is a genuine design question:

| Position | Argument |
|---|---|
| **Under the STEM** | The key's tension is resisted by the stem reinforcement continuing into it — **structurally the easiest to reinforce**, and the usual choice |
| Under the **heel** | Mobilises passive resistance in undisturbed soil |
| Under the **toe** | Passive resistance is in front, but the soil there is the most vulnerable to removal |

**Under the stem is normally preferred** because the stem's main reinforcement can simply be extended down into the key, requiring no special detailing — whereas a key elsewhere must be separately anchored into the base slab.

**Other measures to resist sliding**, in rough order of preference:

| Measure | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Widen the base** | Increases ΣV, hence friction |
| **Shear key** | As above |
| **Batter (incline) the base** | Inclines the resistance favourably, so a component of the weight resists sliding directly |
| **Roughen the base** | Increases δ |
| Rely on **passive resistance** in front | **Usually discounted** — the soil may be removed |
| Piles or anchors | Where the above are insufficient |

**Why the other options are wrong:**

| Option | Actually addressed by |
|---|---|
| Reduce **bearing pressure** | **Widening the base**, or reducing the eccentricity |
| Prevent **overturning** | Widening the base, increasing the weight, or moving the resultant toward the middle third |
| Reduce **earth pressure on the stem** | Free-draining backfill, a relieving platform, or reducing the surcharge |

A key does incidentally affect the pressure distribution slightly, but its purpose is sliding.

**The sliding check:**

> **F_sliding = (ΣV tan δ + c_a B + P_p) / ΣH ≥ 1.5**

where c_a is the base adhesion and P_p the passive resistance — the last term usually **omitted or heavily factored**, for the reasons set out earlier.

**Sliding frequently governs a low, wide wall** while **overturning governs a tall, narrow one** — which is worth knowing when a wall fails a check, because it indicates which dimension to change. If sliding governs, widen the base or add a key; if overturning governs, widen the base or increase the weight.

examTip.trick: The key forces the sliding surface **down into undisturbed soil** instead of along the smooth concrete–soil interface, and it mobilises **passive resistance** on its own face.
examTip.mnemonic: **A shear key buys sliding resistance, not overturning resistance.** Cast it **monolithically** with the base — a key cast later has a construction joint exactly where the shear must cross.

questions.stem: In a braced excavation, the lateral pressure distribution on the sheeting is best represented by:
options: An empirical rectangular or trapezoidal apparent pressure diagram
questions.solution:
**An empirical rectangular or trapezoidal APPARENT PRESSURE diagram** — the Terzaghi and Peck diagrams.

**Why the classical triangular distribution does not apply**, and the reasoning is instructive:

> In a **retaining wall**, the wall is built first and the soil placed against it; the wall then **rotates about its base**, so the top moves most and the classical **triangular active** distribution develops.

> In a **BRACED EXCAVATION**, the sequence is reversed. The **top strut is installed FIRST**, before much excavation, so the **top of the wall CANNOT MOVE**. Excavation then proceeds downward, and each successive level of the wall moves progressively more before its strut is installed.

**The result is that the wall rotates about its TOP rather than its base** — the opposite of a retaining wall — so:

| Zone | Movement | Pressure |
|---|---|---|
| **Top** | **Restrained** by the first strut | **Higher** than active — near at-rest |
| **Bottom** | Freer to move inward | Closer to active |

The pressure distribution is therefore **not triangular** but roughly **rectangular or trapezoidal**, with substantial pressure at the top where the triangular diagram predicts almost none.

**Terzaghi and Peck's apparent pressure diagrams** were derived **empirically from MEASURED STRUT LOADS** on real excavations, not from theory — which is why they are called *apparent* pressure diagrams. They are envelopes for **designing the struts**, not predictions of the actual pressure at any point:

| Soil | Diagram | Maximum pressure |
|---|---|---|
| **Sand** | **Rectangular** | **0.65 K_a γ H** |
| **Soft to medium clay** | **Trapezoidal** | γH − 4c, or 0.3γH, whichever is greater |
| **Stiff fissured clay** | Trapezoidal | 0.2 to 0.4 γH |

**They are envelopes, not distributions** — an important qualification. The actual pressure varies from strut to strut and from excavation to excavation; the diagram is drawn to **envelope** the observed loads so that **every strut** designed from it is adequate. Summing the diagram to get a total thrust and comparing it with the Rankine value is therefore not meaningful.

**The other design checks for a braced excavation:**

| Check | Concern |
|---|---|
| **Strut loads** | From the apparent pressure diagram |
| **BASE HEAVE** in soft clay | The excavation bottom **heaves upward** as the surrounding soil's weight pushes it in — a bearing capacity failure in reverse |
| **Piping / quick condition** at the base | Upward seepage where the water table is above formation |
| Wall bending and embedment | Structural |
| **Ground movement outside** | Settlement damaging adjacent buildings — often the governing criterion in an urban site |

**Base heave** deserves a note because it is peculiar to this situation and can be sudden: in a deep excavation in soft clay, the **weight of soil outside** the excavation acts as a surcharge, and if it exceeds the bearing capacity of the clay at formation level, the clay **flows inward and upward**, heaving the base and drawing the walls in. The factor of safety is checked as **F = N_c c_u / (γH + q)**, and the remedy is a deeper wall embedment, ground improvement, or reducing the surcharge outside.

**Ground movement outside the excavation** is frequently the real constraint in a city: even a wall that is entirely stable may allow enough settlement behind it to damage adjacent buildings, and predicting that movement — rather than merely proving stability — is what governs the design of a deep basement in a built-up area.

examTip.trap: The classic triangular Rankine diagram is wrong here and is the natural wrong answer.
examTip.trick: A braced cut is held at the **top first**, so it cannot rotate about its base and the classical active state never develops. The measured pressure is roughly **uniform with depth**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Struts change the shape of the pressure diagram.** Terzaghi and Peck's apparent-pressure envelopes are an **envelope of maxima for strut design**, not a real pressure distribution at any one moment — so never use them to compute a total thrust.

questions.stem: Negative skin friction on a pile:
options: Increases the load carrying capacity of the pile
Acts upward and adds to the pile's resistance
Acts downward and is an additional load on the pile
questions.solution:
**It acts DOWNWARD and is an ADDITIONAL LOAD on the pile.**

**When it occurs:**

> Where the **surrounding SOIL SETTLES MORE than the PILE**, the soil **hangs on the pile** and drags it down.

In normal circumstances the pile settles relative to the soil, so the shaft friction acts **upward** and helps carry the load. Negative skin friction is the **reversal** of that relationship — and with it, the reversal of the direction of the friction force.

**Causes:**

| Cause | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **A recently placed FILL** consolidating over soft ground | The commonest case — the fill settles as it consolidates |
| **Lowered water table** | Increases effective stress, so the soil consolidates |
| A **soft clay layer consolidating** under a new surcharge | — |
| **Remoulding during driving**, followed by reconsolidation | The disturbed soil around the pile reconsolidates and settles |
| Ground **subsidence** from any cause | — |

**The consequence for design:**

> **Q_net = Q_ultimate − Q_negative**

It must be **SUBTRACTED**, never added — and the magnitude can be very large, sometimes exceeding the structural load the pile was designed to carry. A pile that appeared adequately designed can be overloaded entirely by drag-down.

**Estimating it**: over the depth of the settling layer, **Q_n = perimeter × depth × unit negative friction**, with the unit friction taken as **α c_u** in clay (the same adhesion as positive friction) or **K σ′_v tan δ** in granular fill.

**Mitigation:**

| Measure | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Bitumen (slip) COATING** on the shaft through the settling layer | Reduces the adhesion to a small fraction — the standard solution |
| **Isolation sleeve or casing** | Physically separates the pile from the settling soil |
| **Design for the extra load** | Accept it and lengthen or enlarge the pile |
| **Preload the fill** before piling | Lets the settlement occur first |
| Use fewer, larger piles | Reduces the total perimeter |

**The bitumen coating is the elegant solution**, and it works because the negative friction depends on the **adhesion at the shaft**: a soft bitumen layer allows the soil to slide past the pile with very little shear transfer, reducing the drag to perhaps a tenth of its unprotected value. It must of course be applied **only over the settling layer** — coating the bearing length would remove the positive friction as well.

**A subtlety worth noting**: negative skin friction develops only where the **relative movement** is in that direction, so there is a **NEUTRAL POINT** on the shaft above which the soil settles more than the pile (negative friction) and below which the pile settles more than the soil (positive friction). Its position depends on the relative stiffnesses, and a more refined analysis locates it rather than assuming the whole settling layer contributes.

**A group effect also applies**: for a **group** of piles, the negative friction cannot exceed the **weight of the settling soil enclosed by the group** — so for a large group the drag-down per pile is less than for an isolated pile, and taking the lesser of the two calculations avoids a grossly conservative result.

examTip.trap: "Increases the capacity" is the natural but exactly backwards reading — friction normally helps, so people assume all friction helps.
examTip.trick: Ask which moves more. Normally the **pile** settles relative to the soil, so friction acts **upward**. Where the **soil** settles more — consolidating fill, lowered water table — the relationship reverses and the soil hangs on the pile.
examTip.mnemonic: **Q_net = Q_ult − Q_negative — SUBTRACT it, never add.** The remedy is a **bitumen slip coating** over the settling layer only; coating the bearing length would remove the useful friction too.

questions.stem: By Rankine's formula, the minimum depth of a shallow foundation is:
questions.solution:
**D_min = (q/γ)[(1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ)]² = (q/γ) K_a².**

**Where it comes from.** Rankine reasoned that at the minimum depth, the soil beneath the footing should be in a state of **plastic equilibrium** — with the applied pressure q as the major principal stress and the horizontal stress at that depth as the minor one. Setting the horizontal stress equal to the **active** value gives

> **D = (q/γ) K_a²**

**Note the K_a is SQUARED**, which is what distinguishes the correct option: two applications of the active state, one for the transfer of the applied pressure into horizontal stress and one for the resulting depth.

**But the formula is rarely what actually governs.** In practice the minimum depth is set by whichever of the following is deepest:

| Requirement | Reason |
|---|---|
| **At least 0.5 m below ground** | A practical minimum |
| **Below the zone of seasonal MOISTURE change** | Avoids shrink–swell movement, especially in expansive clay |
| **Below any FILL** | Fill is variable and continues to settle |
| **Below the FROST line** | Where relevant — the high hills |
| **Below the SCOUR depth** | Beside a watercourse — this often governs by a large margin |
| Below the topsoil and organic layer | — |
| Below the influence of adjacent excavations | — |

**The scour requirement is the one that dominates for a bridge or any structure near a river**, and it is computed from **Lacey's formula** with a multiplier:

> **R = 0.473(Q/f)^{1/3}**, and the foundation taken below **1.5 to 2 R** at a pier — plus a grip length

A foundation founded above the scour depth will be **undermined in the first large flood**, however adequate its bearing capacity, which is why scour rather than bearing usually fixes the depth of a bridge foundation.

**The four requirements a foundation must satisfy**, of which depth is the first:

| Requirement | Check |
|---|---|
| **1. Adequate DEPTH** | As above |
| **2. Safety against SHEAR (bearing) failure** | Factor of safety 2.5 to 3 on ultimate capacity |
| **3. SETTLEMENT within tolerable limits** | Total and, more importantly, **differential** |
| **4. Adequate structural strength and durability** | The footing itself must resist its bending and shear |

**Requirements 2 and 3 must BOTH be checked, and either may govern:**

| Soil | Usually governed by |
|---|---|
| **Dense sand and gravel** | **SETTLEMENT** — capacity is ample |
| **Soft to medium clay** | **SHEAR** — capacity is low |
| Stiff clay | Either |

Assuming that bearing capacity always governs is one of the commonest conceptual errors in foundation design, and it leads to footings on dense sand that are perfectly safe against failure and unacceptable in settlement.

examTip.trick: Note the **K_a is SQUARED** — that is what separates the right option from the plausible ones.
examTip.mnemonic: **D = (q/γ)K_a².** But in practice this formula rarely governs: **SCOUR** almost always demands a greater depth near any watercourse, and seasonal moisture change governs in expansive soil. Compute it, then check what really controls.

questions.stem: A foundation is generally classified as shallow when the ratio of its depth to its width is:
options: Less than or about equal to 1
questions.solution:
**Less than or about equal to 1**, that is **D_f/B ≤ 1**.

**The distinction is not merely one of depth**, and that is the substance worth understanding:

| | **SHALLOW foundation** | **DEEP foundation** |
|---|---|---|
| **D_f/B** | **≤ about 1** | **> 1**, often ≫ 1 |
| **Load transferred** | **Mainly through the BASE**, onto soil near the surface | Through **SHAFT FRICTION and END BEARING**, to strata well below |
| Side resistance | **Neglected** | **Essential** |
| Construction | Open excavation | Driven, bored or sunk |
| Types | Isolated, combined, strap, strip, **raft** | **Pile**, pier, well/caisson |

**So the classification reflects the LOAD TRANSFER MECHANISM**, and the depth ratio is simply the geometric condition under which one mechanism or the other dominates. A shallow foundation's side friction over a depth less than its width is negligible; a pile's side friction over tens of diameters is the greater part of its capacity.

**Selecting the type — the discriminator is the PROBLEM, not the depth:**

| Problem | Foundation |
|---|---|
| Single column, reasonable soil | **Isolated (spread) footing** |
| Two columns too close for separate footings | **Combined footing** |
| Column at a **BOUNDARY**, footing cannot be centred | **STRAP (cantilever) footing** |
| A load-bearing **wall** | **Strip / continuous footing** |
| **WEAK soil over a LARGE loaded area** — footings would cover > half the plan | **RAFT (mat)** |
| Firm stratum **OUT OF REACH** of a shallow foundation | **PILES** |
| Deep water, heavy concentrated load (bridge pier) | **WELL / caisson** |
| Very weak soil over a firm stratum, heavy structure | **Piled raft** |

**The pairing most often confused is RAFT versus PILES**, and the distinction is a matter of strategy:

> A **RAFT SPREADS** the load over the greatest available area — and it is a **SHALLOW** foundation.
> **PILES TRANSFER** the load **downward** to a deeper, stronger stratum.

**Spreading and transferring are different strategies for different problems.** A raft does nothing to reach a deeper stratum; piles do nothing to reduce the pressure on the soil near the surface. Choosing between them is choosing which problem you have.

**The raft's economic threshold** is worth carrying:

> A raft becomes economical when individual footings would cover **more than about HALF the plan area** — at which point casting one continuous slab is both cheaper (no separate excavations, less formwork) and structurally better.

**Its second and often decisive advantage** is that it **ties the whole structure together**, greatly reducing **DIFFERENTIAL** settlement: the raft settles more or less as one body. That matters more than total settlement, because a building settling **50 mm uniformly is undamaged** while one settling **10 mm unevenly cracks**.

examTip.trick: The ratio is a proxy for the **load transfer mechanism**: a shallow foundation delivers load through its **base**; a deep one adds **shaft friction**, which only becomes significant over many diameters.
examTip.mnemonic: **D_f/B ≤ 1 is shallow.** Below that ratio the side friction over a depth less than the width contributes almost nothing, so ignoring it is reasonable.

questions.stem: A raft foundation becomes economical when the individual footings would otherwise cover more than about:
questions.solution:
**About 50% of the plan area.**

**The reasoning is direct.** As the soil weakens, each footing must grow to keep the pressure within the allowable value:

> **A = total service load / net allowable bearing pressure**

When the footings become so large that they **nearly touch**, the separate excavations, the separate formwork and the awkward gaps between them cost more than a single continuous slab would — and the slab is structurally better. **Half the plan area** is the conventional threshold at which the balance tips.

**A raft's two distinct benefits:**

| Benefit | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Spreads the load over the greatest possible area** | **q = total load / total area** — the lowest pressure achievable on a shallow foundation |
| **TIES the structure together, reducing DIFFERENTIAL settlement** | The raft settles more or less **as one body** |

**The second is often the decisive one**, and it is worth stating why:

> **DIFFERENTIAL settlement damages a structure; TOTAL settlement generally does not.** A building settling **50 mm uniformly** needs its services and approaches adjusted and is otherwise undamaged. One settling **10 mm unevenly** cracks.

A raft converts a set of independently settling footings into a single stiff body, so the differential movement across the building is greatly reduced even if the total settlement is unchanged.

**Types of raft:**

| Type | Form | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **Flat plate** | Uniform slab | Light loads, closely spaced columns |
| Plate **thickened under columns** | Local thickening | Where **punching shear** governs locally |
| **Beam and slab** | Slab stiffened by beams | Heavier or unequal loads |
| **Cellular / box** | Two slabs with intersecting walls | Very stiff, and **BUOYANT** |
| **Piled raft** | Raft plus piles | Very weak soil, heavy structure |

**The BUOYANCY (floating) raft** is worth understanding for its ingenuity:

> Excavating a deep basement **REMOVES a weight of soil**. If that removed weight approaches the weight of the building, the **NET increase in pressure at foundation level is near ZERO** — so a heavy building can be carried on soil that would not otherwise support it.

A **fully compensated** foundation removes exactly the building's weight; a **partially compensated** one removes some of it. The concept converts an unsuitable site into a suitable one at no cost beyond the basement that was often wanted anyway.

**Its check is UPLIFT**: an empty basement below the water table will **FLOAT**, and swimming pools, sewage tanks and empty basements have all done so. The uplift case — the structure complete but unloaded, water table high — must be checked, and the remedies are added dead weight, tension piles or anchors, or a controlled relief valve.

**Design methods for a raft:**

| Method | Assumption |
|---|---|
