| **Rigid (conventional)** | The raft is **perfectly stiff**, so the pressure distribution is **linear** — simple and conservative for stiff rafts with regular column layouts |
| **Flexible** | The soil is a **bed of springs** of stiffness **k**, the modulus of subgrade reaction — a beam-on-elastic-foundation analysis |
| Finite element | Full soil–structure interaction |

**The rigid method is used where the raft is genuinely stiff** relative to the soil — the usual case for a thick raft on soft soil — and it has the merit of requiring only statics. Where the raft is thin and the columns irregularly spaced, the flexible method is needed, and the modulus of subgrade reaction becomes the governing parameter.

examTip.trick: Once separate footings nearly touch, the separate excavations, formwork and awkward gaps cost more than one continuous slab — which is also structurally better.
examTip.mnemonic: **Half the plan area is the tipping point.** The raft's second and often decisive benefit is that it **ties the structure together**, cutting *differential* settlement — and it is differential settlement, not total, that cracks buildings.

questions.stem: A strap (cantilever) footing is used when:
options: A column is located at a property boundary and its footing cannot be centred
questions.solution:
**When a column is located at a property boundary and its footing cannot be centred beneath it.**

**The problem it solves.** A footing under a boundary column cannot extend beyond the property line, so it must be **eccentric** — its centroid offset from the column. That eccentricity produces:

| Consequence | Effect |
|---|---|
| A **non-uniform pressure** distribution | High pressure at one edge, possibly tension at the other |
| An **overturning moment** on the footing | The footing tends to **tilt** |
| Possible **loss of contact** at the far edge | Reducing the effective area and worsening the pressure |

**The strap footing's solution** is to link the eccentric boundary footing to an **interior footing** by a rigid **strap beam**, which **transfers the moment** to the interior footing and allows both to bear uniformly.

**The key design points:**

| Point | Requirement |
|---|---|
| The **strap beam is designed for BENDING ONLY** | It is a **flexural link**, not a bearing element |
| The strap is often **cast clear of the soil**, or the soil beneath it loosened | So it does **not bear** — otherwise it attracts pressure and the analysis fails |
| The strap must be **RIGID** | A flexible strap does not transfer the moment effectively |
| Both footings are proportioned for **uniform pressure** | Which is the object of the arrangement |

**Casting the strap clear of the soil is the detail most often misunderstood.** If the strap bears on the ground it carries load directly, the assumed distribution is wrong, and the moment transfer is incomplete. The design assumes the strap acts purely as a beam, and the construction must make that true.

**The alternatives for a boundary column**, and each has its place:

| Solution | When |
|---|---|
| **Strap footing** | An interior column is available within a reasonable distance |
| **Combined footing** | The two columns are **close enough** for one footing to span both |
| **Eccentric footing** designed for the moment | Small load, or the eccentricity is modest |
| Cantilever from a pile cap | Where piles are used anyway |

**Combined footings** deserve a note alongside, since they solve the related problem of two columns too close for separate footings:

> A combined footing must be shaped — **rectangular or TRAPEZOIDAL** — so that its **CENTROID COINCIDES with the RESULTANT of the two column loads**.

If it does not, the pressure is non-uniform and the footing tilts. A **trapezoidal** shape is used where the loads are **unequal and the space is constrained**, since a rectangle of the required length would place its centroid in the wrong position.

**The general principle behind all of these** is worth stating, because it recurs:

> **A foundation bears uniformly only when the RESULTANT of the loads passes through the CENTROID of its bearing area.** Every combined, strap and trapezoidal footing is a device for arranging that where the column positions alone would not.

**Structural design** of a strap footing: the **strap beam** for the transferred moment and the shear, the **boundary footing** for the reduced (now concentric) pressure, and the **interior footing** for its own load plus the reaction from the strap — which may be **upward or downward** depending on the geometry, and which is easy to get wrong in sign.

examTip.trick: A boundary footing cannot be centred, so it is eccentric, so it tilts. The strap beam transfers that moment to an interior footing and lets both bear uniformly.
examTip.mnemonic: **The strap is a BEAM, not a bearing element — cast it clear of the soil.** If it bears, it attracts load and the whole analysis is invalid. That single detail is what the design depends on.

questions.stem: The minimum centre-to-centre spacing of friction piles in a group is generally:
questions.solution:
**2.5 to 3 times the pile diameter** (and not less than **750 mm** for friction piles under IS 2911).

**Why a minimum spacing is needed at all** — three distinct reasons:

| Reason | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **Overlapping stress zones** | Each pile stresses a zone of soil around it. Too close, and the zones **overlap**, so the piles compete for the same soil and the group carries less than the sum of its parts |
| **Construction difficulty** | Driving a pile close to one already installed can **damage or heave** it; bored piles can break into one another |
| **Group behaves as a BLOCK** | At very close spacing the group and the soil between it act as a single large pier |

**Group efficiency** quantifies the first:

> **η = group capacity / (n × single pile capacity)**

| Soil | Efficiency | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **CLAY** | **LESS than 1** | The group acts as a **BLOCK**; the perimeter-to-area ratio falls as the group grows |
| **Dense sand** | About 1 | — |
| **LOOSE sand, DRIVEN piles** | **MAY EXCEED 1** | **Driving DENSIFIES** the soil between the piles |

**The loose sand case is the interesting one**: driving a group of displacement piles into loose sand compacts the soil between them, so the group can be **stronger than the sum of the individual piles** — an efficiency above 100%, which surprises candidates but follows directly from the compaction effect.

**For a group in CLAY, the capacity must be checked BOTH ways** and the **lesser taken**:

| Check | Capacity |
|---|---|
| **Individual pile action** | n × (single pile capacity) |
| **BLOCK action** | The group treated as one large pier: **perimeter shear + base bearing** of the block |

For a closely spaced group in soft clay the **block** value is usually the smaller, and it governs.

**Converse–Labarre's formula** gives an empirical group efficiency, though it is now regarded as crude:

> **η = 1 − θ[(n−1)m + (m−1)n] / (90 m n)**, with θ = tan⁻¹(d/s) in degrees

**Other spacing considerations:**

| Pile type | Minimum spacing |
|---|---|
| **Friction piles** | **3 d**, minimum 750 mm |
| **End bearing piles** | **2.5 d** — less, because the load is delivered at the tip where the stress zones overlap less |
| Piles through soft clay to rock | 2 d may suffice |
| Under-reamed piles | **2 × the bulb diameter** |

**End bearing piles can be spaced closer** because their load is transferred at the **tip**, into a firm stratum, rather than distributed along the shaft — so the overlapping of shaft stress zones matters less.

**Maximum spacing** is limited too, by the **pile cap** economics: a widely spaced group needs a large and heavily reinforced cap, so spacing beyond about **4 d** is rarely economical.

**The pile cap** itself is designed as a thick slab or as a **strut-and-tie** system, and IS 2911 requires it to extend at least **150 mm beyond the outer piles** and to have the pile heads **embedded 50 to 75 mm** into it.

examTip.trick: Too close and the stress zones overlap so the piles compete for the same soil; too far and the pile cap becomes huge. Practice lands at **3d for friction piles, 2.5d for end bearing** (which deliver load at the tip, so their zones overlap less).
examTip.mnemonic: **3d friction, 2.5d end bearing, minimum 750 mm.** Group efficiency is **below 1 in clay** (block action) but can **exceed 1 in loose sand**, because driving densifies the soil between the piles.

questions.stem: A friction (floating) pile is used when:
options: No firm bearing stratum exists within reachable depth
Rock is present at 3 m depth
The water table is very deep
questions.solution:
**When no firm bearing stratum exists within reachable depth.**

**The two load-transfer mechanisms:**

| Pile type | Carries load by | Used when |
|---|---|---|
| **END BEARING (point bearing)** | **Tip resistance** on a **hard stratum** | A firm stratum exists at a **reachable depth** |
| **FRICTION (floating)** | **Shaft friction** along its length | **NO firm stratum within reach** — the pile is supported entirely by the soil around it |
| Combination | Both | **Most real piles** |

**The name "floating" captures it**: the pile does not reach anything solid; it is held up by the friction of the soil it passes through, as a nail is held in wood.

**Capacity:**

> **Q_u = Q_p (end bearing) + Q_s (shaft friction) − W (pile weight)**
> **Q_allowable = Q_u / F**, with **F = 2.5**

| Soil | End bearing Q_p | Shaft friction Q_s |
|---|---|---|
| **Clay** | **9 c_u A_p** | **α c_u A_s**, with the adhesion factor **α ≈ 0.5 – 1.0** |
| **Sand** | **σ′_v N_q A_p** | **K σ′_v tan δ A_s** |

**The adhesion factor α** falls as the clay gets stiffer — about 1.0 for soft clay, 0.5 or less for stiff clay — because a stiff clay is disturbed and gapped by pile installation, so the full undrained strength cannot be mobilised at the interface.

**A caution about sand that is genuinely important:**

> The end bearing in sand does **NOT grow indefinitely with depth**. Beyond a **CRITICAL DEPTH of about 15 to 20 pile diameters**, the tip resistance becomes **approximately CONSTANT**.

So a longer pile in uniform sand gains capacity mainly through **friction**, not end bearing — and calculations that apply σ′_v N_q at great depth, with σ′_v continuing to increase linearly, **grossly overestimate** the capacity. The same critical-depth limit applies to the unit shaft friction.

**Classification of piles by function**, the full set:

| Type | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **End bearing** | Transfers load to a hard stratum |
| **Friction** | Load carried by shaft resistance |
| **Compaction** | **Densifies loose granular soil** — ground improvement, not load transfer |
| **Tension (uplift)** | Resists **uplift** — transmission towers, buoyant structures |
| **Batter (raker)** | Inclined; resists **lateral** load — wharves, abutments |
| **Sheet** | **Retains** soil or water; not load bearing |
| Anchor | Provides anchorage |
| Fender, dolphin | Absorbs impact |

**By installation**, which affects the capacity as much as the geometry:

| Installation | Effect on the soil |
|---|---|
| **DRIVEN (displacement)** | **DENSIFIES** granular soil, so capacity may **exceed** prediction; but causes **vibration and noise**, and risks damaging adjacent structures |
| **BORED (non-displacement, cast in situ)** | **No vibration**; can pass obstructions and be inspected; but **no densification**, and quality depends on workmanship |
| Driven cast in situ | Casing driven, then filled |
| Jacked | No vibration; used for **underpinning** |

**In dense urban Kathmandu, BORED piles are usually preferred** despite their higher cost, because driving vibration damages adjacent masonry buildings — many of them old, unreinforced and already weakened. The choice is dictated by the neighbours rather than by the soil.

examTip.trick: The name says it: a floating pile reaches nothing solid and is held by the friction of the soil it passes through, as a nail is held in wood.
examTip.mnemonic: **No firm stratum in reach → float.** Watch the **critical depth** in sand: beyond about **15–20 diameters** the unit tip and shaft resistances stop increasing, so σ′_v N_q applied at great depth grossly overestimates capacity.

questions.stem: The safe load on a pile determined from an initial pile load test is taken as the lesser of two thirds of the load at failure and the load causing a settlement of:
questions.solution:
**12 mm** (or **10% of the pile diameter** for a bored pile).

**The pile load test (IS 2911 Part 4)** is the definitive verification of capacity, because it tests the actual pile in the actual ground rather than relying on correlations.

**Two kinds of test:**

| Test | Load | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **INITIAL (preliminary)** test | **2.5 × working load** | Establishes the **ultimate capacity**; done on a **test pile** before the working piles are installed |
| **ROUTINE test** | **1.5 × working load** | **Verifies construction quality** on selected **working** piles — typically 0.5 to 2% of them |

**Determining the safe load from an initial test** — the **lesser** of:

| Criterion | Value |
|---|---|
| **Two thirds of the load at which total settlement is 12 mm** | Settlement criterion |
| **Half the load at which total settlement equals 10% of the pile diameter** | Failure criterion |

and for a **routine** test, the acceptance criteria are a maximum total settlement of **12 mm** at 1.5 × working load and a **residual (net) settlement** not exceeding **6 mm** or 20% of the total.

**Both a total and a NET settlement criterion are applied**, and the reason is instructive: the **total** settlement includes elastic compression of the pile shaft, which is recoverable and harmless; the **net (residual)** settlement after unloading is the **permanent** movement, and it is what indicates whether the soil has been overstressed.

**Methods of loading:**

| Method | Character |
|---|---|
| **Kentledge** — a stacked dead load platform | Simple; needs a large weight, and is hazardous if it topples |
| **Reaction piles** with a beam | Tension piles either side provide the reaction; cleaner and safer |
| **Ground anchors** | Where suitable |

**Load is applied in increments** of about 20% of the working load, each held until the settlement rate falls below a stated value, with the final load held for a longer period.

**Why a load test is worth its considerable cost:**

| Reason | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **Static formulae are unreliable** | They depend on soil parameters that are hard to measure and on empirical factors |
| **Dynamic formulae are worse** | Engineering News and similar formulae are notoriously inaccurate |
| **It tests the ACTUAL pile in the ACTUAL soil** | Including all the effects of the installation method |
| It verifies **construction quality** | A bored pile with a necked shaft or a soft toe is revealed |

**The timing matters and is a real design consideration:**

> A pile driven into a **sensitive clay** temporarily **remoulds** the soil around it, destroying much of its capacity. The clay then **regains strength with time by THIXOTROPY**, so the pile's capacity **increases over days or weeks** — the **set-up** period.

Testing too soon therefore **understates** the capacity, sometimes by a large factor. IS 2911 specifies a minimum waiting period, and in a very sensitive clay the capacity may double between one day and one month.

**Conversely in dense sand**, driving can generate **relaxation** — a reduction of capacity over time — so the direction of the effect depends on the soil, and the waiting period must be chosen accordingly.

**Non-destructive integrity testing** complements the load test: **low-strain (pile echo / sonic) testing** on a large proportion of the piles detects **necking, bulging, discontinuities and soft toes**, at a small fraction of the cost of a load test. Modern practice combines a few load tests with widespread integrity testing.

examTip.trick: The safe load is the **lesser** of two criteria — two thirds of the load at 12 mm settlement, and half the load at a settlement of 10% of the diameter.
examTip.mnemonic: **12 mm total, 6 mm net (residual).** Both are checked because total settlement includes recoverable elastic shortening of the shaft; only the **net** movement shows the soil has been overstressed. Test too early in sensitive clay and you understate the capacity — thixotropic set-up can double it in weeks.

questions.stem: Under-reamed piles are particularly suited to:
options: Expansive soils, where uplift from swelling must be resisted
questions.solution:
**Expansive soils, where uplift from swelling must be resisted.**

**An under-reamed pile** is a bored cast-in-situ pile with one or more **enlarged bulbs (under-reams)** formed near its base by a special expanding cutting tool. The bulb diameter is typically **2 to 3 times** the shaft diameter.

**Why it suits expansive (black cotton) soil**, which is the point of the question:

> An expansive clay **SWELLS on wetting**, and the swelling exerts an **UPLIFT force on the pile shaft** in the active zone near the surface. A plain shaft, relying only on friction, can be **lifted bodily** — heaving the structure above and cracking it.

> The **BULB provides ANCHORAGE**: to lift the pile, the swelling force must lift the **cone of soil above the bulb** as well, which it cannot. The bulb is located **below the active zone**, in soil whose moisture content does not change seasonally.

That is a mechanism a straight-shafted pile simply cannot provide, and it is why under-reamed piles were developed (by the CBRI in India) specifically for the black cotton soils of the subcontinent.

**Their other advantages:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Increased bearing area** at the base | Greater end bearing for the same shaft |
| **Resists UPLIFT** | Wind uplift on light structures, transmission towers |
| **Economical** | A modest increase in excavation gives a large increase in capacity |
| No vibration | Bored, so suitable near existing structures |
| **Multi-under-reamed** piles | Two or more bulbs give further capacity |

**Design requirements (IS 2911 Part 3):**

| Requirement | Value |
|---|---|
| **Bulb diameter** | **2 to 3 × the shaft diameter** (2.5 usual) |
| **Spacing of bulbs** (multi-under-reamed) | **1.25 to 1.5 × the bulb diameter** |
| **Minimum depth** below ground to the topmost bulb | **2 × the bulb diameter**, and **below the active zone** |
| Minimum pile spacing | **2 × the BULB diameter** |
| Shaft diameter | Typically 200 – 500 mm |

**Locating the bulb below the ACTIVE ZONE is the essential requirement**, and it defines the depth of the pile. The active zone is the depth over which the moisture content changes seasonally — typically **1.5 to 3.5 m** in a black cotton soil, and it must be established for the site rather than assumed.

**Expansive soil more generally.** The problem is **montmorillonite** clay, whose **activity** (PI ÷ % finer than 2 μ) exceeds 1 and which can swell enormously:

| Damage | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Cracking of light structures** | **Differential heave** beneath a footing |
| **Breaking of pavements and floors** | Seasonal heave and shrinkage |
| **Distortion of canal linings and pipelines** | — |
| Deep **desiccation cracks** in the dry season | Which then admit water rapidly at the next rain |

**Treatments, of which under-reamed piles are one:**

| Treatment | Character |
|---|---|
| **Under-reamed piles** | Anchor below the active zone |
| **Remove and replace** | With non-expansive fill |
| **Granular capping** — a cushion layer | Absorbs the movement |
| **LIME stabilisation** | Calcium replaces sodium on the exchange sites, **reducing plasticity** |
| **MOISTURE CONTROL** — impervious apron, drainage, avoiding trees near the building | Keeps the water content **stable so the soil never cycles** |
| Deep foundations below the zone | — |

**Moisture control is the most fundamental**, because the soil only moves when its water content changes. A stable moisture regime — achieved by an apron preventing infiltration next to the building, proper surface drainage, and avoiding vegetation that seasonally dries the soil — removes the cause rather than resisting the effect.

examTip.trick: Expansive clay **swells on wetting** and drags a plain shaft **upward**. The bulb anchors the pile by requiring the swelling force to lift the cone of soil above it as well — which it cannot.
examTip.mnemonic: **The bulb must sit BELOW the active zone** (the depth over which moisture changes seasonally, typically 1.5–3.5 m). Bulb diameter 2–2.5 × shaft; pile spacing 2 × the BULB diameter, not the shaft.

questions.stem: In a well (caisson) foundation for a bridge pier, the grip length is normally taken as:
options: One half of the maximum scour depth
One third of the maximum scour depth, below that depth
questions.solution:
**One third of the maximum scour depth, measured BELOW that depth.**

**Grip length** is the depth of the well **below the maximum anticipated scour level**, and it provides the **lateral stability** of the foundation — resisting the horizontal forces from water current, wind, braking, earthquake and earth pressure.

**Why it is measured below the SCOUR level and not below the bed** is the essential point:

> In flood the bed **scours away**, and whatever depth of soil is removed provides **no lateral support at all**. The foundation's stability must therefore be assessed on the ground **remaining after the worst scour** — which is why the grip is measured from that level, not from the existing bed.

A foundation designed on the present bed level and then subjected to 5 m of scour has lost 5 m of its assumed lateral support, and may be unstable at exactly the moment the current is strongest.

**Maximum scour depth** from **Lacey's formula**:

> **R = 0.473 (Q/f)^{1/3}**  (or 1.35(q²/f)^{1/3} per unit width)

multiplied by a factor for the location:

| Location | Multiplier on R |
|---|---|
| Straight reach | 1.25 |
| **Nose of a bridge PIER** | **2.0** |
| Severe bend | 1.75 – 2.0 |
| Upstream curved head of a guide bank | 2.0 – 2.75 |

**Components of a well foundation**, examined by name:

| Component | Function |
|---|---|
| **Cutting edge** | The sharp steel-shod bottom edge that **cuts into the soil** as the well sinks |
| **Curb** | The tapered RCC section above the cutting edge |
| **Steining** | The **wall** of the well — provides weight for sinking and resists earth pressure |
| **Bottom plug** | Concrete sealing the base after sinking, transferring load to the soil |
| **Sand filling** | Fills the dredge hole; adds weight and stability |
| **Top plug** | Seals the top of the sand filling |
| **Well cap** | Transfers the pier load to the steining |

**How a well is sunk**: the curb and steining are built at the surface, and soil is **excavated (dredged) from inside** the dredge hole. The well then **sinks under its own weight**, and further steining is added as it descends. Where the weight is insufficient, **kentledge** is added on top or the skin friction is reduced by **water jetting** or a **bentonite slurry**.

**Tilt and shift** are the characteristic construction problems:

| Problem | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **TILT** | The well leans from the vertical |
| **SHIFT** | Its centre has moved horizontally from the intended position |

Permissible values are typically **tilt 1 in 80** and **shift 150 mm or 1% of the depth**. They are corrected during sinking by **eccentric dredging** (excavating more on the high side), **eccentric kentledge**, **water jetting** on one side, or **pulling** with hawsers. Correcting them **later is impossible**, which is why sinking is monitored continuously.

**Why wells rather than piles for a major bridge in a large river:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Large lateral capacity** | The massive section resists current and impact |
| **Can be sunk through boulders** and variable strata | Where piles would be deflected or damaged |
| **Resists scour** by its own depth and mass | — |
| Well proven in the subcontinent's alluvial rivers | Extensive precedent |

Against which: sinking is **slow**, tilt and shift are hard to control, and the work is difficult in deep water. **Large-diameter bored piles** are increasingly used instead where the geology permits, being faster and more predictable.

examTip.trap: "The full scour depth" is the plausible wrong answer, and it misses the point of the definition.
examTip.trick: Grip is measured **below the scoured level**, because whatever soil scours away provides **no lateral support at all** — and it disappears exactly when the current is strongest.
examTip.mnemonic: **Grip = R/3 below maximum scour**, with scour from Lacey's **R = 0.473(Q/f)^⅓** times **2.0 at a pier nose**. Design on the ground that will still be there after the flood.

questions.stem: Bored cast-in-situ piles are generally preferred to driven piles in a dense urban area because they:
options: Cause no vibration and can be installed close to existing structures
questions.solution:
**They cause no vibration and can be installed close to existing structures.**

**The comparison:**

| | **DRIVEN (displacement)** | **BORED (non-displacement, cast in situ)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Vibration and noise** | **SEVERE** | **NEGLIGIBLE** |
| Effect on surrounding soil | **DENSIFIES** granular soil — capacity may exceed prediction | **No densification** |
| Ground **heave** | Can lift adjacent piles and structures | None |
| **Obstructions** | Cannot pass boulders; the pile may be damaged or deflected | **Can be drilled through** |
| **Inspection** | The pile is pre-made and inspectable **before** driving | The bore can be **inspected before concreting** |
| **Quality risk** | Damage during driving | **Depends on WORKMANSHIP** — necking, soft toe, contamination |
| Speed and cost | Generally **faster and cheaper** | Slower, dearer |
| Spoil | None | **Spoil to dispose of**; slurry if used |

**Why vibration is decisive in Kathmandu** and similar dense urban settings:

> Much of the building stock is **old, unreinforced masonry**, already weakened, on shallow foundations and built right up to the boundary. **Pile driving vibration cracks such buildings** — and the damage claims, the disputes and the delay cost far more than the difference in piling method.

There is also **ground heave** from displacement piling, which can lift neighbouring foundations, and **noise**, which in a residential area attracts restrictions on working hours.

**The bored pile's own risks** are worth knowing, because they are real and they are all matters of workmanship:

| Risk | Cause | Prevention |
|---|---|---|
| **NECKING** | The bore collapses inward before or during concreting | **Casing or bentonite slurry** to support the bore |
| **Soft toe** | Debris left at the base of the bore | **Clean the base** before concreting; airlift or bailer |
| **Contamination of the concrete** | Concrete placed through water or slurry without a tremie | **TREMIE** placement, the pipe kept embedded in the concrete |
| **Voids and honeycombing** | Poor concrete workability | High-slump, self-compacting mix — the concrete **cannot be vibrated** |
| Reinforcement displaced | Cage not centred or lifted during concreting | Spacers; secure the cage |

**The concrete for a bored pile must be highly workable** — a slump of **150 to 180 mm**, sometimes self-compacting — because it **cannot be compacted by vibration** once placed at depth. It must flow around the reinforcement and fill the bore under its own weight. That is the opposite of the low-slump concrete used above ground, and specifying an ordinary structural mix for a bored pile produces a honeycombed shaft.

**Tremie placement** deserves the detail because it is where bored piles are lost: the concrete is placed through a pipe whose **outlet remains buried in the concrete already placed**, so that fresh concrete **displaces** the water or slurry upward rather than mixing with it. If the tremie is lifted clear of the concrete surface, water enters and a **defective plane** forms across the pile — which the load test may not detect and the integrity test will.

**Integrity testing** is therefore routine for bored piles: **low-strain sonic (pile echo) testing** on a large proportion of them detects necking, discontinuities and soft toes cheaply, and **cross-hole sonic logging** through pre-installed tubes gives a more detailed picture for large-diameter piles.

**Where DRIVEN piles remain preferable**: an open site away from structures, **loose granular soil** (where driving densifies and improves it), **marine** work, and where **speed and cost** dominate. The choice is site-specific, and it is decided as much by the neighbours as by the soil.

examTip.trick: The decisive factor is usually the **neighbours**, not the soil. Kathmandu's building stock is largely old unreinforced masonry on shallow foundations, built to the boundary — and driving vibration cracks it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bored piles for crowded ground; driven piles for open sites and loose sand** (where driving densifies and helps). Bored piles have their own risks, all of workmanship: **necking, soft toe, and washed-out concrete** — hence casing or bentonite, a cleaned base, and **tremie** placement with the pipe kept buried.

questions.stem: In a combined footing carrying two columns of unequal load, the shape is chosen so that:
options: The centroid of the footing coincides with the resultant of the column loads
The heavier column is at the centre
questions.solution:
**So that the CENTROID of the footing coincides with the RESULTANT of the column loads.**

**Why.** A footing bears **uniformly** on the soil only when the **resultant of the applied loads passes through the centroid of the bearing area**. If it does not, the pressure distribution is **non-uniform** — trapezoidal or triangular — and:

| Consequence | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Higher pressure at one end** | May exceed the allowable bearing pressure |
| **Differential settlement** across the footing | The footing **TILTS** |
| Tilting redistributes the load | Which can make matters worse progressively |
| Additional moments in the columns | From the tilt |

**The shapes used, and why:**

| Shape | When |
|---|---|
| **RECTANGULAR** | When the footing can be **extended beyond the lighter column** far enough to bring its centroid under the resultant |
| **TRAPEZOIDAL** | When space is **constrained at both ends** — the wider end is placed under the **heavier** column |
| **Strap (cantilever)** | When the columns are **far apart** — two separate footings linked by a beam is cheaper than one long slab |

**The trapezoid is used when a rectangle will not fit**, which is the case worth understanding: with a boundary at one end and the heavier column near it, a rectangle long enough to place its centroid correctly would have to extend past the boundary. A **trapezoid puts more area under the heavier load** without extending further, achieving the same centroid position within the available length.

**The geometry of a trapezoidal footing**: with end widths **b₁** (under the heavier column) and **b₂**, and length L,

> **Area A = (b₁ + b₂)L/2 = ΣP / q_allowable**
> **Centroid from the b₁ end: x̄ = (L/3)(2b₂ + b₁)/(b₁ + b₂)**

and the two equations are solved for b₁ and b₂ once L is fixed and x̄ is set to place the centroid under the resultant. A trapezoid is only feasible if the resultant falls between **L/3 and L/2** from the heavy end — outside that range, a rectangle or a strap footing is needed.

**Structural behaviour of a combined footing** is worth noting because it differs from an isolated footing:

> A combined footing acts as a **BEAM spanning between the two columns**, loaded **UPWARD** by the soil pressure — so it has **HOGGING moment between the columns** and **sagging at the cantilever ends**.

That means the **main reinforcement between the columns is at the TOP**, which is the reverse of an isolated footing and a frequent detailing error. A drawing showing bottom steel throughout a combined footing is wrong.

**The transverse direction** is designed as a series of cantilevers from the column faces, with the reinforcement concentrated in **band widths** beneath each column, since the load spreads only a limited distance along the footing.

**When a combined footing is used at all:**

| Situation | Reason |
|---|---|
| Two columns **too close** for separate footings | Their footings would overlap |
| A column at a **boundary** with an interior column nearby | The boundary footing cannot be centred |
| **Weak soil** requiring large footings | Which then merge |
| Very **unequal loads** on adjacent columns | To equalise the pressure |

And when the columns are **far apart**, the **strap footing** is preferred, because a long combined slab spanning between them is heavily loaded in bending and expensive — while a strap beam carries only the moment and needs no bearing area.

examTip.trick: A footing bears uniformly **only** when the resultant passes through the centroid of the bearing area. Every combined, strap and trapezoidal footing is a device for arranging exactly that.
examTip.mnemonic: **Trapezoidal when space is tight at both ends** — put the wide end under the heavier column. And note the structural surprise: a combined footing spans as a beam **loaded upward by the soil**, so the main steel between the columns goes in the **TOP**, opposite to an isolated footing.

questions.stem: A fully compensated (floating) foundation is one in which:
options: The weight of soil excavated equals the weight of the structure
The foundation is supported on piles
The building is lighter than water
questions.solution:
**The weight of soil excavated equals the weight of the structure.**

**The principle:**

> Excavating a basement **REMOVES a weight of soil**. If the removed weight equals the weight of the building, the **NET increase in pressure at foundation level is ZERO** — so the soil beneath experiences no more stress than it did before construction, and there is theoretically **no settlement at all**.

> **Net pressure q_net = (weight of structure / area) − (weight of soil excavated / area) = 0** for full compensation.

**The consequence is remarkable and genuinely useful:**

> A **HEAVY building can be carried on soil that would not otherwise support it**, because the soil is being asked to carry nothing new.

**Degrees of compensation:**

| Type | Condition |
|---|---|
| **Fully compensated** | Excavated weight **= structure weight**; net pressure zero |
| **Partially compensated** | Excavated weight **< structure weight**; net pressure positive but reduced |
| **Over-compensated** | Excavated weight **> structure weight**; net pressure **negative** — the ground may **HEAVE** |

**Over-compensation is a real condition, not a theoretical curiosity**: a deep basement under a light structure removes more weight than it replaces, and the soil beneath **swells and heaves** — lifting the basement slab, which must then be designed for uplift.

**The design considerations:**

| Consideration | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **UPLIFT / flotation** | An **empty basement below the water table will FLOAT**. Check the structure complete but unloaded, water table high |
| **HEAVE during excavation** | The excavation bottom rises as the overburden is removed; it must be allowed for, and it partly reverses when the building is placed |
| **Base stability** | A deep excavation in soft clay can fail by **base heave** — a bearing capacity failure in reverse |
| **Groundwater control** | Dewatering during construction, and permanent tanking afterwards |
| **Effect on neighbours** | Excavation removes lateral support from adjacent foundations — **underpinning** may be required |
| Waterproofing | The basement must resist hydrostatic pressure |

**Flotation is the check most often overlooked** and it has caught real projects: an empty basement, a swimming pool or a sewage tank, complete but not yet loaded, and the water table rising after rain — the structure floats out of the ground. The remedies are **added dead weight** (a thicker base slab), **tension piles or ground anchors**, or a **pressure relief valve** admitting groundwater in a controlled way.

**The cellular or box raft** is the natural form for a compensated foundation: two slabs with intersecting walls between them, giving a very **stiff** structure that is also **hollow and therefore light** — maximising the excavated weight relative to the structure's own.

**Where it is used:** heavy buildings on **soft compressible clay** where piling to a firm stratum is impossible or uneconomical, and where a basement is wanted in any case for parking or plant. The basement is then not a cost but the foundation itself — which is what makes the concept so economical when it applies.

**Its limitation** is that it requires a **deep excavation**, with all its attendant difficulties: dewatering, temporary support, effect on neighbours, and the risk of base heave. In a congested urban site those may cost more than the piling avoided.

examTip.trick: Excavating removes weight. If the weight removed equals the weight added, the soil below sees **no net increase in pressure** — so a heavy building can sit on ground that could not otherwise carry it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Dig out as much as you put back.** The check that catches people is **FLOTATION**: an empty basement below the water table will float. Swimming pools and sewage tanks have done exactly that.

questions.stem: The thickness of an isolated footing is most often governed by:
options: One-way shear at d from the column face
Two-way (punching) shear on a perimeter at d/2 from the column face
questions.solution:
**Two-way (punching) shear**, on a perimeter at **d/2 from the column face**.

**The four checks on an isolated footing**, and the order in which they usually govern:

| Check | Critical section | Usually governs |
|---|---|---|
| **TWO-WAY (punching) shear** | Perimeter at **d/2 from the column face** | **THE THICKNESS** |
| **One-way shear** | At **d from the column face** | Occasionally, for a wide footing |
| **Bending** | **At the column face** | **The reinforcement** |
| Development length, bearing | — | Detailing |

**Punching shear** is the mechanism by which the **column punches through the slab**, pushing out a truncated pyramid of concrete. It is checked as

> **τ_v = V_u / (perimeter at d/2 × d) ≤ k_s × 0.25 √f_ck**

with **k_s = (0.5 + β_c) ≤ 1.0**, where β_c is the ratio of the short to the long side of the column.

**Why it governs the thickness rather than bending** — the reasoning is worth having:

> Punching shear is resisted by the **concrete alone** (shear reinforcement in a footing is possible but rarely used, being difficult to fix and inspect). The **only variable available** is therefore the **depth d** — so the check is satisfied by making the footing thicker.

> Bending, by contrast, is satisfied by **adding reinforcement**, which is cheap and easy. So bending fixes the **steel** and punching fixes the **depth**.

That division surprises candidates who size the footing for moment first and then find the shear check fails by a wide margin.

**Note the different critical sections**, and each has a physical reason:

| Check | Section | Why there |
|---|---|---|
| **Punching** | **d/2** from the face | The assumed failure surface spreads at 45° through the depth, so its average perimeter is at d/2 |
| **One-way** | **d** from the face | The diagonal tension crack forms at roughly 45°, so a load within d of the support is carried directly by arch action |
| **Bending** | **At the face** | The maximum moment in the cantilever projection |

**Design sequence for an isolated footing:**

1. **Area** from the **SERVICE** load and the **net allowable bearing pressure**: **A = P/q_a**.
2. Compute the **net upward pressure from the FACTORED load**: **q_u = P_u/A**.
3. Assume a depth and check **punching shear** — revise until satisfied.
4. Check **one-way shear**.
5. Design the **bending** reinforcement at the column face.
6. Check **development length** and **bearing** on the column.

**Step 1 uses SERVICE loads and step 2 FACTORED loads**, and mixing them is a standard error. The **area** is fixed by the soil's allowable pressure, which is itself a working-stress quantity with its own factor of safety; the **structural design** of the footing then uses factored loads and limit-state material strengths. Applying factored loads to the soil pressure would double-count the safety factor and give a footing twice the necessary area.

**Minimum thickness** at the edge is **150 mm** for a footing on soil (300 mm on piles), and the **cover** is **50 mm** — greater than for other members, because the concrete is cast **against the ground** and cannot be as well controlled.

**For a rectangular footing**, IS 456 requires the reinforcement in the **short** direction to be **concentrated in a central band** of width equal to the short dimension, in the proportion **2/(β+1)**, where β is the ratio of the long to short side — because the load does not spread uniformly along the length.

examTip.trap: Bending is the instinctive answer because it feels like the primary action — but bending is satisfied by **adding steel**, which is cheap.
examTip.trick: Punching shear is resisted by the **concrete alone**, so the only variable available is the **depth**. That is why it fixes the thickness while bending fixes the reinforcement.
examTip.mnemonic: **Punching at d/2, one-way shear at d, bending at the face.** Three checks, three different critical sections.

questions.stem: Compaction piles are installed primarily to:
options: Carry the structural load to a deep stratum
questions.solution:
**To densify loose granular soil.**

**Compaction piles are a GROUND IMPROVEMENT technique, not a load-transfer element** — which is the distinction the question tests. They are driven not to carry the structure but to **improve the soil**, and the structure may then be founded on a shallow foundation on the improved ground.

**How they work:**

> Driving a **displacement** pile into loose sand **displaces the soil sideways**, densifying the zone around it. A **grid of such piles** densifies the whole treated area, raising its **relative density**, its **bearing capacity** and — most importantly — its **resistance to LIQUEFACTION**.

The piles themselves are often left in place, but they may also be **sand or stone columns** formed by driving a casing and withdrawing it while filling.

**The pile classification by FUNCTION**, of which this is one:

| Type | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **End bearing** | Transfers load to a hard stratum |
| **Friction (floating)** | Load carried by shaft resistance |
| **COMPACTION** | **Densifies loose granular soil** — ground improvement |
| **Tension (uplift)** | Resists uplift — transmission towers, buoyant structures |
| **Batter (raker)** | Inclined; resists **lateral** load — wharves, abutments |
| **Sheet** | **Retains** soil or water; not load bearing |
| Anchor | Provides anchorage |
| Fender, dolphin | Absorbs impact from vessels |

Each option in the question names a different one of these — end bearing (a), tension (b), sheet (d) — which is why the set is instructive.

**Ground improvement techniques more broadly**, since compaction piles are one of a family:

| Technique | Suits | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| **Vibro-compaction (vibroflotation)** | **Clean sand** | A vibrating probe densifies the sand around it |
| **Vibro-replacement / STONE COLUMNS** | Silty sand, soft clay | Columns of compacted stone; **densify AND drain AND reinforce** |
| **Dynamic compaction** | Loose fills, granular soil | A heavy weight dropped repeatedly from height |
| **Compaction piles** | Loose sand | Displacement densification |
| **PRELOADING with vertical drains** | **Soft clay** | Consolidates the clay before construction |
| **Grouting** — permeation, compaction, jet | Various | Fills voids, cements particles |
| **Lime or cement stabilisation** | Clays, silts | Chemical modification |
| Geosynthetic reinforcement | Fills, embankments | Tensile reinforcement |
| Dewatering | — | Increases effective stress |

**Stone columns deserve emphasis for liquefaction mitigation**, because they work in **three ways at once**:

| Function | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Densification** during installation | Raises relative density, so the sand **dilates rather than contracts** |
| **DRAINAGE** — the column is a permanent vertical drain | Lets excess pore pressure **dissipate as fast as it builds** |
| **Reinforcement** | The stiff column carries a share of the load and the shear |

That combination is why stone columns are the standard treatment for liquefiable ground beneath a structure — and why they are relevant to Kathmandu Valley sites under NBC 105.

**Choosing the technique follows the soil**, and the pairing is examinable:

> **GRANULAR soil → DENSIFICATION** (vibro-compaction, dynamic compaction, compaction piles).
> **SOFT CLAY → CONSOLIDATION** (preloading with vertical drains) or **REINFORCEMENT** (stone columns).

Applying vibro-compaction to a clay achieves nothing — clay cannot be densified by vibration, because the water cannot escape quickly — which is exactly the compaction-versus-consolidation distinction encountered earlier in the chapter.

examTip.trick: Every other option names a different pile *function* — end bearing, tension, sheet. Compaction piles are **ground improvement**, not load transfer; the structure may then sit on a shallow foundation on the improved ground.
examTip.mnemonic: **Granular soil → DENSIFY. Soft clay → CONSOLIDATE or REINFORCE.** Vibro-compaction on clay achieves nothing, because clay cannot be densified by vibration. **Stone columns** are the liquefaction remedy of choice — they densify, drain and reinforce at once.

questions.stem: The end bearing capacity of a pile in uniform sand:
options: Becomes approximately constant beyond a critical depth of about 15 to 20 diameters
Is independent of the sand density
questions.solution:
**It becomes approximately constant beyond a critical depth of about 15 to 20 pile diameters.**

**The naive expectation and why it is wrong.** The end bearing in sand is usually written

> **Q_p = σ′_v N_q A_p**

and since **σ′_v increases linearly with depth**, the formula appears to predict that end bearing grows without limit. **It does not.** Beyond a **critical depth** the tip resistance **levels off**, and applying the linear formula at great depth **grossly overestimates** the capacity.

**Why it levels off** — the accepted explanations:

| Reason | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **Arching** | The soil above the tip forms an arch, so the full overburden is not transmitted to it |
| **Reduction in φ at high stress** | The friction angle **falls** as the confining stress rises, because particles **crush** rather than ride over one another |
| **Compressibility** at high stress | The sand becomes more compressible, changing the failure mode |

**The same limit applies to the unit SHAFT FRICTION**, which also becomes approximately constant beyond the critical depth — so both components of capacity are affected.

**The practical consequence:**

> **Driving a pile deeper into uniform sand yields diminishing returns.** Beyond about 20 diameters, additional length adds capacity only through the **additional shaft area at a constant unit friction** — not through any increase in unit resistance.

So a very long pile in uniform sand is inefficient, and where greater capacity is needed the answer is a **larger diameter** or **more piles**, not a longer one.

**Critical depth values**, which vary with density:

| Sand | Critical depth |
|---|---|
| **Loose** | ~10 diameters |
| **Medium** | ~15 diameters |
| **Dense** | ~20 diameters |

**Pile capacity in sand**, with the limit applied:

> **Q_p = σ′_v N_q A_p**, with **σ′_v LIMITED to its value at the critical depth**
> **Q_s = K σ′_v tan δ A_s**, with the same limit

where **K** is the earth pressure coefficient (higher for driven piles, which densify the soil, than for bored) and **δ** the pile–soil friction angle (about **⅔φ to φ**).

**Contrast with CLAY**, where no such limit applies:

| | **Sand** | **Clay** |
|---|---|---|
| End bearing | **σ′_v N_q**, limited beyond critical depth | **9 c_u** — depends on the **strength**, not the depth |
| Shaft friction | **K σ′_v tan δ**, limited | **α c_u** |
| Depends on | **Effective stress** (hence depth) | **Undrained strength** (hence the soil itself) |

In clay the capacity increases with depth only insofar as **c_u increases with depth** — which it usually does in a normally consolidated deposit, but as a property of the soil rather than of the confinement.

**Why the distinction matters for design:** in **sand**, a pile is essentially a **friction** pile beyond the critical depth, and the tip contributes a fixed amount. In **clay**, both components scale with the strength profile. Estimating either with the other's formula produces errors of a factor of two or more — which is one reason **pile load tests** are relied on so heavily rather than static formulae alone.

examTip.trap: The formula **σ′_v N_q** appears to grow without limit, and applying it at depth is a genuine and serious over-estimate.
examTip.trick: Arching and grain crushing cap the tip resistance. Beyond the critical depth, extra length adds capacity only through **more shaft area at constant unit friction**.
examTip.mnemonic: **15–20 diameters and it stops growing.** So a very long pile in uniform sand is inefficient — for more capacity, use a **larger diameter or more piles**, not a longer one. In clay there is no such limit, because capacity follows c_u, not confinement.

questions.stem: For a pile group in soft clay, the ultimate capacity should be taken as:
options: The sum of the individual pile capacities
Twice the sum of the individual capacities
The lesser of the sum of individual capacities and the block capacity
questions.solution:
**The LESSER of the sum of the individual pile capacities and the BLOCK capacity.**

**The two possible failure modes**, and the group will fail in whichever is weaker:

| Mode | Capacity |
|---|---|
| **Individual pile failure** | **n × (single pile capacity)** — each pile punches through independently |
| **BLOCK failure** | The group and the soil **between** the piles move as a **single large pier**: **perimeter shear + base bearing of the block** |

> **Block capacity = c_u × (perimeter of the group × length) + 9 c_u × (plan area of the group)**

**Why block failure can govern.** Consider the ratio of resisting surface to volume as the group grows: the **individual** capacity grows with **n** (the number of piles), but the **block** perimeter grows only with the **square root** of the plan area. So for a **closely spaced group in soft clay**, the block value falls below the sum of individual capacities, and it governs.

**Group efficiency** expresses the same thing:

> **η = group capacity / (n × single pile capacity)**

| Soil | Efficiency | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **CLAY** | **< 1** | Block action; overlapping stress zones |
| Dense sand | ≈ 1 | — |
| **Loose sand, DRIVEN piles** | **> 1** | Driving **densifies** the soil between the piles |

**Group SETTLEMENT is a separate and often more serious matter**, and it is the point most often missed:

> A **pile GROUP settles considerably MORE than a single pile carrying the same load per pile** — because the group's stress bulb is **far deeper**, reaching compressible layers that a single pile's does not.

A single test pile may settle 5 mm at working load while the group of which it is a member settles 50 mm — and the load test, which is done on a single pile, gives no warning of it.

**The equivalent raft method** is the standard way of estimating group settlement:

| Pile type | Equivalent raft placed at |
|---|---|
| **Friction piles** | **Two thirds of the pile length** below the ground |
| **End bearing piles** | At the **pile tip level** |

The load is assumed to spread from the equivalent raft at **2 vertical to 1 horizontal**, and the settlement computed by ordinary consolidation theory for the layers below.

**That method is what reveals the problem**: the equivalent raft is a **large loaded area**, so its pressure bulb extends far deeper than any individual pile's, and a compressible layer at depth that no single pile would notice governs the group's settlement entirely.

**Pile cap design** completes the group: it distributes the column load to the piles, and is designed as a **thick slab** (checking punching shear around the column and around each pile) or by a **strut-and-tie** model for a deep cap. IS 2911 requires it to project **at least 150 mm** beyond the outer piles, with the pile heads embedded **50 to 75 mm**.

**A note on the eccentric group**: where the column load is eccentric to the group centroid, the pile loads are found as for a footing under combined axial load and moment,

> **P_i = ΣP/n ± M x_i/Σx²**

and the **corner piles** take the greatest load — which must be checked against the individual pile capacity, and which may govern the group's design even when the average is comfortable.

examTip.trick: Both mechanisms must be checked because either can govern: **n × individual capacity**, or the **block** (perimeter shear plus base bearing of the whole group as one pier). For a close group in soft clay the block value is usually smaller.
examTip.mnemonic: **Individual capacity grows with n; block perimeter grows only with √area.** So the bigger the group, the more likely the block governs. Separately, remember a **group SETTLES far more than a single test pile** — its stress bulb reaches much deeper (equivalent raft at ⅔ the pile length).

questions.stem: In Terzaghi's bearing capacity equation q_u = cN_c + γD_f N_q + 0.5γBN_γ, the third term represents the contribution of:
options: The self-weight of the soil in the failure wedge
questions.solution:
**The self-weight of the soil in the failure wedge — hence the footing WIDTH.**

**The three terms and what each represents:**

| Term | Contribution from | Depends on |
|---|---|---|
| **c N_c** | **COHESION** of the soil | c |
| **γ D_f N_q** | **SURCHARGE** — the weight of soil above founding level | **DEPTH** D_f |
| **0.5 γ B N_γ** | **SELF-WEIGHT of the soil in the failure wedge** | **WIDTH** B |

Understanding what each term *is* makes the two most important consequences immediate:

**For a PURE CLAY (φ = 0):**

> **N_q = 1** and **N_γ = 0**, so **q_u = c N_c + γD_f** with **N_c = 5.7** (Terzaghi) or **5.14** (Prandtl)

> **The WIDTH TERM VANISHES — so the bearing capacity of clay is INDEPENDENT of the footing width.**

That is a striking and examinable result: **widening a footing on clay does NOT increase the pressure it can carry**, only the total load. On sand, where c = 0 and the width term is all that remains besides depth, it does.

**For a PURE SAND (c = 0):**

> **q_u = γD_f N_q + 0.5 γ B N_γ** — capacity grows with **both depth and width**

**Terzaghi's assumptions**, which define where the equation applies:

| Assumption | Note |
|---|---|
| **Strip (continuous)** footing | Other shapes need **shape factors** |
| **Shallow** foundation, D_f ≤ B | Deeper needs depth factors |
| **Homogeneous, isotropic** soil | A layered profile needs separate treatment |
| **General shear** failure | Local or punching shear needs reduced parameters |
| The soil **above founding level is a surcharge only** — its shear strength is ignored | Conservative |
| **Vertical, concentric** load | Inclined or eccentric loads need further factors |
| Base **rough** | — |

**The bearing capacity factors** depend only on **φ**:

| φ | N_c | N_q | N_γ |
|---|---|---|---|
| **0** | **5.7** | **1.0** | **0** |
| 10° | 9.6 | 2.7 | 1.2 |
| 20° | 17.7 | 7.4 | 5.0 |
| **30°** | **37.2** | **22.5** | **19.7** |
| 40° | 95.7 | 81.3 | 100.4 |

**Note how steeply they rise with φ** — roughly doubling for every 5° — which is why the friction angle is the parameter to which bearing capacity is most sensitive, and why an optimistic φ is so dangerous. An error of 5° in φ can change the computed capacity by a factor of two.

**Later theories** — **Meyerhof, Hansen, Vesic** — extend the equation with factors for **shape, depth, load inclination and ground slope**, and use a fuller failure surface. **IS 6403** follows the same pattern and is what Nepali and Indian practice uses.

examTip.trick: Read the three terms by what each depends on: **c** (cohesion), **D_f** (depth/surcharge), **B** (width/self-weight of the wedge).
examTip.mnemonic: **For pure clay N_γ = 0, so bearing capacity is INDEPENDENT of footing width.** Widening a footing on clay carries more total load but not more pressure. On sand the width term is everything.

questions.stem: General shear failure of a foundation is characterised by:
options: A well-defined failure surface reaching the ground surface, with heave beside the footing
Progressive settlement with no failure surface
The footing punching vertically downward with no heave
questions.solution:
**A well-defined failure surface reaching the ground surface, with heave beside the footing.**

**The three modes of bearing failure**, distinguished by the soil's density or stiffness:

| Mode | Occurs in | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **GENERAL shear** | **Dense sand, stiff clay** | A **well-defined failure surface reaches the ground surface**; **HEAVE beside the footing**; **sudden, catastrophic** failure with a **clear peak load** |
| **LOCAL shear** | **Medium dense sand, medium clay** | Failure surface only **partly developed**; **some heave**; **no clear peak** |
| **PUNCHING shear** | **Very loose sand, very soft clay** | The footing simply **punches down**; **NO heave**, no surface reaching the ground |

**The practical significance of the distinction:**

> **General shear gives WARNING** — a clear peak load, visible heave, and a definable ultimate capacity.
> **Punching failure gives none** — it is a progressive settlement with **no identifiable ultimate load at all**.

So for a very loose or very soft soil, the design criterion becomes **SETTLEMENT rather than capacity**, because there is no capacity to speak of: the footing simply goes on settling as the load increases, and choosing an "ultimate" load from the load–settlement curve is arbitrary.

**How the mode is identified:**

| Indicator | General shear | Punching shear |
|---|---|---|
| **Relative density** | I_D > 70% | I_D < 35% |
| **SPT N** | > 30 | < 5 |
| **Void ratio** | Low | High |
| Load–settlement curve | **Clear peak** | Continuous, no peak |

**The LOCAL SHEAR reduction** is how the intermediate case is handled:

> **c′ = ⅔ c** and **tan φ′ = ⅔ tan φ**

The reduced parameters are then used in the ordinary Terzaghi equation. The **two-thirds** factor is empirical, and it reflects the fact that only part of the failure surface develops so only part of the strength is mobilised.

**Vesic's criterion** relates the mode to the **rigidity index** of the soil, providing a rational basis rather than the empirical density thresholds — but the density-based rule is what is used in practice and examined.

**A note on the load–settlement curve**, which is how the mode is actually recognised in a plate load test:

| Mode | Curve |
|---|---|
| **General shear** | Rises to a **distinct peak**, then falls or flattens abruptly |
| **Local shear** | Bends over gradually; the "failure" load is taken at a defined settlement |
| **Punching** | Nearly **straight**, continuing to settle indefinitely |

For the last two, the ultimate load is defined by convention — commonly the load at a settlement of **10% of the footing width**, or the intersection of the initial and final tangents on a log–log plot.

**The mode also affects the choice of design approach**: for general shear, a **bearing capacity** calculation with a factor of safety is appropriate; for punching, a **settlement** calculation is the meaningful one, and the allowable pressure is whatever produces a tolerable settlement.

examTip.trick: Three modes by density: **general** (dense — sudden, clear peak, visible heave), **local** (medium), **punching** (very loose/soft — no heave, no peak at all).
examTip.mnemonic: **General shear gives warning; punching gives none.** Where punching applies there is no identifiable ultimate load, so the design criterion becomes **SETTLEMENT**, not capacity.

questions.stem: The net safe bearing capacity is obtained by dividing by the factor of safety the:
questions.solution:
**The NET ultimate bearing capacity.**

> **q_nu = q_u − γD_f**
> **q_ns = q_nu / F**, with **F = 2.5 or 3**
> **q_safe (gross) = q_nu/F + γD_f**

**The terms, kept apart** — and most wrong answers in this topic come from mixing gross and net rather than from any error in the theory:

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **GROSS pressure** | The **TOTAL** pressure at founding level, **INCLUDING** the weight of soil previously there |
| **NET pressure** | The **INCREASE** over the original overburden: **q_net = q_gross − γD_f** |
| **Ultimate bearing capacity q_u** | The **GROSS** pressure at which shear failure occurs |
| **Net ultimate q_nu** | **q_u − γD_f** |
| **Net safe bearing capacity** | **q_nu / F** |
| **Safe bearing capacity (gross)** | q_nu/F **+ γD_f** |
| **ALLOWABLE bearing pressure** | The **LESSER** of the safe bearing capacity and the pressure limited by **SETTLEMENT** |

**Why the factor of safety applies to the NET value** — this is the substance of the question, and the reason is physical rather than conventional:

> The overburden pressure **γD_f was ALREADY THERE** before construction, and the soil has carried it for geological time. It needs **no factor of safety**. Only the **INCREASE** — the net pressure — is new, and only that requires a margin.

Applying F to the **gross** value would apply a safety factor to a load the soil has demonstrably carried, which is **over-conservative** and, for a deep foundation where γD_f is large, absurdly so. It is a genuine error, not merely a convention.

**A worked illustration.** A footing at 2 m depth in soil of γ = 18 kN/m³, with q_u = 400 kPa and F = 3:

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Overburden γD_f | 18 × 2 = **36 kPa** |
| **Net ultimate** q_nu | 400 − 36 = **364 kPa** |
| **Net safe** q_ns | 364/3 = **121 kPa** |
| **Safe (gross)** | 121 + 36 = **157 kPa** |

Had F been applied to the gross value: 400/3 = 133 kPa gross, or only **97 kPa net** — **20% less** than the correct answer, and the difference grows with depth.

**The allowable bearing pressure** is then the **lesser** of the safe bearing capacity and the settlement-limited value:

| Soil | Usually governed by | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Dense sand and gravel** | **SETTLEMENT** | Shear capacity is ample; settlement is immediate and can be excessive under a wide footing |
| **Soft to medium clay** | **SHEAR** | Capacity is low; settlement, though large, occurs over years |
| Stiff clay | Either | Both must be checked |
| Rock | Neither | Capacity vastly exceeds requirement |

**Assuming that shear always governs is a common conceptual error**, and it produces footings on dense sand that are perfectly safe against collapse and unacceptable in settlement — which is why both checks are mandatory and why the allowable pressure is defined as the lesser.

examTip.trap: Applying the factor of safety to the **gross** value is a real and common error, and it grows worse with depth.
examTip.trick: The overburden γD_f was already there and the ground has carried it for geological time. Only the **increase** is new, so only the increase needs a margin.
examTip.mnemonic: **q_ns = (q_u − γD_f)/F, then add γD_f back for the gross safe value.** Using the gross value throughout can under-rate the soil by 20% or more.

questions.stem: Where local shear failure governs, the shear strength parameters are reduced to:
options: c′ = ⅔c and tan φ′ = ⅔ tan φ
questions.solution:
**c′ = ⅔c and tan φ′ = ⅔ tan φ.**

Note carefully that it is **tan φ** that is reduced to two thirds, **not φ itself**. So for φ = 30°:

> tan 30° = 0.577; ⅔ × 0.577 = 0.385; **φ′ = tan⁻¹(0.385) = 21°** — not 20°

Reducing the **angle** rather than its tangent is a small but real error, and it is why the formula is stated in terms of tan φ.

**When the reduction applies:**

| Mode | Soil | Parameters |
|---|---|---|
| **General shear** | **Dense sand (I_D > 70%, N > 30), stiff clay** | **Full** c and φ |
| **LOCAL shear** | **Medium dense sand, medium clay** | **Reduced: ⅔c and ⅔tan φ** |
| **Punching shear** | **Very loose sand (I_D < 35%, N < 5), very soft clay** | Settlement governs; capacity is ill-defined |

**Why a reduction is needed at all.** Terzaghi's theory assumes a **fully developed failure surface** reaching the ground surface, with the **full shear strength mobilised along its whole length**. In a loose or soft soil the surface only **partly develops**, so only part of the strength is available — and using the full parameters would overestimate the capacity substantially.

The **two thirds** factor is **empirical**, chosen by Terzaghi to bring the computed capacity into line with observation. It has no theoretical derivation, which is worth knowing: it is a calibration, not a physical constant.

**The full set of corrections applied to Terzaghi's equation in practice (IS 6403):**

| Correction | For |
|---|---|
| **Local shear reduction** | Loose or soft soil |
| **SHAPE factors** | Square, circular, rectangular footings |
| **DEPTH factors** | Where D_f is significant |
| **INCLINATION factors** | Inclined loading |
| **WATER TABLE correction** | R_w1 and R_w2 |

**Shape factors** convert the strip result:

| Shape | N_c | N_γ |
|---|---|---|
| **Strip** | **1.0** (the base case) | **1.0** |
| **Square** | **× 1.3** | **× 0.8** |
| **Circular** | **× 1.3** | **× 0.6** |
| **Rectangular** | × (1 + 0.2B/L) | × (1 − 0.2B/L) |

**Note the OPPOSITE directions**: the cohesion term is **increased** for a square footing while the width term is **reduced**. The reason is geometric — a square footing's failure surface is confined on all four sides, which helps the cohesive resistance, while its wedge is smaller relative to its width, which reduces the self-weight contribution.

**The water table correction** reduces the capacity because the **effective** unit weight in the failure zone falls from γ to **γ′ ≈ γ/2**:

| Water table position | R_w1 (surcharge term) | R_w2 (width term) |
|---|---|---|
| **At or above founding level** | **0.5** | **0.5** |
| At depth B below the base | 1.0 | **1.0** |
| Between | Interpolated | Interpolated |

> **A high water table can nearly HALVE the bearing capacity of a sand** — which is worth remembering for the Terai and the Kathmandu Valley, and which means the **worst credible water table**, not the level found on the day of the investigation, must be used in design.

examTip.trap: Reducing **φ** rather than **tan φ** is a small but real slip: for φ = 30°, ⅔tan30° gives **21°**, not 20°.
examTip.trick: The failure surface only partly develops in a loose or soft soil, so only part of the strength is available. The ⅔ is **empirical**, chosen to match observation — not derived.
examTip.mnemonic: **Two thirds of c, and two thirds of TAN φ.**

questions.stem: A rise of the water table to founding level reduces the bearing capacity of a sand by approximately:
questions.solution:
**Approximately half.**

**The reason is the effective unit weight.** Both the surcharge term and the width term of Terzaghi's equation contain γ, and below the water table the **effective (submerged) unit weight** applies:

> **γ′ = γ_sat − γ_w ≈ 20 − 10 = 10 kN/m³**, against a moist unit weight of about **18–19 kN/m³**

So **γ′ ≈ γ/2**, and since a sand's capacity depends **entirely** on γ (with c = 0), the capacity is **roughly halved**.

**Formally, IS 6403 applies two correction factors:**

| Factor | Applies to | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **R_w1** | The **surcharge** term γD_f N_q | **0.5** when the water table is at or above **founding level**; 1.0 when at depth D_f or more above it |
| **R_w2** | The **width** term 0.5γBN_γ | **0.5** when the water table is at or above founding level; **1.0** when at depth **B below the base** |

> **q_u = c N_c + γ D_f N_q R_w1 + 0.5 γ B N_γ R_w2**

**The two factors respond to different water table positions**, which is the detail worth noting: R_w1 concerns water **above** founding level (affecting the surcharge), while R_w2 concerns water **within a depth B below** the base (affecting the failure wedge). A water table between the base and B below it therefore reduces only the width term.

**For a CLAY the effect is quite different**, and it is a useful contrast:

| Soil | Effect of a rising water table on bearing capacity |
|---|---|
| **SAND** | **Halved** — capacity depends entirely on γ |
| **CLAY (undrained, φ = 0)** | **Almost NO immediate effect** — capacity is c N_c, and c_u does not depend on the water table in the short term |

The clay's **long-term** capacity does fall, as the effective stresses reduce and the clay softens — but the immediate undrained capacity is essentially unchanged.

**The design implication is important and often mishandled:**

> The **WORST CREDIBLE water table** must be used — **not the level found on the day of the investigation**.

A site investigated in the dry season may show a water table 5 m down and be designed accordingly; the monsoon table may be at the surface, and the bearing capacity then half what was assumed. In Nepal, where the seasonal variation is large, this is a real and recurring source of under-design.

**The correct practice:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Install piezometers** and monitor over a full year if the programme permits | The only reliable method |
| Look for **evidence of the seasonal high** | Staining, mottling, vegetation, local knowledge |
| Ask **local residents** | Wells, flooding history — often the best available information |
| Assume the water table at or near the **surface** where evidence is lacking | Conservative and usually right in the Terai |

**A related effect**: a rising water table also **reduces the effective stress** throughout the profile, which in a **normally consolidated clay** reduces its strength and in a **loose saturated sand** creates the conditions for **liquefaction**. So the water table is not merely a bearing capacity parameter but a governing variable for several distinct failure modes at once.

examTip.trick: Sand's capacity depends entirely on γ, and below the water table the **effective** unit weight applies: **γ′ ≈ 10 against 18–20 kN/m³** — about half.
examTip.mnemonic: **Water halves a sand's bearing capacity, and barely touches a clay's** (undrained c_u does not care about the water table in the short term). Design on the **worst credible** water table, not the one found on the day of the survey — in Nepal the seasonal swing is large.

questions.stem: The allowable bearing pressure for a foundation is:
options: The lesser of the safe bearing capacity and the pressure limited by settlement
Always equal to the safe bearing capacity
The greater of the safe bearing capacity and the settlement-limited pressure
questions.solution:
**The LESSER of the safe bearing capacity and the pressure limited by settlement.**

**Two entirely independent criteria must both be satisfied:**

| Criterion | Concerns | Failure mode |
|---|---|---|
| **Safe bearing capacity** | **STRENGTH** — will the soil shear? | **Collapse** |
| **Settlement-limited pressure** | **SERVICEABILITY** — will the structure move too much? | **Damage, not collapse** |

The allowable pressure is the **lesser**, because the foundation must satisfy both — and there is no reason for the two to give the same answer.

**Which one governs depends on the SOIL**, and the pattern is worth knowing:

| Soil | Governed by | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Dense sand and gravel** | **SETTLEMENT** | Shear capacity is **ample**; but settlement is **immediate** and increases with footing width |
| **Soft to medium clay** | **SHEAR** | Capacity is **low**; settlement, though large, develops over years |
| Stiff clay | **Either** | Both must be checked |
| Rock | Neither, usually | Capacity vastly exceeds any requirement |

**"Bearing capacity always governs" is a common and consequential misconception**, and it produces footings on dense sand that are perfectly safe against collapse and unacceptable in service — cracking finishes, jamming doors, distorting drainage.

**Why settlement governs on dense sand** is worth understanding: the shear strength of a dense sand is very high, so the ultimate capacity is enormous — but settlement in sand is **immediate and increases with the loaded width**, and a wide footing at a pressure well within its shear capacity can still settle 40 mm.

**Why shear governs on soft clay**: the undrained capacity is low (q_u ≈ 5.14 c_u + γD_f, so perhaps 150 kPa for c_u = 25), and the factor of safety of 2.5–3 brings the safe value down to perhaps 40 kPa. The settlement at that pressure, though it may be large, is a **long-term** matter and codes permit more of it in clay for exactly that reason.

**Permissible settlements (IS 1904):**

| Structure and soil | Maximum total settlement |
|---|---|
| **Isolated footing on SAND** | **40 mm** |
| **Isolated footing on CLAY** | **65 mm** |
| **Raft on sand** | 40 – 65 mm |
| **Raft on clay** | 65 – 100 mm |

**Clay is allowed MORE**, which surprises candidates until the reason is seen:

> The settlement in clay occurs **SLOWLY, over years** — so the structure can accommodate it by **creep and progressive adjustment**, rather than being strained suddenly. Sand settles almost entirely during construction, when the structure is least able to adjust.

**And rafts are allowed more than isolated footings**, because a raft's stiffness means its settlement is **more uniform** — and it is **differential** settlement that damages structures.

**Which brings the essential point:**

> **DIFFERENTIAL settlement matters far more than TOTAL.** A building settling **50 mm uniformly** is undamaged; one settling **10 mm unevenly** cracks.

The governing measure is the **angular distortion δ/L**, limited to about **1/500** where cracking is not permissible, with cracking of panel walls beginning around **1/300**.

examTip.trap: "Bearing capacity always governs" is a widespread misconception, and it produces footings on dense sand that cannot fail but settle unacceptably.
examTip.trick: Two independent criteria, and the **lesser** wins: strength (will it shear?) and serviceability (will it move too much?).
examTip.mnemonic: **Dense sand → SETTLEMENT governs. Soft clay → SHEAR governs.** Both must be checked, every time.

questions.stem: For a structure founded on sand, the settlement is:
options: Essentially complete by the end of construction
Spread over ten to twenty years
questions.solution:
**Essentially complete by the end of construction.**

**The three components of settlement and where each dominates:**

| Component | Cause | Timescale | Dominant in |
|---|---|---|---|
| **IMMEDIATE (elastic)** | Distortion at essentially constant volume | **During construction** | **SAND and gravel** |
| **PRIMARY CONSOLIDATION** | **Expulsion of pore WATER**; effective stress rising | **Months to years** | **Saturated CLAY** |
| **Secondary compression (creep)** | Creep of the soil structure at **constant** effective stress | Years to decades | **Organic soils, PEAT** |

> **Total settlement = immediate + primary consolidation + secondary compression**

**Why sand settles immediately.** Sand's **permeability is high** (10⁻² to 10⁻⁵ m/s), so the pore water **escapes as fast as the load is applied**. There is no build-up of excess pore pressure, the effective stress rises at once, and the soil compresses at once.

**The practical consequences of that**, which are considerable:

| Consequence | Explanation |
|---|---|
| **Most of the settlement occurs DURING construction** | So it is absorbed by the structure before finishes are applied |
| **Little settlement after occupation** | Finishes, cladding and services are not distressed |
| It can be **observed and measured** as construction proceeds | Giving early warning if it exceeds prediction |
| **Consolidation theory does not apply** | Settlement is computed by **elastic** methods, or from **SPT/CPT correlations** |

**Computing settlement in sand** is done by:

| Method | Basis |
|---|---|
| **Elastic (Boussinesq-based)** | **S = qB(1 − μ²)I_f/E_s** — needs E_s, which is hard to measure |
| **SPT correlations** (Terzaghi & Peck, Meyerhof, Burland & Burbidge) | The practical standard |
| **CPT correlations** (Schmertmann) | Better, using the continuous profile |
| **Plate load test** with size scaling | Direct but limited by the shallow bulb |

**The size effect in sand** is worth stating, because it is why settlement rather than capacity governs:

> **S_footing / S_plate = [2B_f/(B_f + B_p)]²**

so settlement **increases with footing width** even at the same pressure — approaching a limit of four times the plate settlement for a very large footing. A wide raft on sand at a modest pressure can therefore settle appreciably.

**The contrast with CLAY:**

| | **SAND** | **CLAY** |
|---|---|---|
| Dominant component | **Immediate** | **Consolidation** |
| Timescale | **Construction period** | **Years** |
| Theory | **Elastic** | **Terzaghi consolidation** |
| Observed during construction? | **Yes** | Barely begun |
| Can be accelerated? | Not needed | **Yes — vertical drains** |

**Option (d) is wrong** and worth correcting: settlement in sand is **not negligible**. It is immediate, which is convenient, but for a wide foundation on medium-dense sand it can readily reach the 40 mm permissible limit — which is precisely why **settlement, not bearing capacity, governs the allowable pressure on sand**.

examTip.trick: Sand's permeability is high, so pore water escapes as fast as the load is applied — no excess pore pressure, no time lag.
examTip.mnemonic: **Sand settles as you build; clay settles for years afterwards.** The practical benefit is that sand settlement happens **before the finishes go on**, so it damages nothing — but it is not negligible, and it is exactly why settlement governs the allowable pressure on sand.

questions.stem: The consolidation settlement of a normally consolidated clay layer is proportional to:
options: The square of the stress increase
The logarithm of the ratio of final to initial effective stress
questions.solution:
**The LOGARITHM of the ratio of final to initial effective stress.**

> **S_c = (C_c H / (1 + e₀)) × log₁₀[(σ′₀ + Δσ)/σ′₀]**

**The logarithm has two important consequences**, both examinable:

**1. Settlement is NOT proportional to the load.** Doubling Δσ does **not** double the settlement. For σ′₀ = 100 kPa:

| Δσ | Ratio | log₁₀ | Relative settlement |
|---|---|---|---|
| 100 kPa | 2.0 | 0.301 | **1.00** |
| 200 kPa | 3.0 | 0.477 | **1.58** |
| 400 kPa | 5.0 | 0.699 | **2.32** |

So **quadrupling the load increases the settlement by only 2.3 times** — a strongly diminishing return.
