**2. The same increment causes FAR LESS settlement at depth.** Because σ′₀ is larger there, the ratio is closer to 1 and its logarithm smaller. An increment of 50 kPa at σ′₀ = 50 gives log(2) = 0.301; the same 50 kPa at σ′₀ = 400 gives log(1.125) = 0.051 — **six times less**.

**That is why the layers near the foundation dominate the settlement**, and why the pressure bulb concept works: the stress increase falls with depth *and* its effect falls further because the existing stress is higher.

**The parameters:**

| Parameter | Meaning | Typical |
|---|---|---|
| **C_c** — compression index | Slope of the **VIRGIN** portion of the **e – log σ′** curve | 0.2 – 0.8 for clays |
| **C_r** — recompression index | Slope of the **reloading** curve | **C_c/5 to C_c/10** |
| **e₀** | Initial void ratio | — |
| **H** | Thickness of the compressible layer | — |

**Skempton's correlation** for a first estimate:

> **C_c = 0.009 (LL − 10)** for remoulded, normally consolidated clay

**For an OVER-CONSOLIDATED clay the calculation splits**, and getting this right can change the answer by an order of magnitude:

> **If σ′₀ + Δσ ≤ σ′_c:  use C_r throughout**
> **If σ′₀ + Δσ > σ′_c:  S = (C_r H/(1+e₀))log(σ′_c/σ′₀) + (C_c H/(1+e₀))log[(σ′₀+Δσ)/σ′_c]**

Using C_c throughout for an over-consolidated clay **grossly overestimates** the settlement — by a factor of five or more — and can lead to an unnecessary and very expensive foundation.

**Note what the equation does NOT contain: TIME.** It gives the **magnitude** of the settlement, not its rate. The rate comes from a separate relation:

> **T_v = c_v t / d²**

with **T_v = 0.197 at U = 50%** and **0.848 at U = 90%**.

**The two questions are answered by different parameters**, and keeping them apart is the organising idea of consolidation:

> **C_c (or m_v) determines HOW MUCH. c_v determines HOW FAST.**

A clay may be highly compressible but drain quickly, or only moderately compressible but drain extremely slowly — and only the second is helped by vertical drains.

examTip.trick: The **log** has two consequences worth carrying: settlement is **not proportional to load** (quadrupling Δσ only about doubles the settlement), and the **same increment at depth causes far less settlement**, because σ′₀ is already large.
examTip.mnemonic: **Layers near the footing dominate.** And for an **over-consolidated** clay the calculation splits at σ′_c — using C_c throughout can overestimate settlement five-fold and buy a foundation you never needed.

questions.stem: The measure that best indicates whether settlement will damage a structure is the:
options: Maximum settlement of any one footing
questions.solution:
**The angular distortion between adjacent supports.**

> **Angular distortion = δ / L**, the **differential settlement between two points** divided by the **distance between them**

**Why it, and not total settlement, is the damaging quantity:**

> A building settling **50 mm UNIFORMLY** is **undamaged** — it has simply moved down. Services and approaches need adjusting; the structure is unstrained.
> A building settling **10 mm UNEVENLY** **cracks** — because the differential movement **distorts the frame and strains the finishes**.

The structure is strained by the **difference** in settlement, not by its magnitude — so a measure of difference relative to distance is the right one.

**Limiting values:**

| Angular distortion | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **1/500** | **Safe limit** for buildings where cracking is **not permissible** |
| **1/300** | **Cracking of panel walls** begins; difficulty with overhead cranes |
| 1/250 | **Structural damage** to be expected; tilting of tall buildings visible |
| 1/150 | Considerable cracking; danger of structural damage |
| 1/1000 | Limit for machinery sensitive to settlement |

**Note how small these are**: 1/500 over a 6 m bay is only **12 mm** of differential settlement — which is why the permissible **total** settlements (40–65 mm) are set on the expectation that only a fraction of that will be differential.

**Causes of differential settlement**, each with a design response:

| Cause | Response |
|---|---|
| **Non-uniform soil** across the site | Proportion footings for **EQUAL SETTLEMENT**, not equal pressure |
| **Unequal column loads** on similar footings | Same |
| **Varying founding depths** | Keep the founding level consistent where possible |
| Local variation in the **water table** | Investigate adequately |
| **Non-uniform load history** — an extension to an old building | **Separate with a MOVEMENT JOINT** |
| Different foundation types under one structure | Avoid — piles and pads under one building settle differently |

**"Proportion for equal settlement, not equal pressure" is the key design idea**, and it is counter-intuitive: designing every footing to the same allowable pressure gives **different settlements** where the loads differ, because settlement increases with footing width. Deliberately using a **lower** pressure under the more heavily loaded (hence larger) footings equalises the settlement instead.

**Mixing foundation types under one structure** is the error worth naming explicitly: a building part on piles and part on pad footings will settle differentially at the junction, however carefully each part is designed — because their settlement mechanisms and timescales differ entirely. Either use one system throughout, or separate the parts with a **movement joint** that allows them to move independently.

**Reducing differential settlement:**

| Measure | Effect |
|---|---|
| **RAFT foundation** | **Ties the structure together** so it settles as one body — the most effective |
| **Increase the depth** | Mobilises stronger soil and reduces the net pressure |
| **Piles to a firm stratum** | Removes the variable layer from the load path |
| **Ground improvement** | Makes the soil more uniform |
| **Design the structure to TOLERATE it** | A jointed or statically determinate structure is far less sensitive |
| Movement joints | Divide the structure into independently settling units |

**The last is worth emphasis**: a **statically determinate** or jointed structure develops **no stress** from differential settlement, because it can adjust. A stiff, highly indeterminate frame develops large secondary stresses. So the choice of structural form is itself a settlement measure — and it is why long buildings on variable ground are divided into blocks by movement joints rather than being made stiffer.

examTip.trap: Total settlement is the natural answer and is largely irrelevant to damage.
examTip.trick: A building settling **50 mm uniformly** is undamaged; one settling **10 mm unevenly** cracks. The structure is strained by the **difference**, not the magnitude.
examTip.mnemonic: **δ/L limited to 1/500** where cracking is not acceptable; panel walls start cracking around **1/300**. Over a 6 m bay, 1/500 is just **12 mm** of differential — which is why the total limits (40–65 mm) assume only a fraction is differential.

questions.stem: Presumptive bearing capacity values given in codes should be used:
options: For the final design of all structures
Only for structures over ten storeys
In place of a site investigation
questions.solution:
**For preliminary sizing only — never for final design where a site investigation is possible.**

**Presumptive values (IS 1904)** give a safe bearing capacity by **soil description alone**:

| Soil / rock | Presumptive safe bearing capacity (kN/m²) |
|---|---|
| **Hard rock** | **3300 and above** |
| Soft rock | 440 |
| **Gravel, dense sand** | **440** |
| Medium sand | 245 |
| **Loose sand** | **100** |
| Hard / stiff clay | 440 / 245 |
| **Soft clay** | **100** |
| **Very soft clay, peat** | **50, or to be determined** |

**Why they must not be used for final design** — they take **no account of** the factors that actually govern:

| Ignored factor | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **Footing WIDTH** | Governs the capacity of sand and the settlement of everything |
| **Founding DEPTH** | The surcharge term |
| **WATER TABLE** | Can **halve** the capacity of a sand |
| **SETTLEMENT** | Which usually governs on sand, and is not addressed at all |
| **Layering** | A soft layer below is invisible to a soil description |
| The **actual strength** of this particular soil | A "stiff clay" spans a wide range of c_u |

**The last row is the fundamental objection**: a presumptive value is keyed to a **verbal description**, and descriptions are imprecise. Two soils both correctly described as "medium sand" may differ in capacity by a factor of two.

**Their legitimate uses:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **Preliminary sizing** and cost estimating | Before the investigation is complete |
| **Very small structures** where an investigation is disproportionate | A boundary wall, a small single-storey building |
| A **sanity check** on a computed value | If the calculation gives 800 kPa on a soft clay, something is wrong |
| Where **no investigation is possible** | And then with a large margin and explicit acknowledgement |

**The sanity-check use is genuinely valuable** and worth keeping: presumptive values give a feel for the plausible range, and a computed capacity far outside it should prompt a review of the input parameters rather than being accepted.

**How bearing capacity is properly determined:**

| Method | Character |
|---|---|
| **Analytical** (Terzaghi, IS 6403) | From **c and φ** obtained by laboratory or field testing — the standard |
| **Plate load test** | Direct, but a **shallow** pressure bulb; good for sand, misleading for clay |
| **SPT correlations** | Rapid, widely used for sand |
| **CPT correlations** | A continuous profile |
| **Pile load test** | For piles, definitive |
| Presumptive values | **Preliminary only** |

**A closing caution that applies to all of them.** Bearing capacity and settlement calculations are only as good as **c, φ, E_s and c_v** — parameters measured on small specimens of a variable natural material. **Two significant figures is generous precision.**

The professional response is not false precision but: **bracket the answer** with sensible parameter ranges, **choose conservatively** where the consequence of error is severe, **state the assumptions**, and — for an important structure — **verify by plate load test, pile load test or instrumented monitoring** rather than trusting the arithmetic alone.

Never for final design where investigation is possible.

examTip.trick: A presumptive value is keyed to a **verbal description** and takes no account of footing width, depth, water table, layering or settlement — every factor that actually governs.
examTip.mnemonic: **Presumptive values are for a first sketch and a sanity check, never for a final design.** They remain genuinely useful for the sanity check: if your calculation gives 800 kPa on soft clay, something is wrong with the inputs.

questions.stem: Preloading a soft clay site with vertical drains before construction:
options: Increases the total settlement that will occur
Reduces the total settlement that will occur
Has no effect on the settlement
Accelerates the settlement so that most of it occurs before construction
questions.solution:
**It accelerates the settlement so that most of it occurs BEFORE construction.**

**The principle.** A **surcharge** (usually a temporary fill) is placed on the site to impose a stress at least equal to that of the future structure. The clay consolidates under it, and the surcharge is then removed and the structure built — on ground that has **already done most of its settling**.

**Vertical drains accelerate the process**, and the mechanism is the drainage path:

> **T_v = c_v t / d²** — time varies as the **SQUARE of the drainage path**

| Without drains | With drains |
|---|---|
| Drainage is **VERTICAL**, over the layer thickness — perhaps **10 m** (or 5 m if double-drained) | Drainage is **RADIAL**, to the nearest drain — perhaps **1 m** |
| Consolidation takes **years to decades** | **Months** |

> Reducing the drainage path from 10 m to 1 m reduces the time by a factor of about **100**.

**The essential point, and the reason the other options are wrong:**

> **Drains change HOW FAST the settlement occurs — NOT HOW MUCH.**

The total settlement is determined by the **stress increase and the compressibility (C_c, e₀, H)**, none of which the drains affect. A question suggesting that drains reduce the total settlement is offering a plausible but wrong answer.

**What DOES reduce the total settlement is the SURCHARGE**, and specifically **over-surcharging**: placing a surcharge **greater** than the eventual structure load causes the clay to consolidate **beyond** what the structure will require, so that when the structure is built the clay is **over-consolidated** with respect to it and follows the flat **recompression** curve. The residual settlement is then very small.

That is the real design refinement: **surcharge = structure load + an excess**, held long enough to achieve the required degree of consolidation, then removed.

**Types of vertical drain:**

| Type | Character |
|---|---|
| **Sand drains** | Boreholes filled with sand; 200–400 mm diameter |
| **Prefabricated vertical drains (PVD, band drains, wick drains)** | A plastic core wrapped in geotextile, **100 mm × 4 mm**; installed by a mandrel |

**PVDs have largely replaced sand drains** because they are **far quicker to install** (a rig can place hundreds of metres a day), cause **less disturbance** (a thin mandrel rather than a bored hole), and cost less.

**Design parameters**: spacing **1 to 3 m** on a triangular or square grid, depth through the compressible layer, with a **horizontal drainage blanket** at the surface to carry the water away.

**Smear and well resistance** are the two effects that degrade performance and must be allowed for: **smear** is the zone of remoulded, less permeable soil around the drain caused by the mandrel, and **well resistance** is the finite capacity of the drain itself over a long length. Both are accounted for in the radial consolidation analysis (Barron's solution).

**Monitoring is essential** and is what makes preloading a controlled operation rather than a hope: **settlement plates** track the settlement, and **piezometers** track the pore pressure dissipation. Plotting settlement against time (Asaoka's method) predicts the ultimate settlement, and the surcharge is removed when the **required degree of consolidation** has been demonstrated — not when a predicted period has elapsed.

**Where preloading is used**: **embankments on soft ground**, **highway and railway formations**, **airport runways**, **storage tank farms** and **reclaimed land** — anywhere with a large area, a soft compressible layer, and enough time in the programme. Its limitation is exactly that: it takes **months**, and a project without that time in its programme must pile instead.

examTip.trap: "Reduces the total settlement" is the plausible wrong answer, and it confuses the drain with the surcharge.
examTip.trick: Drains change **how fast**, not **how much** — the magnitude is fixed by the stress increase and the compressibility, neither of which a drain affects. What *does* reduce residual settlement is **over-surcharging**.
examTip.mnemonic: **t ∝ d², so cutting the drainage path from 10 m to 1 m cuts the time by a hundred.** That square law is the whole reason vertical drains work.

questions.stem: For a strip footing on a purely cohesive soil with φ = 0, Terzaghi's bearing capacity factor N_c is:
questions.solution:
**5.7** (Terzaghi), or **5.14** by Prandtl's plasticity solution which later theories adopt.

**For φ = 0 the three factors become:**

| Factor | Value at φ = 0 |
|---|---|
| **N_c** | **5.7** (Terzaghi) / **5.14** (Prandtl, Meyerhof, Vesic) |
| **N_q** | **1.0** |
| **N_γ** | **0** |

so the equation reduces to

> **q_u = 5.7 c + γD_f**, and **q_nu = 5.7 c**

**Two consequences follow immediately:**

1. **The bearing capacity of clay is INDEPENDENT of the footing WIDTH**, since N_γ = 0 removes the width term entirely.
2. **q_nu depends only on c_u**, so the undrained strength is the single parameter that matters.

**Why 5.7 rather than 5.14.** Terzaghi assumed a **rough** footing base and a particular shape for the elastic wedge beneath it, giving 5.7. **Prandtl's** exact plasticity solution for a **smooth** base gives **(π + 2) = 5.14**. Modern practice generally uses **5.14**, and IS 6403 follows it — the difference of about 10% being small relative to the uncertainty in c_u itself.

**Option (c), 9.0**, is worth noting because it is a **real and related value**: **N_c = 9** is used for the **END BEARING of a deep pile** in clay:

> **Q_p = 9 c_u A_p**

The factor is higher for a deep foundation because the failure surface is **fully confined** by the surrounding soil — it cannot reach the ground surface as a shallow footing's does, so more resistance must be overcome. The progression is instructive:

| Situation | N_c |
|---|---|
| **Shallow strip footing** on the surface | **5.14** |
| Shallow **square** footing | 5.14 × 1.3 ≈ **6.7** |
| Footing at depth (Skempton) | Rising with D/B |
| **Deep pile tip** (fully confined) | **9** |

**Skempton's N_c for clay** captures the depth variation explicitly, rising from **5.14 at the surface to about 7.5 at D/B = 4** for a strip, and from 6.2 to 9.0 for a square or circle — reaching the deep-foundation value of 9 at D/B ≈ 4.

**A worked case.** A 2 m square footing at 1.5 m depth on clay with c_u = 60 kPa, γ = 18 kN/m³:

> N_c = 5.14 × 1.3 (shape) ≈ **6.7**
> **q_nu = 6.7 × 60 = 402 kPa**
> **q_ns = 402/3 = 134 kPa** (net safe)
> **q_safe (gross) = 134 + 27 = 161 kPa**

and the settlement must then be checked separately, since a bearing capacity check alone does not establish that the footing is acceptable.

**The φ = 0 analysis applies to the SHORT TERM only** — the undrained condition immediately after loading. For a **permanent** structure on clay the **long-term drained** case must also be considered, using **c′ and φ′** — though for a **loaded** clay the short-term case usually governs, since consolidation subsequently strengthens the soil.

examTip.trick: For φ = 0 the whole equation collapses: **N_q = 1, N_γ = 0, N_c = 5.7** (Terzaghi) or **5.14** (Prandtl, and what IS 6403 uses).
examTip.mnemonic: **5.14 shallow strip, 9 at a deep pile tip.** Those are the two ends of the same relationship — N_c rises with depth as the failure surface becomes confined, reaching 9 at about D/B = 4.

questions.stem: Increasing the depth of a foundation generally:
options: Increases the bearing capacity and reduces the net pressure
Has no effect on the bearing capacity
questions.solution:
**It increases the bearing capacity and reduces the net pressure.**

**Two independent benefits, and they compound:**

**1. The bearing capacity increases**, through the surcharge term:

> **q_u = c N_c + γ D_f N_q + 0.5 γ B N_γ**

the second term grows directly with **D_f**. For a sand with N_q = 22 (φ = 30°) and γ = 18, each additional metre of depth adds **18 × 22 = 396 kPa** to the ultimate capacity — a very large gain.

**2. The NET pressure falls**, because the soil excavated is soil no longer bearing on the ground:

> **q_net = q_gross − γD_f**

So deepening reduces the increase in stress the soil experiences, which reduces the **settlement** as well.

**Taken to its limit, the second effect becomes the COMPENSATED (floating) foundation**: excavate enough that **γD_f equals the structure's pressure**, and the net increase is **zero** — a heavy building carried on soil that could not otherwise support it.

**Other reasons a foundation is taken deeper:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| To reach a **stronger stratum** | The commonest reason |
| Below the **zone of seasonal moisture change** | Expansive soil |
| Below the **frost line** | High altitude |
| **Below the SCOUR depth** | Beside a watercourse — often the governing requirement |
| Below **fill or organic** material | — |
| To provide a **basement** | Which may then serve as compensation |

**The costs of going deeper**, which is why it is not done indiscriminately:

| Cost | Note |
|---|---|
| **Excavation** volume and disposal | Rises rapidly with depth |
| **Temporary support** — timbering, sheeting | Required beyond about 1.2 m |
| **DEWATERING** | Often the dominant cost below the water table |
| Effect on **adjacent structures** | Loss of lateral support; underpinning may be needed |
| **Time** | — |
| Working space and safety | — |

**Option (d) is the reverse of the truth** and worth correcting explicitly: deepening **reduces** settlement, for two compounding reasons — the **net pressure** is lower, and the soil at depth is generally **stronger and less compressible** than at the surface. It is one of the standard remedies for excessive settlement.

**The full set of remedies for excessive settlement**, in rough order of preference:

| Measure | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Increase the DEPTH** | Reduces net pressure and mobilises better soil |
| **Increase the AREA** | Reduces the pressure — though on sand a wider footing settles more at the same pressure, so the benefit is less than expected |
| **RAFT** foundation | Ties the structure together, reducing **differential** settlement |
| **PILES** to a firmer stratum | Bypasses the compressible layer |
| **Ground improvement** — preloading, drains, stone columns, densification | Improves the soil itself |
| **Design the structure to TOLERATE** the movement | Joints, a determinate form |

**The second entry carries a caution worth stating**: on **sand**, widening a footing at constant pressure **increases** the settlement (S ∝ [2B/(B+B_p)]²), because the pressure bulb reaches deeper. So enlarging a footing to reduce settlement works on **clay** but can be counterproductive on **sand** — where reducing the pressure by enlargement is partly offset by the greater depth of influence.

examTip.trap: "Increases the settlement" is exactly backwards, and it is offered because deeper *sounds* like more load on the soil.
examTip.trick: Two effects compound: the **surcharge term γD_f N_q** raises capacity, and the **net pressure q − γD_f** falls. Deeper soil is usually stronger and stiffer as well.
examTip.mnemonic: **Deeper is stronger AND settles less.** Taken to its limit this becomes the **compensated foundation**, where the excavated weight equals the building's.

questions.stem: Skempton's bearing capacity factor N_c for a clay increases with the depth to width ratio because:
options: The clay becomes stronger with depth
The failure surface becomes increasingly confined by the surrounding soil
questions.solution:
**Because the failure surface becomes increasingly confined by the surrounding soil.**

**Skempton's N_c** rises with the **depth to width ratio D/B**:

| D/B | N_c, strip | N_c, square or circle |
|---|---|---|
| **0** (surface) | **5.14** | **6.2** |
| 1 | 6.4 | 7.7 |
| 2 | 7.0 | 8.4 |
| **4 and above** | **7.5** | **9.0** |

**The physical reason.** A footing at the **surface** fails by pushing up a wedge of soil that **escapes to the ground surface** on either side — a relatively easy path. As the footing is placed **deeper**, that escape path must pass through **more and more soil**, and eventually the failure surface is **fully confined** and cannot reach the surface at all. More soil must be sheared, so more resistance is available.

**The value converges on N_c = 9**, which is exactly the factor used for the **END BEARING OF A DEEP PILE** in clay:

> **Q_p = 9 c_u A_p**

So the progression from 5.14 at the surface to 9 at depth is **continuous**, and the pile value is simply the fully confined limit of the same phenomenon. That connection is worth seeing: the shallow and deep foundation formulae are not separate theories but two ends of one relationship.

**Note that option (a) is a real effect but not the reason here.** Clay strength **does** commonly increase with depth in a normally consolidated deposit — c_u/σ′_v is roughly constant, so c_u rises with overburden. But that is a property of the **soil profile**, entered separately through the value of c_u used at founding level. **N_c is a geometric factor**, and it rises because of **confinement**, not because the clay is stronger.

Distinguishing a **soil property** from a **geometric factor** is the substance of the question, and confusing them leads to double-counting: using both a depth-increased c_u and a depth-increased N_c without recognising they represent different things.

**Skempton's formulation for clay** in full:

> **q_nu = c_u N_c** (net ultimate)
> **q_u = c_u N_c + γD_f** (gross)

with N_c from the table above. It is simpler than Terzaghi's for clay because **N_γ = 0** and the surcharge term is just γD_f (N_q = 1) — so the whole capacity rests on one soil parameter and one geometric factor.

**Where the depth effect matters practically:**

| Situation | Effect |
|---|---|
| A **basement** or deep footing in clay | Substantially higher N_c than a surface footing |
| **Pile end bearing** | The limiting value, 9 |
| A shallow raft | Little benefit — D/B is small for a wide raft |

**The last row is worth noting**: for a **wide raft**, D/B is small even at appreciable depth, so N_c stays near 5.14 and the depth benefit comes almost entirely from the **reduced net pressure** rather than from an increased capacity factor. For a **narrow deep footing**, the reverse.

**A caution on using the deep values**: they assume the soil **above** founding level remains in place and provides the confinement. If it can be **excavated later** — for services, or by scour — the confinement is lost and the capacity with it. Where that is credible, the surface value should be used.

examTip.trap: "The clay gets stronger with depth" is true of most deposits but is **not the reason** — that is a soil property entering separately through c_u. N_c is a **geometric** factor.
examTip.trick: At the surface the failure wedge escapes easily to open ground. Deeper, it must shear through more soil to reach the surface, and eventually cannot reach it at all.
examTip.mnemonic: **5.14 at the surface rising to 9 when fully confined** — the deep value is exactly the pile end-bearing factor. Shallow and deep foundation theory are two ends of one curve.

questions.stem: In an eccentrically loaded footing, the effective area method replaces the actual footing by one of:
options: Reduced dimensions B′ = B − 2e, so that the load acts at its centroid
The same dimensions but reduced bearing pressure
questions.solution:
**Reduced dimensions B′ = B − 2e, so that the load acts at the centroid of the reduced area.**

> **B′ = B − 2e_B** and **L′ = L − 2e_L**
> **Effective area A′ = B′ × L′**

**The idea (Meyerhof's effective area method)** is elegant: rather than analysing a non-uniform pressure distribution, the footing is **replaced by a smaller, CONCENTRICALLY loaded one** whose centroid coincides with the load. The bearing capacity is then computed for that reduced footing in the ordinary way.

**Why B − 2e.** The reduced footing must be **symmetrical about the load**, so the amount trimmed from the loaded side must equal the amount trimmed from the other — hence **twice** the eccentricity is removed from the width.

**Note what is reduced**: the **B′ used in the width term** of Terzaghi's equation is the reduced value, so the capacity per unit area falls as well as the area itself — a double penalty, which is the correct reflection of how damaging eccentricity is.

**The alternative approach**, valid only for small eccentricity:

> **p_max, p_min = (ΣV/A)(1 ± 6e/B)**

valid while **e ≤ B/6** — the **middle third rule**. Beyond that:

| Condition | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **e ≤ B/6** | Resultant within the **middle third**; **whole base in compression**; trapezoidal pressure |
| **e = B/6** | Pressure just reaches **zero at one edge**; triangular distribution |
| **e > B/6** | **PART OF THE BASE LIFTS OFF**; pressure over a reduced contact width **x = 3(B/2 − e)**, with **p_max = 2ΣV/(3 b x)** |

**The lift-off case is the dangerous one**, and its consequences compound:

| Consequence | Effect |
|---|---|
| The **contact area is reduced** | Pressure over the remaining area rises sharply |
| The **resultant moves further toward the edge** | Which reduces the contact further |
| **Overturning resistance falls** | The stabilising lever arm is shortened |
| Progressive tilting | Which increases the eccentricity, and so on |

That feedback is why the middle-third rule is enforced rather than merely recommended: outside it, the behaviour is **progressive** rather than stable.

**Sources of eccentricity:**

| Source | Example |
|---|---|
| **Moment** transferred from the column | A frame with lateral load |
| **Boundary constraint** | A footing that cannot be centred — hence the **strap footing** |
| **Lateral load** at height | Wind or earthquake on a retaining wall or a tall structure |
| Unequal adjacent loads | — |
| **Construction tolerance** | Which is why IS 456 requires a **minimum eccentricity** on every column |

**Combined with an INCLINED load**, the effective area method is used together with **inclination factors**, which reduce the bearing capacity further — an inclined load being resisted less efficiently than a vertical one. Meyerhof's and Hansen's formulations include both.

**The design responses to eccentricity:**

| Response | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Enlarge the footing** so the resultant falls within the middle third | The simplest |
| **Offset the footing** so its centroid lies under the resultant | Where space allows |
| **STRAP footing** | Transfers the moment to an adjacent footing |
| Combined footing | Shaped so its centroid matches the resultant |
| Accept the reduced capacity | Using the effective area method |

The general principle behind all of them is the one that recurs throughout foundation design: **a footing bears uniformly only when the resultant passes through the centroid of the bearing area** — and every device above is a way of arranging that where the loads alone would not.

examTip.trick: **B − 2e**, not B − e, because the reduced footing must be **symmetrical about the load** — so the same amount comes off both sides.
examTip.mnemonic: **Trim twice the eccentricity.** And the penalty is double: the reduced B′ also goes into the width term, so capacity per unit area falls too. Keep e within **B/6** (the middle third) or part of the base lifts off — after which the process is progressive and unstable.

questions.stem: The immediate settlement of a footing on an elastic soil is given by an expression proportional to:
questions.solution:
**S_i = q B (1 − μ²) I_f / E_s.**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **q** | Net applied pressure |
| **B** | Footing **width** |
| **μ** | **Poisson's ratio** — 0.3 to 0.4 for sand, **0.5 for saturated clay undrained** |
| **I_f** | **Influence factor** — depends on the footing **shape and rigidity** |
| **E_s** | **Modulus of elasticity** of the soil |

**A dimensional check confirms the form**: q has units of kPa, B of m, E_s of kPa — so qB/E_s has units of **m** ✓. Options (b) and (c) fail this check immediately, and (d) gives kPa²·m, which is meaningless.

**Note that μ = 0.5 for a saturated clay under UNDRAINED conditions**, because the volume cannot change — and a Poisson's ratio of exactly 0.5 is the mathematical statement of incompressibility. The factor (1 − μ²) then becomes 0.75.

**Influence factors I_f** for a flexible footing (at the centre):

| Shape | I_f |
|---|---|
| **Circle** | 1.00 (rigid) / 1.00 at centre (flexible) |
| **Square** | **1.12** at centre, 0.56 at corner |
| Rectangle L/B = 2 | 1.53 |
| Rectangle L/B = 5 | 2.10 |
| **Strip** | Large — settlement grows with length |

**Flexible and rigid footings settle differently**, and the distinction is instructive:

| Footing | Pressure distribution | Settlement |
|---|---|---|
| **FLEXIBLE** (a thin slab, an embankment) | **Uniform** | **Non-uniform** — maximum at the centre, less at the edges (on clay); the reverse on sand |
| **RIGID** (a thick footing) | **Non-uniform** | **UNIFORM** |

> A **rigid** footing settles uniformly and its pressure distribution adjusts; a **flexible** one applies uniform pressure and its settlement adjusts. The **average** settlement of a flexible footing is roughly the settlement of a rigid one of the same size — conventionally **I_f(rigid) ≈ 0.8 × I_f(flexible, centre)**.

**On CLAY, a flexible loaded area dishes downward** (more settlement at the centre), while **on SAND it settles more at the EDGES** — because the sand at the edge is less confined and therefore less stiff. That contrast surprises people and is a genuine observed effect.

**Obtaining E_s is the practical difficulty**, and it is why immediate settlement calculations are treated as approximate:

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **Correlations with SPT N** | E_s ≈ 500(N + 15) kPa for sand — very approximate |
| **Correlations with CPT q_c** | E_s ≈ 2 to 4 q_c |
| **Plate load test** | Direct, but shallow |
| Pressuremeter | In situ, better |
| Laboratory triaxial | Disturbance affects it greatly |

**E_s is strongly stress-dependent and strain-dependent**, which is the fundamental problem: the soil is much stiffer at small strain than at large, so a single "modulus" is a considerable simplification. Modern practice uses a strain-dependent stiffness, but for routine work a value appropriate to the expected strain range is chosen.

**Where immediate settlement matters:**

| Soil | Significance |
|---|---|
| **SAND** | **The whole settlement** — it is essentially all immediate |
| **CLAY** | A **component only** — the consolidation settlement usually dominates |
| Rock | Negligible |

So for a footing on sand this expression is the settlement calculation; for one on clay it is the first of three terms, and generally the smallest.

examTip.trick: Check the units and three of the four options die instantly: **q** in kPa × **B** in m ÷ **E_s** in kPa gives **metres** ✓. Nothing else does.
examTip.mnemonic: **μ = 0.5 for saturated clay undrained** — incompressible, so (1 − μ²) = 0.75. A **rigid** footing settles uniformly with non-uniform pressure; a **flexible** one does the reverse.

questions.stem: The factor of safety normally applied to the net ultimate bearing capacity of a shallow foundation is:
questions.solution:
**2.5 to 3.0.**

**Why so much larger than the factors used in structural design**, where 1.5 on loads and 1.15 to 1.5 on materials are typical? The reason is the **quality of the information**:

| Source of uncertainty | Structural material | Soil |
|---|---|---|
| **Variability of the material** | Steel is **manufactured to specification**; concrete is tested cube by cube | Soil is a **natural material**, variable over a few metres |
| **Knowledge of properties** | Measured directly on the actual material | **Inferred** from small specimens, or from correlations |
| **Sampling** | The whole member is the material | A **tiny fraction** of the soil mass is ever tested |
| **Theory** | Well-established mechanics | **Simplified models** with empirical factors |
| Consequence of failure | Serious | **Serious, and hard to remedy** |

> A structural engineer knows the strength of the steel. A geotechnical engineer **infers** the strength of the ground from a few boreholes and some laboratory tests on specimens that were disturbed in the taking.

The larger factor of safety buys back that difference in knowledge — it is a factor on **ignorance** as much as on strength.

**Factors of safety across geotechnical design:**

| Application | Factor |
|---|---|
| **Shallow foundation bearing capacity** | **2.5 – 3.0** on the **NET ultimate** |
| **Pile capacity** | **2.5** |
| **Slope stability, long term** | **1.5** |
| Slope stability, transient (drawdown, seismic) | 1.2 – 1.3 |
| **Retaining wall overturning** | **2.0** |
| **Retaining wall sliding** | **1.5** |
| **Retaining wall bearing** | **3.0** |
| Uplift / flotation | 1.2 – 1.5 |
| Piping (exit gradient) | 4 – 7 (expressed as the ratio i_c/i_exit) |

**Note that the factors differ by application, and the pattern is rational**: they are **highest where the failure is sudden and the analysis crudest** (bearing capacity, piping) and **lowest where the failure is gradual and observable, or the load is transient** (slope stability, drawdown).

**Slope stability's 1.5 looks low against bearing capacity's 3.0**, and the reason is worth understanding: a slope analysis uses **measured shear strength parameters directly** in a well-understood limiting-equilibrium calculation, and the failure is usually **preceded by visible movement**. A bearing capacity calculation adds an empirical theory and its factors on top of the same parameters, and the failure can be sudden.

**Remember also that the factor applies to the NET value:**

> **q_ns = q_nu / F**, where **q_nu = q_u − γD_f**

Applying F to the **gross** capacity double-counts the overburden — which the soil had already carried for geological time and which needs no safety factor.

**And that bearing capacity is only half the check.** The allowable pressure is the **lesser** of the safe bearing capacity and the **settlement-limited** pressure — and on dense sand the latter usually governs, so a generous factor of safety on capacity contributes nothing to the design.

**The honest closing point** about all these numbers: soil parameters are known to perhaps **two significant figures at best**. The factor of safety is not a precision instrument but a recognition of that, and the professional response is to **bracket the answer with sensible parameter ranges**, choose conservatively where the consequence of error is severe, **state the assumptions**, and verify by **load test or monitoring** where the structure warrants it.

examTip.trick: Compare with structural design, where 1.15–1.5 suffices. Steel is manufactured to specification and tested; soil is a natural material, sampled at a few points and inferred through a simplified theory.
examTip.mnemonic: **2.5–3 on the NET ultimate.** The factor buys back ignorance as much as strength — which is also why slope stability gets only 1.5 (measured parameters, gradual failure) while piping gets 4–7 (sudden, progressive, catastrophic).
